Name: concept_language_binding_ledger
Title: Where Does the Concept Meet the Language? A Causal Audit of Language Re-binding Failures in Multilingual Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual reasoning errors in non-dominant languages are not caused by faulty language-agnostic concept computation, but by a localized failure to *re-bind* the correct language identity onto correctly-computed concepts in late layers. We hypothesize that (a) concept computation and language re-binding are causally separable stages, (b) most cross-lingual reasoning failures occur at the re-binding stage rather than the concept stage, and (c) re-binding failure rate grows monotonically with script/typological distance while concept-stage accuracy stays roughly constant.
Related Work: Prior work established that LLMs form shared semantic/concept spaces in middle layers with language-specific decoding in late layers (Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025), that grammatical concepts are shared (Brinkmann et al. 2025), and that shared geometry extends to meta-cognitive difficulty (Civelli et al. 2026). Beneath the Surface of Consistency (2024) shows script similarity dominates knowledge sharing, and Tracing the Roots of Facts (2024) categorizes facts as independent/shared/transferred. However, all these works either (i) study single-token word translation or static concept probes, or (ii) demonstrate the two-stage structure descriptively. None decomposes *multi-step reasoning* errors in a language into a concept-stage vs. binding-stage causal attribution, nor quantifies what fraction of downstream task failures are attributable to each stage. Our contribution is a causal error-attribution framework ('binding ledger') applied to reasoning chains, distinguishing 'the model got the reasoning right but spoke the wrong language / degraded fluency' from 'the model genuinely reasoned wrong in this language.'
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs answer factual and reasoning questions far more reliably in their dominant pretraining language than in low-resource languages. Interpretability work suggests models compute in a shared, language-agnostic concept space in middle layers and then decode into a target language in late layers. We ask a sharper causal question: when a model fails a reasoning task in language X, does it fail because the concept-stage computation was wrong, or because the late-stage re-binding of the target language onto a correctly-computed concept failed? We introduce the Binding Ledger, a causal attribution procedure that, for each reasoning failure, uses activation patching to swap late-layer language-identity features and mid-layer concept representations between a correct dominant-language run and the failing target-language run, classifying each failure as concept-stage or binding-stage. We evaluate on multi-step arithmetic, multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA), and short chain-of-thought tasks across 20+ languages spanning several scripts and families in Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We predict that (1) a large fraction of failures in typologically-close, different-script languages are binding-stage, recoverable by a lightweight late-layer language-vector correction with no retraining; (2) concept-stage accuracy is far more uniform across languages than end-task accuracy, quantifying an upper bound on gains from fixing binding alone; and (3) binding failure scales with script/typological distance while concept accuracy does not. The framework yields both mechanistic insight and a cheap, training-free intervention for narrowing the multilingual gap.
Experiments: 1. Task suite: multilingual multi-step arithmetic (numbers verbalized per language), multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA), and 2-3 step chain-of-thought word problems (translated GSM-style subset), each in 20+ languages covering Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari scripts and 4+ families. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Localize the two stages: replicate the two-stage layer split (concept mid-layers, language identity late-layers) via logit-lens and linear probes for language identity; extract per-language 'language vectors' as mean late-layer activation differences. 3. Binding Ledger construction: for each item, run in dominant language (correct) and target language (incorrect). (a) Concept-stage test: patch the mid-layer concept representation from the correct dominant run into the target-language run; if the answer becomes correct in the target language -> failure was concept-stage. (b) Binding-stage test: keep target-language concept representation, but inject the correct answer only when late-layer language re-binding is corrected via language-vector steering; measure recovery. Classify each failure. 4. Metric: fraction concept-stage vs binding-stage per language; correlate binding-stage fraction with lang2vec typological distance and a binary same-script indicator. 5. Concept-accuracy upper bound: measure task accuracy achievable when concept stage is forced correct, comparing across languages to quantify uniformity. 6. Training-free intervention: apply the extracted late-layer language-vector correction at inference to failing target-language items; report accuracy gain, fluency (perplexity of output), and answer-language correctness. Compare against a translate-to-English baseline. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where binding is most malleable; effect of model scale; effect of prompting in-language vs cross-lingual. Evaluation metrics: exact-match accuracy, per-stage failure attribution rate, recovery rate under intervention, correlation coefficients with distance measures, output-language identification accuracy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The clean two-stage (concept then binding) decomposition may not hold for all models or deeper reasoning, making attribution noisy; we mitigate by validating the split with probes before attribution. 2. Activation patching across languages can produce degenerate outputs (as noted by When Meanings Meet 2024, some 'gains' are behavioral shifts like copying vs translating); we include manual/automatic error analysis to avoid mislabeling. 3. Tokenizer differences across scripts complicate representation alignment for concept patching; we restrict concept swaps to items with matched answer-token structure or use last-token-of-answer representations. 4. The training-free intervention may trade fluency for correctness; we report both. 5. Findings may be model-specific; using three model families addresses generality but not exhaustively. 6. Low-resource-language ground truth translations may contain noise, affecting labels; we use human-verified benchmark subsets where possible.

Name: latent_language_suppression
Title: The Ghost in the Machine Translation: Automatic Co-activation and Active Suppression of Non-target Languages in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Like the bilingual brain, multilingual LLMs automatically co-activate the non-target language's answer as a latent competitor during monolingual generation, and must *actively suppress* it in late layers. We hypothesize that (a) the non-target (typically English) answer is linearly decodable from internal states even during purely target-language generation, (b) a specific, identifiable late-layer suppression mechanism damps this competitor, and (c) both the strength of co-activation and the failure of suppression (causing code-switching / wrong-language leakage errors) scale with typological/script distance between the target language and the model's dominant language.
Related Work: Interpretability work frames LLMs as computing in a language-agnostic concept space (Semantic Hub 2024) and 'transitioning' to the target language in final layers, with failures at this transition causing inconsistency (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025). These works model the dominant language as an intermediate *pivot* that is translated away, and non-target languages as simply absent. Cross-lingual knowledge-conflict work (CLEAR 2026) studies conflict between explicit external evidence, not internal automatic co-activation. In contrast, decades of cognitive neuroscience (Language Conflict in the Bilingual Brain 2008; RLD & Bilingual Control 2019) show non-target languages are *automatically and involuntarily co-activated* and must be *actively inhibited*, with cost scaling with relative language distance. No ML paper tests whether LLMs implement an analogous automatic-activation-plus-inhibition control mechanism, nor operationalizes 'suppression cost' as a measurable, causally-manipulable circuit. We reframe cross-lingual leakage errors not as a passive translation failure but as an active *interference-control* failure, and provide the first causal characterization of a suppression mechanism in LLMs.
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions in many languages, and interpretability work describes an English-centric internal pipeline that is 'translated away' before output. We propose a fundamentally different, cognitively-inspired lens: drawing on bilingualism neuroscience, we hypothesize that the non-target language is not passively absent but *automatically co-activated* as a latent competitor, which the model must *actively suppress* to produce fluent monolingual text. We test three claims. First, during purely target-language generation, the correct answer token in the model's dominant language remains linearly decodable from hidden states well into late layers (co-activation). Second, there exists an identifiable suppression mechanism (specific late-layer attention heads / directions) that damps the competitor; ablating it induces code-switching and wrong-language leakage. Third, both co-activation strength and suppression failure scale with typological and script distance from the dominant language, mirroring the neuroscience 'relative language distance' effect. We operationalize a per-item Suppression Cost (logit-space distance the competitor is pushed down over late layers) and a Leakage Rate (wrong-language output). Experiments span multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA) and translation-free generation across 20+ languages and Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We predict a clean dose-response between lang2vec distance and suppression cost, causal identification of a suppression circuit, and that steering along the recovered suppression direction reduces code-switching in low-resource languages at inference with no retraining. This bridges cognitive theories of bilingual control with mechanistic interpretability and yields a training-free fix for language leakage.
Experiments: 1. Co-activation probe: On monolingual target-language QA/generation, at each layer apply logit-lens and trained linear probes to detect the dominant-language (English) answer token. Metric: layer-wise decodability (probe accuracy / logit-lens rank of English answer) while output is verified to be in the target language. Compare across 20+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. Baseline: random/unrelated-language answer decodability. 2. Suppression trajectory & Suppression Cost: track the English competitor token's logit across late layers; define Suppression Cost = drop in competitor logit rank from peak-activation layer to output. Test whether the competitor is actively pushed down (suppression) vs. simply never boosted. 3. Localize suppression mechanism: use attention-head attribution and activation patching to find heads/MLP directions responsible for damping the competitor; ablate them and measure (a) rise in competitor logit, (b) Leakage Rate = fraction of outputs that switch to the dominant language or code-switch. 4. Distance dose-response: correlate co-activation strength and Suppression Cost with lang2vec typological distance and a same-script binary indicator; test monotonic scaling (Spearman). Prediction: distant/different-script languages show higher co-activation and higher suppression cost/leakage. 5. Recover a 'suppression direction' (mean activation difference between clean monolingual and leakage-prone runs); at inference, steer along it on low-resource languages. Metrics: Leakage Rate reduction, output-language ID accuracy, fluency (perplexity), and task accuracy — verifying we reduce leakage without harming correctness. 6. Ablations: model scale, dominant-language-forced vs in-language prompting, and whether the competitor is always English or the highest-resource typologically-nearest language (tests whether suppression targets the *dominant* vs *nearest* language). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The 'competitor' might be decodable simply because the concept space is shared, not because of genuine co-activation of a specific language's token; we control by comparing dominant-language decodability against unrelated languages and by testing whether it is actively suppressed (dynamic drop) rather than merely present. 2. Logit-lens/probe decodability can reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal ablation (leakage induction) to confirm functional relevance. 3. Suppression may be diffuse rather than localized to identifiable heads, weakening the circuit story; we report degree of localization honestly and fall back on a direction-based (not head-based) account. 4. Leakage may be rare in strong models, limiting statistical power; we include low-resource languages and adversarial prompts to elicit it. 5. Distinguishing 'dominant language' from 'typologically nearest high-resource language' as the suppression target requires careful language selection; experiment 6 is designed for this. 6. Findings may vary across model families; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: storage_topology_via_edit_propagation
Title: Shared or Duplicated? Using Knowledge Edits to Map the Cross-Lingual Storage Topology of Facts, and Predicting Transfer Before Editing
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs store facts along a spectrum from language-shared (single parameter locus serving all languages) to language-duplicated (redundant per-language copies). Which regime a given fact occupies determines whether an edit in one language propagates to others, and this regime is measurable by an intrinsic PRE-edit mechanistic signature (overlap of causally-important components across languages). Consequently, cross-lingual edit propagation is predictable per-fact and per-language-pair from this signature alone, without performing the edit.
Related Work: A large body of work shows factual edits fail to propagate across languages, especially across script families (Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing 2024, Bi-ZsRE; XME 2024; MLaKE 2024), and proposes better editing methods (MEMLA, LU-LAFNs via language-agnostic factual neurons, LangEdit null-space, MEMAT attention editing, ReMaKE retrieval). ECLeKTic (2025) shows SOTA models fail to share knowledge across languages behaviorally. These works either (i) measure propagation post-hoc as a benchmark, or (ii) propose fixes; LU-LAFNs identifies shared neurons but uses them only to improve editing. None treats editing as a causal probe to reverse-engineer a per-fact storage topology, nor establishes that an intrinsic PRE-edit mechanistic signature predicts which facts/language-pairs will transfer. Our contribution is diagnostic and predictive: a taxonomy (shared vs. duplicated vs. hybrid) grounded in causal tracing, a demonstration that edit-propagation patterns causally validate this taxonomy, and a cheap pre-edit predictor of transferability that generalizes across facts, languages, and models.
Abstract: Editing a fact in one language of a multilingual LLM often fails to update the same fact when queried in another language, particularly across different scripts. Prior work treats this as a benchmark failure and proposes better editing algorithms. We instead use knowledge editing as a causal probe to reverse-engineer how facts are stored across languages. We hypothesize a storage spectrum: some facts live at a single, language-shared parameter locus that serves all languages, while others are redundantly duplicated into language-specific copies; a fact's position on this spectrum dictates whether an edit propagates. We first derive, for each fact, an intrinsic PRE-edit signature by causal tracing (activation patching) the components most responsible for recalling the fact independently in each language, and computing their cross-language overlap (a sharedness score). We then perform locate-and-edit updates in a single source language and measure recovery in every other language, building a propagation matrix. Our central claim is that the pre-edit sharedness score predicts post-edit propagation per fact and per language-pair, with high overlap yielding transfer and low overlap yielding language-locked edits. We test on mLAMA and Bi-ZsRE across 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. We further show sharedness correlates with typological/script distance, that many facts are hybrid (shared for near languages, duplicated for far ones), and that editing at the causally-shared locus (rather than the default) improves propagation. This yields a mechanistic map of cross-lingual knowledge and a training-free predictor of transferability.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: parallel factual QA from mLAMA and Bi-ZsRE (subject-relation-object triples) in 12+ languages covering 5 scripts and 4+ families; models Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Pre-edit sharedness signature: for each fact, run causal tracing (activation patching / causal mediation, ROME-style) independently in each language to find the top-k MLP/attention components whose restoration recovers the object token. Define per-language-pair sharedness = overlap (Jaccard / rank correlation) of causally-important components; aggregate to a per-fact sharedness profile. 3. Edit-propagation matrix: apply locate-and-edit (ROME/MEMIT) to change each fact in a single source language; query in all target languages. Metrics: edit success (source), cross-lingual propagation (target reliability), and locality (unrelated facts unchanged). Build fact x source x target propagation tensor. 4. Core test: regress/predict per-pair propagation from pre-edit sharedness; report AUC/correlation for predicting transfer vs. no-transfer purely from the pre-edit signature (train predictor on a fact split, test on held-out facts and held-out language pairs). 5. Taxonomy: cluster facts into shared / duplicated / hybrid based on sharedness profiles; report distribution and characterize which relation types and entity types fall into each. 6. Distance analysis: correlate sharedness and propagation with lang2vec typological distance and same-script indicator; test the hybrid prediction (shared for near, duplicated for far). 7. Causal validation via intervention: for low-sharedness (duplicated) facts, edit at each language's own locus vs. at the union/most-shared locus; measure whether editing the shared locus (when one exists) or multi-locus editing improves propagation, confirming the topology is causally real. 8. Ablations: model scale, tracing granularity (layer vs neuron), and robustness of the predictor across models (train on one model, test transfer of the predictive relationship qualitatively). Metrics throughout: propagation reliability, locality, predictor AUC/Spearman, Jaccard overlap, correlations with distance.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Causal tracing localization is noisy and can be diffuse, weakening the sharedness signal; we mitigate with multiple tracing methods (patching + causal mediation) and report stability. 2. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate identifying comparable causal components and matching object tokens; we restrict to facts with clean object tokenization and use last-token-of-object representations. 3. Locate-and-edit methods have their own artifacts (may fail to edit at all in low-resource languages), confounding propagation with edit success; we condition analyses on successful source-language edits. 4. Sharedness and propagation could both simply track resource level rather than a genuine storage topology; we control by matching facts across resource levels and testing predictor generalization to held-out language pairs. 5. The shared/duplicated dichotomy may be a continuum with no clean clusters; we present it as a spectrum and report continuous predictive power rather than forcing discrete classes. 6. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: reasoning_language_mismatch
Title: Thinking in One Language, Writing in Another: Measuring the Cost of Surface-Latent Reasoning-Language Mismatch in Multilingual CoT
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs have a per-item 'latent reasoning language' (the language whose token representations dominate hidden states during the reasoning steps), which is often but not always English. Reasoning accuracy is governed less by the surface language of the prompt and more by the *mismatch* between the surface CoT language the model is forced to write in and its latent reasoning language: the larger this mismatch (measured in the model's own representation space and by typological distance), the greater the 'reasoning drag' (accuracy loss). Consequently, per-item alignment of the surface CoT language to the model's latent language should improve multilingual reasoning more than uniformly forcing English or the prompt language.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-centric latent space (Do Llamas Work in English? 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English? 2025; Transfer Neurons Hypothesis 2025), that latent multilingual reasoning is English-aligned but uneven (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026), that language mixing in traces reflects internal preferences and constrained decoding to Latin/Han helps (Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025), and that ablating language-specific components boosts reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025). All of these characterize the latent language as a global, largely fixed English-centric pivot, and treat improvements as either removing language (ablation) or forcing a single reasoning script for everyone. None (i) measures a *per-item* latent reasoning language that varies across items and languages, (ii) causally quantifies a 'mismatch cost' between the forced surface CoT language and the model's own per-item latent language, or (iii) proposes per-item surface-language selection aligned to the latent language rather than one global choice. We reframe multilingual CoT failure as a surface-latent language *alignment* problem and provide a causal, item-level account plus a training-free per-item intervention.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are widely believed to 'think in English' internally while writing chain-of-thought (CoT) in the prompt's language. We challenge the assumption that this latent reasoning language is a fixed, global, English-centric pivot. Instead, we hypothesize that each reasoning problem induces a *latent reasoning language*—the language whose token representations dominate hidden states during the reasoning steps—that varies across items, and that multilingual reasoning accuracy is driven by the *mismatch* between the surface language the model is forced to verbalize CoT in and this per-item latent language. We introduce two measurements: (1) a per-item Latent Language Profile, obtained by applying logit-lens/probing to hidden states at reasoning-step token positions to identify which language's tokens are most decodable; and (2) a Mismatch Cost, the accuracy change when the model is constrained (via constrained decoding / instruction) to reason in a surface language that agrees vs. disagrees with its latent profile. We predict Mismatch Cost grows with the representational and typological distance between surface and latent languages. We validate on multilingual math (MGSM), commonsense (XCOPA), and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a distilled reasoning model. Finally we test a training-free per-item intervention that selects the surface CoT language matching the model's measured latent language, comparing against uniform-English, prompt-language, and forced-Latin/Han baselines. The framework yields a mechanistic, item-level view of where language helps or hurts reasoning and a cheap, self-selected multilingual reasoning strategy.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: MGSM (multilingual grade-school math), XCOPA (commonsense), and a translated multi-hop QA subset, in 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (a reasoning model). 2. Latent Language Profile: run each item with CoT; at the token positions of reasoning steps, apply logit-lens and trained linear language-ID probes at middle-to-late layers to compute a per-item, per-layer distribution over which language's answer/step tokens are most decodable. Aggregate to a dominant latent language per item; report how often it is English vs. prompt language vs. another language, and its variance across items (testing that it is NOT globally fixed). 3. Mismatch Cost (behavioral/causal): for each item, elicit CoT under surface languages that (a) match the measured latent language, (b) equal the prompt language, (c) equal English, (d) are a maximally-distant language; use constrained decoding to enforce the script/language of reasoning steps. Metric: exact-match accuracy per condition; Mismatch Cost = accuracy(matched) - accuracy(mismatched). 4. Distance dose-response: correlate Mismatch Cost with (i) representational distance between surface and latent languages (cosine distance of mean reasoning-step activations / mean language vectors) and (ii) lang2vec typological distance and a same-script indicator (Spearman). Prediction: monotonic increase. 5. Causal steering control: rather than only constraining output, steer late-layer language vectors to align/misalign the internal language while keeping surface language fixed, isolating whether the *internal* alignment (not just surface tokens) drives accuracy; measure accuracy and output-language fidelity. 6. Per-item intervention: at inference, measure the latent language from a short forced CoT prefix, then generate full CoT in that language; compare accuracy against uniform-English, prompt-language, and forced-Latin/Han baselines, plus an oracle upper bound (best language per item). Report accuracy gain, extra compute, and output-language fidelity. 7. Ablations: layer choice for latent measurement; short-prefix vs full-trace latent estimation; model scale; whether the effect is stronger in the reasoning-distilled model; robustness of the probe across models (train probe on one, test on another). Metrics throughout: exact-match accuracy, Mismatch Cost, Spearman correlations with distance measures, language-ID probe accuracy, output-language fidelity, and intervention gain vs. oracle.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens/probe decodability at reasoning-step positions may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally-used latent language; we require the causal steering control (Exp. 5) to confirm functional relevance rather than relying on decodability alone. 2. The per-item latent language may in practice be almost always English for some models, collapsing the hypothesis to a global-pivot story; even so, quantifying the small non-English fraction and its predictive value for accuracy is a contribution, and we include a reasoning-distilled model where language mixing (hence latent variability) is documented to be larger. 3. Constrained decoding can degrade fluency and confound accuracy with generation difficulty; we report output-language fidelity and use steering as a fluency-preserving alternative. 4. Tokenization/script differences complicate cross-language logit-lens comparison; we restrict probes to answer/step tokens with clean tokenization and validate probes with held-out data. 5. The per-item intervention adds a short extra forward pass; we report its compute overhead and compare to the oracle to bound achievable gains. 6. Findings may be model-specific; four models across families and one reasoning model address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: cultural_frame_register
Title: Which Answer Is True Here? A Mechanistic Study of How Multilingual LLMs Select Among Culturally-Relative Truths
Short Hypothesis: For claims whose truth value is genuinely relative to a cultural/geographic frame (e.g., 'people drive on the left', 'the head of state is a monarch', 'the school year starts in spring'), multilingual LLMs store multiple mutually-contradictory candidate answers simultaneously and select among them via an internal 'frame register' set in mid layers. We hypothesize that (a) the query language acts as an implicit, weak frame selector that competes with explicit textual frame cues, (b) this selection is mediated by a small, causally-identifiable set of directions/components separable from the answer-content computation, and (c) selection failures (giving the answer correct for the wrong frame) scale with typological/script distance between the query language and the language canonically associated with the intended frame.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work localizes 'culture neurons' separable from language neurons (Isolating Culture Neurons 2025), finds cultural localization in middle layers steerable by cultural vectors (Localized Cultural Knowledge is Conserved 2025), documents a Cultural-Linguistic Synergy where in-language cultural queries activate more specialized neurons (Disentangling Language and Culture 2025), shows cross-lingual alignment causes cultural erasure fixable by layer-specific Surgical Steering (Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment 2025), and finds internal paths are more language- than content-driven (Language over Content 2025). Factual-storage work (Tracing the Roots of Facts 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025) categorizes facts as shared/independent and finds a language-agnostic concept space with late-layer decoding. All of this treats cultural knowledge as static localized content or measures bias toward one canonical (often Western) answer. None studies claims with NO single correct answer—where multiple contradictory answers are simultaneously true under different frames—nor characterizes the mechanism that *selects* among stored competing answers as a function of an explicit-vs-implicit (language) frame cue. We reframe cultural knowledge as a frame-conditioned selection problem and provide the first causal account of a 'frame register' plus a diagnostic of when language overrides explicit context.
Abstract: Many claims about the world have no universal truth value: whether people drive on the left, whether the head of state is a monarch, or when the school year begins depends on the cultural or geographic frame in which the question is asked. Multilingual LLMs must therefore not merely recall facts but *select* which stored, frame-dependent answer applies. We investigate this selection mechanism. We construct FRAME-REL, a controlled dataset of culturally-relative claims for which several countries have known, mutually-contradictory ground-truth answers, and probe models under two orthogonal frame cues: an explicit textual cue (naming the country) and an implicit cue (the query language). We first show that multiple contradictory candidate answers are simultaneously linearly decodable from mid-layer hidden states before selection collapses to one output, evidencing parallel storage rather than a single canonical answer. Using activation patching, we localize a compact 'frame register'—mid-layer components that, when swapped between a same-question run under frame A and under frame B, flip the selected answer without altering answer content. We then quantify a competition between explicit and implicit (language) cues: how often does asking in language L override an explicit country cue, and does this override scale with typological/script distance between L and the frame's canonical language? Experiments span 15+ languages and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. We further test a training-free intervention that steers the frame register to fix mismatched selections without harming fluency, and compare against explicit-prompting baselines. The work recasts multilingual cultural knowledge as frame-conditioned selection and delivers a causal, controllable account.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (FRAME-REL): assemble culturally-relative claim templates with verifiable per-country ground truth that differs across countries (driving side, monarchy vs republic, currency, primary school start season, calendar/new-year timing, measurement units, dominant religion, plug voltage, tipping norms). For each claim, collect >=6 countries with contradictory answers and their canonical languages. Render each claim in 15+ query languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families, crossed with explicit country cues (present/absent). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Parallel-storage probe: for each claim, apply logit-lens and trained linear probes at each layer to test whether multiple countries' answers are simultaneously decodable in mid layers before the output answer emerges. Metric: layer-wise decodability rank of each candidate answer; report co-decodability of contradictory answers vs. a single-answer factual baseline. 3. Locate the frame register: run the identical question under explicit frame A (country A) and frame B (country B), producing different answers. Activation-patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run; identify the minimal set whose patching flips the selected answer to A's answer. Metric: flip rate vs. number/location of patched components; verify content (which candidates exist) is preserved while selection changes. 4. Explicit-vs-implicit (language) competition: with the explicit country cue set to country C but the query posed in language L (canonical language of a different country D), measure how often the output matches C (explicit wins), D (language wins), or neither. Metric: language-override rate. 5. Distance dose-response: correlate language-override rate and frame-selection error with lang2vec typological distance and same-script indicator between L and the intended frame's canonical language (Spearman). Prediction: override/error rises with distance. 6. Causal steering intervention: extract a 'frame direction' per country from mean activation differences at the frame register; at inference, steer the register to the intended frame on mismatched items. Metrics: selection-correction rate, output fluency (perplexity), answer-content preservation, and comparison against explicit-country-prompt and translate-to-English baselines. 7. Separability check: test whether the frame register overlaps with previously reported language-specific and culture-specific neurons (compute overlap) to establish it as a distinct selection (not storage) mechanism. 8. Ablations: model scale; register layer sweep; single-answer factual controls (should show no parallel storage / no flippable register); robustness of probes across models (train on one, test on another). Metrics throughout: candidate decodability rank, flip rate, language-override rate, Spearman with distance, steering-correction rate, fluency, neuron-overlap.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground truth for culturally-relative claims can be ambiguous or change over time; we restrict to unambiguous, stable, verifiable claims (driving side, monarchy status, plug voltage) and have annotators validate per-country answers. 2. Logit-lens/probe decodability of multiple candidates may reflect the readout basis rather than functional parallel storage; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 3) to confirm functional relevance. 3. The frame register may be diffuse rather than compact, weakening the localization story; we report degree of localization honestly and fall back to a direction-based account. 4. Some models may simply always default to the canonical/Western answer regardless of frame, collapsing selection; even so, quantifying the near-absence of frame sensitivity and its language dependence is a contribution, and multiple models mitigate this. 5. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate cross-language probing and answer matching; we restrict to claims with clean, short answer tokens and use last-token-of-answer representations. 6. Steering may trade content preservation for correct selection; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: numeral_morphology_magnitude_leak
Title: Four-Twenty-Ten Is Not Ninety: How Numeral-System Morphology Distorts the Shared Magnitude Representation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a number is written as words, multilingual LLMs are supposed to recover a language-agnostic magnitude, but the surface *morphology* of a language's numeral system leaks into the internal representation. Specifically, for languages with opaque/non-decimal numeral construction (e.g., French vigesimal 'quatre-vingt-dix' = 90, Danish 'halvfems', Georgian, Basque), the model's internal magnitude estimate is systematically pulled toward the values of the literal component morphemes, and this compositional-leakage grows with the typological distance of the numeral system from a transparent base-10 system. This predicts (a) a measurable, direction-consistent magnitude distortion, (b) that distortion tracks numeral-system opacity rather than general language resource level, and (c) that a training-free steering correction along the recovered magnitude direction can repair the leak.
Related Work: A rich interpretability literature shows LLMs encode numbers as digit-wise base-10 (Zhu et al. 2024), sinusoidally (2025), as log-magnitude linear directions (LLMs Know More About Numbers 2026), and in low-dimensional monotonic subspaces (Heinzerling & Inui 2024). Multilingual numeracy work shows accuracy drops across scripts/formats (The Effect of Scripts and Formats on LLM Numeracy 2026), that models fail cross-linguistic numeral puzzles because they lack implicit compositional numeral structure (Investigating linguistic-mathematical reasoning 2025), and that embeddings support grammaticality but not value comparison across languages (Probing for Multilingual Numerical Understanding 2020). All of these either study digits/notation in a single language, or study behavioral failure on cross-linguistic puzzles. None asks the sharp mechanistic question: when a value is expressed as *number words* in different natural languages, is the recovered internal magnitude language-agnostic, and does the *morphological transparency* of the numeral system causally distort that internal magnitude? We uniquely use cross-linguistic numeral morphology as a controlled probe of the shared-vs-language-specific magnitude representation, introduce a 'compositional-leakage' distortion metric grounded in numeral-system typology, and provide a causal steering fix.
Abstract: Multilingual language models must map number words in any language onto a shared notion of magnitude: French 'quatre-vingt-dix', literally 'four-twenty-ten', and English 'ninety' should both point to 90. But numeral systems differ dramatically in morphological transparency—some are cleanly decimal (Chinese, English), others vigesimal or idiosyncratic (French, Danish, Georgian, Basque). We ask whether the model recovers a language-agnostic magnitude regardless of surface morphology, or whether the literal values of a numeral's component morphemes leak into the internal representation. Using established magnitude-probing tools (linear log-magnitude probes, monotonic subspaces), we decode the model's internal magnitude for numbers spelled out as words across 12+ languages spanning transparent-decimal, additive, vigesimal, and irregular numeral systems. We define a compositional-leakage score: the systematic bias of the decoded magnitude toward the summed/producted values of the literal component morphemes. We predict (1) that leakage is measurable and direction-consistent, pulling estimates of opaque numerals (e.g., 90) toward morpheme-implied values; (2) that leakage magnitude correlates with a numeral-system opacity index and is dissociable from language resource level (a transparent low-resource language leaks less than an opaque high-resource one); and (3) that steering activations along the recovered clean magnitude direction repairs downstream comparison and arithmetic errors on opaque numerals without retraining. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The study turns numeral-system typology into a precise instrument for measuring where the multilingual magnitude representation is shared versus contaminated by language-specific surface form.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli & typology: build a parallel set of numbers (0-1000, focused on ranges where morphology diverges, e.g., 70-99, teens, hundreds) spelled out as words in 12+ languages chosen to span numeral-system types: transparent-decimal (English, Chinese, Turkish, Japanese), additive/subtractive (Latin-style, Welsh), vigesimal (French, Danish, Basque, Georgian), and irregular teens (German, Dutch inversion 'einundzwanzig'). For each numeral, annotate its component morphemes and their literal values, and compute a per-language numeral-system Opacity Index (e.g., mean absolute difference between morpheme-implied composition and true decimal value, plus non-decimal-base indicator). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Magnitude probing: train linear log-magnitude probes and identify monotonic magnitude subspaces (Heinzerling-style) using digit-format numbers in English as a language-agnostic anchor; then apply the *same* probe to hidden states at the final token of word-form numerals in every language. Metric: decoded magnitude vs. true magnitude, per language, per layer. Validate probe transfer with held-out numbers. 3. Compositional-leakage score: for each opaque numeral, regress the decoded-magnitude error on (true value) and (morpheme-implied value); the coefficient on morpheme-implied value is the leakage. Report per-language leakage and its layer trajectory (does leakage decrease across layers as the model 'resolves' morphology?). 4. Dissociation test: correlate per-language leakage with the Opacity Index vs. with a language resource-level proxy (pretraining token share / mLAMA accuracy). Prediction: leakage tracks opacity, not resource level; include the crucial contrast of a transparent low-resource language (e.g., Turkish/Swahili) vs. an opaque high-resource one (French). Spearman correlations with confidence intervals. 5. Behavioral link: on magnitude-comparison ('which is larger, [word-form A] or [word-form B]?') and simple word-form arithmetic, measure whether items with high internal leakage have higher error rates; test that leakage predicts errors beyond the true value. 6. Causal steering fix: extract the clean magnitude direction from digit/transparent anchors; at inference, project out the morpheme-leakage component or steer the activation toward the correct-magnitude location for opaque numerals. Metrics: reduction in decoded-magnitude error, comparison/arithmetic accuracy gain, and control that non-numeric fluency is unharmed. Compare against a translate-numeral-to-digits prompting baseline. 7. Causal validation of leakage: patch/ablate the component-morpheme token representations and measure whether decoded magnitude shifts toward or away from morpheme-implied values, confirming morphology is causally responsible. 8. Ablations: layer sweep, model scale, digit vs. word format within the same language, and probe-transfer robustness across models (train probe on one model/language, test on another). Metrics throughout: decoded-magnitude relative error, leakage coefficient, Spearman with Opacity Index and resource proxy, comparison/arithmetic accuracy, steering-repair rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used magnitude; we require the causal morpheme-patching (Exp. 7) and the steering-repair behavioral effect (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. Tokenization of number words differs across languages and may split morphemes unevenly, confounding morpheme-value attribution; we curate stimuli with clean morpheme boundaries and use last-token representations, and report tokenization statistics. 3. Leakage might be confounded with frequency (opaque numerals may be rarer strings); we control by matching frequency ranges and including the resource-level dissociation. 4. The Opacity Index is a hand-constructed metric; we report robustness to alternative operationalizations and validate with multiple annotators. 5. Some models may resolve morphology so well that leakage is negligible—still a positive finding (magnitude is genuinely shared) and multiple models/languages give statistical power to detect small effects. 6. Steering may trade repair for fluency; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: tense_grammaticalization_gap
Title: When the Grammar Is Silent: How Multilingual LLMs Represent Time in Tenseless vs. Tensed Languages
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic 'reference-time' representation (the abstract past/present/future ordering a sentence describes) that is distinct from the surface tense-morphology representation. We hypothesize that (a) for morphologically tensed languages the model can lazily read reference time off surface tense features, while for tenseless/aspect-only languages (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba) it must infer reference time from lexical/pragmatic context using a slower, later-layer, more error-prone circuit; (b) this creates a measurable 'grammaticalization gap' in the robustness and localization of the abstract time representation that tracks whether a language grammatically marks tense, NOT its resource level; and (c) the abstract reference-time direction transfers across languages, so it can be causally read from a tensed language and injected to repair temporal inference in a tenseless one.
Related Work: Prior probing work shows tense is easy to decode in morphologically-marked languages (French) but hard in Chinese, attributing the drop to memorization vs. abstraction (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021), and that transformers encode aspect features like telicity/duration (About Time 2022; Verbal Aspect 2024). Recent interpretability shows grammatical concepts (number, gender, tense) share cross-lingual feature directions (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) and that tense/aspect are steerable orthogonal directions (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025). LLMs also encode linear time and 'temporal heads' for factual dates (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Temporal Heads 2025). Cross-linguistic NLI work shows LLMs struggle with perfect-aspect temporal inference in Chinese/Japanese (2025). However, ALL prior work either (i) probes surface tense morphology, or (ii) studies factual event dates, and treats the tenseless-language decoding drop as a probing artifact. None distinguishes the abstract SENTENCE-INTERNAL reference-time representation (the situation's temporal location, present regardless of whether grammar marks it) from surface tense morphology, nor tests whether tenseless languages recruit a distinct, later, error-prone inference circuit, nor uses a tensed language as a causal donor to repair temporal inference in a tenseless one. We reframe the classic French-vs-Chinese gap as a mechanistic grammaticalization-gap phenomenon with a causal cross-lingual fix.
Abstract: Some languages grammatically mark when an event happened (English 'walked' vs 'walks'); others, like Chinese, Indonesian, and Yoruba, are largely tenseless and leave temporal location to be inferred from adverbs, aspect markers, and pragmatics. Yet any comprehending model must recover the same abstract reference time. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this abstract sentence-internal time, and whether the mechanism differs when grammar is silent. We distinguish two representations: surface tense morphology (which verb form appears) and abstract reference time (past/present/future location of the described situation). Using parallel sentences whose reference time is fixed by context across tensed and tenseless languages, we train linear probes and locate the layers and components that encode reference time in each. We predict a 'grammaticalization gap': in tensed languages reference time is decodable early and localizes with surface-tense features, whereas in tenseless languages it emerges only in later layers via a distinct, more error-prone circuit, and this gap tracks whether a language marks tense rather than its resource level (e.g., low-resource tensed Swahili patterns with English, high-resource tenseless Chinese with Indonesian). We causally test whether the abstract reference-time direction is shared: extracting it from a tensed language and steering it into a tenseless-language forward pass should repair temporal-inference errors without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B and 12+ languages of both types. This recasts the classic tense-probing gap as a controllable, cross-lingually transferable mechanistic phenomenon.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli: build parallel minimal-pair sentences where the abstract reference time (past/present/future) is unambiguously fixed by an explicit temporal adverbial ('yesterday'/'now'/'tomorrow') and by a bare-context version (no adverbial, inferable only from lexical/pragmatic cues). Render in 12+ languages split into TENSED (English, Spanish, Russian, Swahili [low-resource but tensed], Hindi) and TENSELESS/aspect-only (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba, Thai, Vietnamese). Annotate surface tense-morphology label and abstract reference-time label separately. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Two-target probing: train separate linear probes for (a) surface tense morphology and (b) abstract reference time, per layer, per language. Metric: probe accuracy vs layer; identify emergence layer (first layer >90% or peak) for reference time in each language. Prediction: tensed languages peak early and reference-time probe correlates with surface-tense probe; tenseless languages peak later and dissociate. 3. Grammaticalization-gap quantification: define gap = (reference-time emergence layer / robustness in bare-context condition) difference between tenseless and tensed languages. Correlate gap with a binary 'grammatically marks tense' typology indicator vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / mLAMA accuracy). Spearman with CIs; key contrast: low-resource tensed (Swahili) vs high-resource tenseless (Chinese) to dissociate typology from resource. 4. Circuit localization: use activation patching / attention-head attribution to find components that carry reference time in tensed vs tenseless languages; measure overlap (Jaccard) between the two circuits and whether tenseless languages recruit additional later components tied to adverbial/context tokens. 5. Shared-direction test & causal transfer: extract abstract reference-time direction (mean activation difference past vs future) from a TENSED donor language; test cross-lingual decodability (donor probe applied to tenseless language) and, crucially, steer the donor-derived direction into a tenseless-language forward pass on bare-context temporal-inference items where the model errs. Metrics: temporal-NLI accuracy gain (using Chinese/Japanese perfect-aspect NLI style items and our bare-context set), output fluency (perplexity), and specificity (no change to unrelated features). Compare to a same-language steering baseline and a translate-to-English baseline. 6. Behavioral link: on a temporal-inference task (order two events / answer when-question), test that low reference-time probe confidence in tenseless bare-context items predicts higher error, beyond the true label. 7. Ablations: adverbial-present vs bare-context; layer sweep; model scale; aspect-marker presence (does an aspect marker in Chinese restore early decodability?); probe-transfer robustness across models. Metrics throughout: probe accuracy, emergence layer, Jaccard circuit overlap, Spearman with typology vs resource, cross-lingual probe transfer accuracy, steering-repair rate, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal steering-repair (Exp. 5) and the behavioral link (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. Separating 'abstract reference time' from 'surface tense' is hard in tensed languages where they nearly coincide; the tenseless languages and the bare-context condition are the crucial dissociating cases and are designed for exactly this. 3. Ground-truth reference time in bare-context tenseless sentences can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to items validated by native-speaker annotators with high agreement. 4. Tokenization/script differences complicate cross-language probing; we use clean sentence-final or verb-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 5. Some models may simply route everything through English tense, collapsing the tenseless circuit into a translation step; even so, showing this (via the shared-direction transfer) is a positive, informative result. 6. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen languages (Swahili tensed low-resource, Chinese tenseless high-resource); we report robustness to alternative language choices. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: grammatical_gender_concept_leak
Title: The Gender You Didn't Ask For: Causal Leakage of Query-Language Grammatical Gender into the Shared Concept Space and Cross-Lingual Semantic Judgments
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM represents an inanimate concept, the grammatical gender that concept happens to carry in the query language covertly enters the model's language-agnostic concept representation and causally biases downstream *semantic* judgments (e.g., attribute association, pronoun choice, adjective selection), even when the answer is produced in a gender-neutral language like English or Chinese. We hypothesize (a) a covert 'concept-gender' direction, distinct from surface agreement features, that inherits the query language's grammatical gender; (b) that this leakage is causally responsible for cross-lingual semantic-gender inconsistencies; and (c) that leakage strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes gender, and can be removed by a training-free projection along a shared concept-gender direction.
Related Work: Prior work shows grammatical gender contaminates static/contextual word embeddings of inanimate nouns (Gonen et al. 2019; embedding-disentangling methods 2020-2022), that gender subspaces are partly shared across languages so classification transfers but removal does not (Analyzing Gender Representation 2022), that grammatical concepts including gender share cross-lingual feature directions in LLMs (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), and that grammatical gender biases text-to-image outputs (Beyond Content 2025). Distributional accounts test whether opposite-gender noun pairs shift embedding semantics (Testing a Distributional Account 2024). All of this is either (i) about static/contextual embeddings and their geometry, or (ii) about behavioral bias in image generation. None asks the sharp causal, generation-time question inside a decoder LLM: does the *query language's* grammatical gender leak into the *shared concept representation* used during reasoning and thereby causally alter *semantic* judgments produced in a gender-neutral output language? We use opposite-gender cross-lingual noun pairs (key: feminine ES / masculine DE) as a controlled natural experiment, provide activation-patching causal evidence for a 'concept-gender' direction separate from surface agreement, quantify leakage vs. degree of grammaticalization, and deliver a training-free debiasing projection whose effect is validated behaviorally in a neutral output language.
Abstract: Many languages grammatically gender inanimate nouns, and these assignments are largely arbitrary and disagree across languages: a bridge is feminine in German but masculine in Spanish. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs, which are widely believed to compute in a shared language-agnostic concept space, keep this concept space free of the query language's grammatical gender, or whether that gender covertly leaks in and biases genuinely semantic judgments. Using cross-lingual noun pairs with opposite grammatical genders as a natural experiment, we ask the model to make semantic-gender judgments (which attribute/adjective/pronoun best fits a concept) in a gender-neutral output language (English or Chinese) while varying the gendered language in which the concept is introduced. We first show that a covert 'concept-gender' direction is linearly decodable from mid-layer representations and inherits the query language's grammatical gender, distinct from surface agreement features. Using activation patching, we causally test whether swapping this direction between a masculine-language run and a feminine-language run flips the model's semantic judgment without changing the concept's identity, establishing that grammatical gender leakage is causally responsible for cross-lingual semantic inconsistency. We predict leakage strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes gender (Slavic/Germanic/Romance vs. English/Chinese controls) and not with resource level. Finally, we recover a shared concept-gender direction and apply a training-free projection that removes leakage, measuring restored cross-lingual consistency without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 8+ languages. The work reveals a subtle language-specific contaminant of the supposedly shared concept space and provides a mechanistic, controllable account.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli: assemble ~300 inanimate concrete nouns with attested grammatical gender across 6 gendered languages spanning the strength of gender marking (Romance: Spanish, French, Italian; Germanic: German [3-gender]; Slavic: Russian, Polish) plus 2 gender-neutral controls (English, Chinese). Crucially select the subset of concepts whose grammatical gender is OPPOSITE across at least two languages (e.g., key/bridge/sun/moon), giving matched minimal pairs that dissociate grammatical from any semantic gender. Annotate per-language grammatical gender. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral leakage test: pose semantic-gender judgment tasks with the answer forced into a gender-NEUTRAL output language (English/Chinese): 'Would you describe [concept, introduced in language L] as more [masculine-associated adjective] or more [feminine-associated adjective]?', personification pronoun choice ('If this object were a person, would it be he or she?'), and adjective-fit ranking. Metric: rate at which the chosen attribute matches the query language's GRAMMATICAL gender; compute cross-lingual inconsistency = fraction of opposite-gender pairs where the judgment flips with the query language. Baselines: English/Chinese query (no grammatical gender). 3. Concept-gender probe: train linear probes at each layer to decode grammatical gender of the concept from the mid-layer hidden state at the concept-token position (or last token of a neutral-language prompt), using held-out nouns. Show the decoded 'concept-gender' inherits the query language's assignment and is distinct from surface agreement features (control probe on languages with no gender should be near chance). Report layer-wise decodability. 4. Causal patching (core test): for an opposite-gender pair concept, run two forward passes introducing the concept in a masculine-marking language vs a feminine-marking language, both answering in English. Activation-patch the mid-layer concept representation (or the isolated concept-gender direction) from the masculine run into the feminine run; measure whether the English semantic judgment flips to match the donor's grammatical gender while concept identity (topic/answer content) is preserved. Metric: flip rate vs. number/location of patched components; identity-preservation check. 5. Grammaticalization dose-response: correlate per-language leakage (behavioral flip rate + probe decodability) with a gender-marking-strength index (number of genders, agreement pervasiveness) and, as a dissociation, with a resource-level proxy. Prediction: leakage tracks grammaticalization strength, not resource level; English/Chinese controls near zero. Spearman with CIs. 6. Training-free debiasing: extract a shared concept-gender direction (mean activation difference masculine vs feminine, pooled across gendered languages) and project it out of the concept representation at inference. Metrics: reduction in cross-lingual inconsistency, restoration of neutral-baseline judgment distribution, output fluency (perplexity), and specificity (unrelated attributes unchanged). Compare against embedding-debiasing-style baselines and a translate-to-English-first baseline. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where concept-gender is malleable; single-direction projection vs full-subspace removal; model scale; whether German's neuter provides a third pole; probe transfer across models (train on one, test on another); and a semantically-gendered control set (man/woman/king/queen) that SHOULD retain gender to verify the intervention is selective to grammatical leakage. Metrics throughout: attribute-match rate, cross-lingual flip/inconsistency rate, probe accuracy, causal flip rate, identity preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, debiasing consistency gain, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of concept-gender may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and behavioral debiasing (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. Some 'semantic gender' judgments may reflect genuine cultural stereotypes rather than grammatical leakage; the opposite-gender minimal pairs and gender-neutral control languages are designed to isolate the grammatical contribution, and we control for stereotype associations of the target concepts. 3. Leakage may be small in strong models that fully abstract away grammar—still an informative positive result (concept space is genuinely clean), and multiple languages/models give statistical power. 4. Tokenization differences across languages/scripts complicate concept-token localization; we use last-token-of-concept or neutral-prompt final-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 5. Debiasing may over-remove and harm legitimately gendered concepts; the semantically-gendered control set (Exp. 7) tests selectivity, and we report specificity/fluency. 6. Behavioral tasks (pronoun/adjective choice) may be prompt-sensitive; we average over multiple paraphrases and report robustness. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: false_friend_meaning_leak
Title: Gift Means Poison: Causally Tracing How Interlingual Homographs Leak the Wrong-Language Meaning Into Multilingual LLM Computation
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM processes an interlingual homograph (a false friend, e.g. German 'Gift' = poison vs English 'gift' = present), the wrong-language meaning is automatically co-activated as a latent competitor in mid layers, and semantic errors occur when the model fails to disambiguate using context. We hypothesize (a) both meanings are simultaneously linearly decodable before disambiguation collapses to one, (b) a causally-identifiable mid-layer 'meaning-selection' step resolves the competition, (c) selection failure scales with the frequency balance between the two meanings and with the mismatch between the query-context language and the model's dominant language, and (d) steering along a recovered meaning direction can causally repair or induce the wrong reading.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs perform below random on interlingual-homograph disambiguation and rely on orthography over semantics (Multilingual LLMs Struggle to Link Orthography and Semantics 2025). Small bilingual-model studies show shared embeddings produce facilitation for BOTH friends and false friends, driven by frequency, failing to reproduce human interference (Skrjanec et al. 2026; Cumulative Frequency 2021). Tokenizer-level work maps false friends to shared subwords and proposes language cues at tokenization (Tokenizing Crosslingual Homographs 2026; False Friends Are Not Foes 2025). Embedding-geometry work characterizes shared vs language-partitioned spaces (Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023; BERT is Not an Interlingua 2019). All of this is either (i) behavioral, (ii) about static embeddings/tokenization, or (iii) in tiny controlled bilingual models. None gives a causal, generation-time mechanistic account inside a large decoder LLM of HOW the wrong-language meaning is co-activated and selected against, WHERE disambiguation happens, and WHAT modulates failure. We use false friends as a controlled natural experiment to probe the shared-vs-specific meaning representation, provide activation-patching causal evidence for a mid-layer meaning-selection step, quantify failure drivers (frequency balance, language dominance, context strength), and deliver a causal steering intervention.
Abstract: Interlingual homographs, or false friends, are words with identical surface form but different meanings across languages: German 'Gift' means poison, but English 'gift' means present. Such words are a natural stress test for the shared subword vocabularies of multilingual LLMs. Behavioral studies show models resolve them poorly, but how the wrong meaning enters computation, where it is (or is not) suppressed, and what governs failure remain unknown mechanistically. We treat false friends as a controlled probe of whether the model computes a single, context-appropriate meaning or covertly co-activates both. Using a curated cross-lingual false-friend set with matched cognate and monosemous controls, we first show via logit-lens and linear probes that in mid layers both meanings of a false friend are simultaneously decodable before selection collapses to one, unlike controls. Using activation patching, we localize a compact mid-layer meaning-selection step: swapping its activation between a context that forces meaning A and one that forces meaning B flips the model's downstream semantic judgment while preserving that the word is a false friend. We then quantify what drives selection failure: the frequency balance between the two meanings, the mismatch between the surrounding-context language and the model's dominant language, and context strength. Finally, we extract a meaning direction and steer it to causally repair mis-selections in disambiguating context, and to induce the wrong reading in weak context, validated behaviorally. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across English-German, English-Spanish, English-French, English-Dutch, and English-Russian false-friend pairs. The work provides the first causal, generation-time account of cross-lingual meaning interference in large LLMs and a controllable fix.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli: build a cross-lingual false-friend set from validated databases (Dutch-English homograph DB 2019, plus curated English-German/Spanish/French/Russian pairs), each with (a) the two meanings and their canonical languages, (b) matched cognate controls (same form, same meaning) and (c) monosemous single-language controls. For each false friend, construct paired disambiguating contexts (one forcing meaning A, one forcing meaning B) and a weak/neutral context, rendered so the surrounding context is in language A vs language B. Estimate per-meaning corpus frequency to compute a frequency-balance score. Annotate the intended meaning per item (native-speaker validation). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral baseline: pose meaning-selection / paraphrase / entailment tasks (e.g. 'Does this sentence say something dangerous?') and measure selection accuracy for false friends vs cognate vs monosemous controls, across context strength and context language. Metric: disambiguation accuracy, wrong-language-meaning error rate. 3. Parallel-activation probe: at the homograph token position, apply logit-lens and trained linear probes at each layer to test whether BOTH meanings (e.g. answer tokens 'poison' and 'present') are simultaneously decodable in mid layers before one dominates. Metric: layer-wise co-decodability rank of each meaning; contrast against monosemous controls (should show single meaning). 4. Localize meaning-selection (core causal test): run the identical false friend under context A (forces meaning A) vs context B (forces meaning B), yielding different downstream answers. Activation-patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run; identify the minimal set whose patching flips the model's semantic judgment to A while preserving lexical identity. Metric: flip rate vs number/location of patched components; identity-preservation check. 5. Failure-driver analysis: regress selection-failure rate on (i) frequency-balance score, (ii) context-language vs dominant-language mismatch (lang2vec/typological distance), and (iii) context strength. Prediction: failure rises with balanced/dominant-competitor frequency and with mismatch. Report standardized coefficients and Spearman with CIs. 6. Causal steering intervention: extract a meaning direction (mean activation difference between meaning-A and meaning-B runs) at the selection layer; (a) in disambiguating context where the model errs, steer toward the correct meaning and measure repair rate; (b) in weak context, steer to induce the wrong reading (proving the direction is causally functional). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, downstream-task accuracy, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (unrelated items unchanged). Compare against a translate-to-context-language baseline and a tokenizer-language-cue prompt baseline. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where selection is malleable; effect of shared vs language-specific tokenization of the homograph (does the model treat it as one token?); model scale; whether the competitor is always the dominant-language meaning or the higher-frequency meaning; probe transfer across models. Metrics throughout: disambiguation accuracy, co-decodability rank, causal flip/repair/induction rates, identity preservation, Spearman with frequency/distance, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe co-decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than functional co-activation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. False-friend meanings often differ in frequency, confounding co-activation with mere frequency; we explicitly model frequency balance (Exp. 5) and include frequency-matched subsets. 3. Tokenization varies: some homographs split into different subwords across contexts, breaking the 'shared surface form' premise; we report per-item tokenization and analyze shared-token vs split-token cases separately (Exp. 7). 4. Strong models may resolve context so well that interference is rare in disambiguating contexts; the weak-context and induction experiments (Exp. 6b) still yield informative causal results, and multiple languages/models give statistical power. 5. Ground-truth intended meaning in weak contexts can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated items with high agreement. 6. Steering may trade correctness for fluency; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: honorific_register_binding
Title: Who Am I Talking To? A Causal Study of How Multilingual LLMs Represent Social Register and Bind It to Honorific Grammar
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic representation of the social relationship between speaker and addressee (relative status/formality), stored separately from surface honorific morphology. When generating in a language that grammatically forces an honorific/register choice (Japanese/Korean honorifics, T-V distinction), the model reads register off this shared 'social-register' variable via a late-layer binding step. We hypothesize (a) an abstract social-register direction that is decodable across languages including register-lax ones like English; (b) that honorific errors in obligatory-honorific languages arise from a binding failure that lazily inherits the register implied by the input/query language rather than re-inferring it from context; and (c) that this inheritance bias scales with how strongly a language grammaticalizes register, not with its resource level, and can be causally repaired by steering the shared register direction.
Related Work: Prior work studies politeness behaviorally and stylistically (TyDiP 2022; Comparing Styles across Languages 2023; Should We Respect LLMs? 2024) and probes negation/passivization/function words in monolingual BERT-era models (Negation Scope 2020; Controlling the Imprint 2020; Function Words 2022). Interpretability work shows LLMs share cross-lingual concept and grammatical-concept directions (Semantic Hub 2024; Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) and decode into the target language in late layers. However, all politeness work is behavioral/stylistic and treats register as an output style, while all mechanistic multilingual work targets semantic content or morphological features like gender/number/tense. None isolates the abstract social-relationship variable (relative speaker-addressee status) as a distinct, causally-manipulable representation, none studies the late-layer binding of this variable onto obligatory honorific grammar, and none tests whether register is lazily inherited from the input language. We uniquely treat honorification/T-V typology as a controlled probe of the shared-vs-specific pragmatic representation, give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a register-binding step, and dissociate grammaticalization strength from resource level.
Abstract: Languages encode the social relationship between speaker and addressee very differently: Japanese and Korean obligatorily mark honorification through verb morphology, Romance/Slavic/German languages force a T-V (informal/formal 'you') choice, and English leaves register largely to lexical and pragmatic cues. Any competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract social relationship and, when the target language demands it, commit to a grammatical register. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this social-register variable and how they bind it onto honorific grammar. We distinguish two representations: an abstract, language-agnostic social-register variable (the relative status/formality of the interlocutors, present regardless of grammatical marking) and the surface honorific/T-V morphology that realizes it. Using parallel dialogues whose social relationship is fixed by context across register-marking and register-lax languages, we train linear probes and localize where register is encoded and where it is bound to grammar. We predict (1) the abstract register direction is decodable across languages, including English; (2) honorific errors in obligatory-honorific languages stem from a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the register implied by the query/input language; and (3) this inheritance bias tracks grammaticalization strength, not resource level (e.g., high-resource register-lax English vs. lower-resource register-heavy Korean). We causally test binding via activation patching and repair errors by steering the shared register direction, measuring restored register correctness without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages. The work provides the first mechanistic, controllable account of pragmatic social register in multilingual LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli: build parallel dialogue/instruction items whose speaker-addressee social relationship is unambiguously fixed by context (e.g., 'a student writing to a professor' [high formality] vs 'texting a close friend' [low formality]; power/status/intimacy dimensions). Render each item in 10+ languages spanning three register-grammar types: OBLIGATORY-HONORIFIC (Japanese, Korean), T-V DISTINCTION (Spanish, French, German, Russian, Hindi), and REGISTER-LAX (English, Chinese, Indonesian). Include a bare-context variant where relationship must be inferred from lexical cues and an explicit-context variant. Annotate the correct target register per item (native-speaker validation) and a per-language 'register-grammaticalization strength' index (obligatory verb morphology > T-V pronoun > lexical-only). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral register-accuracy baseline: generate replies in each language and measure whether the produced honorific/T-V level matches the context-mandated register; report register-error rate by language type, context strength, and by whether the query/prompt framing language matches or mismatches the generation language. 3. Abstract-register probe: train linear probes at each layer to decode the intended social register (formal/informal, or ordinal register level) from mid-layer hidden states, using held-out items. Show it is decodable in register-lax languages (English/Chinese) too and that a probe trained on one language transfers to others (cross-lingual register-direction sharing). Contrast with a surface-morphology probe (which honorific form appears) to establish the abstract-vs-surface dissociation. 4. Locate the register-binding step (core causal test): run the identical item under context forcing FORMAL vs INFORMAL, producing different honorific outputs in an obligatory-honorific language; activation-patch late-layer components from the formal run into the informal run and identify the minimal set whose patching flips the produced register while preserving message content. Metric: register-flip rate vs number/location of patched components; content-preservation check. 5. Lazy-inheritance test: hold the target generation language fixed (e.g., Japanese) but vary the language/framing in which the context is presented (English formal framing vs Japanese informal-context, etc.); measure how often the output register matches the input-language-implied register rather than the context-mandated register. Prediction: inheritance is strongest when generating obligatory-honorific languages from register-lax input languages. 6. Grammaticalization dose-response: correlate register-error and inheritance rate with the grammaticalization-strength index vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy).
