Key dissociation: register-lax high-resource English vs register-heavy lower-resource Korean. Report Spearman with CIs. 7. Causal steering repair: extract a shared social-register direction (mean activation difference formal vs informal, pooled across languages) at the binding layer; on mis-registered items, steer toward the correct register and measure repair rate, and in bare context steer to induce the wrong register (proving functional causality). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, register correctness, content preservation, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (unrelated attributes unchanged). Compare against an explicit register-instruction prompting baseline and a translate-context-first baseline. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where register is malleable; probe transfer across models; power vs intimacy dimension separability; whether Japanese/Korean recruit additional late components tied to verb-ending tokens; model scale. Metrics throughout: register-error rate, inheritance rate, probe accuracy, cross-lingual probe transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of abstract register may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used variable; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 7) to establish functional relevance. 2. Ground-truth register in bare-context items can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated items with high inter-annotator agreement. 3. Separating abstract register from surface morphology is hard in obligatory-honorific languages where they nearly coincide; the register-lax languages and bare-context condition are the crucial dissociating cases. 4. Some models may produce degenerate or under-marked register in low-resource honorific languages (e.g., always default polite), collapsing the effect; quantifying such near-absence of register sensitivity is itself informative, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of honorific verb endings varies across languages; we use verb-final or reply-final token representations and report tokenization statistics; obligatory-honorific vs T-V vs lexical cases are analyzed separately. 6. The grammaticalization-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen languages; we report robustness to alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade register correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: implicit_comparative_method
Title: Does the Model Know the Comparative Method? Causally Isolating an Implicit Sound-Correspondence Engine in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs can predict cognate forms across related languages by internally applying REGULAR sound-correspondence rules (an implicit 'comparative method') rather than only memorizing attested cognate pairs, and this rule-application is driven by an identifiable, causally-manipulable internal mechanism that generalizes to held-out language pairs and even nonce (invented) words.
Related Work: Historical-linguistics NLP shows specialized character-based models learn sound correspondences and latent diachronic information (Probing Multilingual Cognate Prediction, Fournier 2022; List 2018 automatic correspondence inference), and that mBERT/NMT representations cluster by phylogenetic/typological relatedness (Probing mBERT for Genetic/Typological Signals 2020; Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations 2023; Investigating Multilingual NMT Representations 2019). Transfer work exploits cognates and phonetic alignment for low-resource languages (PhoneXL 2023; Transliteration for Morphological Inflection 2020; Hamshentsnag 2025). ALL of this either (i) uses task-specialized character-level cognate/NMT models, or (ii) probes STATIC encoder representations for typology, treating relatedness as a similarity signal. None asks whether a modern GENERATIVE multilingual LLM, prompted in-context, applies REGULAR sound-correspondence rules productively (to nonce/unseen forms), nor gives CAUSAL mechanistic evidence that a specific internal component implements this rule-application distinct from lexical memorization. We reframe cognate prediction as a test of an implicit, causally-real comparative-method engine and provide the first location+intervention account.
Abstract: Historical linguistics reconstructs language history via the comparative method: identifying REGULAR sound correspondences (e.g., Latin 'p' -> English 'f' in pater/father, pisces/fish) and applying them productively. We ask whether multilingual LLMs have implicitly acquired such an engine. The sharp question is whether a model predicts cognates by APPLYING a regular rule that generalizes to words it has never seen paired (including invented nonce forms), or merely RETRIEVES memorized cognate pairs. We first establish the behavior: given a few in-context correspondence exemplars from a language pair, can the model transform a held-out real word, and crucially a NONCE word (which cannot be memorized), into its cognate form obeying the correspondence? We test across language families (Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Indo-Aryan, Turkic) using established cognate resources (NorthEuraLex, CogNet, IELex) and nonce stimuli constructed to obey known correspondences. We predict above-chance productive rule application that degrades gracefully with the number/regularity of correspondences and with typological distance. We then locate the mechanism: probing and vocabulary-projection to find where correspondence rules are represented, and activation patching / steering to test causality. Our central mechanistic claim is that SOME internal component (a small set of mid-layer features/heads) carries the active correspondence rule: patching it from a Latin->English run into a Latin->German run should switch the applied correspondence, and steering along a recovered 'correspondence direction' should induce or repair rule application on nonce words. Experiments use Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. This bridges the comparative method with mechanistic interpretability and dissociates rule-based generalization from lexical memorization in multilingual LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Data & stimuli: (a) Real cognate sets from NorthEuraLex, CogNet, and IELex spanning Romance (Latin/Spanish/French/Italian), Germanic (English/German/Dutch/Swedish), Slavic (Russian/Polish/Czech), Indo-Aryan (Hindi/Bengali), and Turkic (Turkish/Azerbaijani); annotate attested regular sound correspondences per pair. (b) NONCE stimuli: construct invented source words that obey the phonotactics of the source language and to which a known correspondence set applies, yielding a deterministic 'correct' target form no model could have memorized. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral test (establish the phenomenon): in-context prompt with k correspondence exemplars (source->target cognate pairs), then ask the model to produce the cognate of a held-out REAL word and of a NONCE word. Metrics: exact-match and edit-distance to the rule-predicted form; correspondence-obedience rate (fraction of relevant segments transformed per the rule). Baselines: (i) copy-source baseline, (ii) random-correspondence baseline, (iii) memorization ceiling on seen pairs. Key contrast: real-word vs nonce-word accuracy isolates productive rule application from retrieval. 3. Condition sweep (when it holds): vary number of exemplars k, correspondence regularity (regular vs irregular/exceptional), and typological/lang2vec distance; test predicted graceful degradation and correlate accuracy with distance and regularity (Spearman). 4. Location: train linear probes and apply vocabulary projection (logit lens) at each layer to detect (i) whether the source segment's corresponding target segment is decodable before output, and (ii) which layers carry the active correspondence identity; attention-attribution to find heads reading exemplar pairs. Output: ranked candidate components. 5. Causal intervention (core): (a) Activation patching / swap: run the same source word under correspondence set A (Latin->English) vs set B (Latin->German); patch the candidate mid-layer component from the A-run into the B-run and test whether the applied correspondence switches to A while lexical identity is preserved. (b) Steering: extract a 'correspondence direction' (mean activation difference between correct-rule and wrong-rule runs) and steer on NONCE words to induce correct rule application where the model errs, and to induce a WRONG correspondence where it was correct (proving functional causality). Metrics: correspondence-switch/repair/induction rate, specificity (unrelated segments unchanged), fluency of output. 6. Dissociation control: compare intervention effects on nonce words (pure rule) vs high-frequency memorized cognates (retrieval) to confirm the located component drives RULE application, not lexical lookup. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where the rule is malleable; exemplar order/count; model scale; probe transfer across models (train probe on one, apply to another); proto-form reconstruction as a bonus productive task. Metrics throughout: exact-match, edit distance, correspondence-obedience/switch/repair/induction rates, Spearman with distance/regularity, specificity, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Nonce words may still partially overlap memorized substrings, blurring the rule-vs-memorization line; we control by using segments/positions where the correspondence is the only cue and by comparing against a copy baseline. 2. Probe/logit-lens decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; the causal patching-switch and steering induction (Exp. 5) are required to establish functional relevance. 3. The correspondence mechanism may be diffuse rather than localized; we report degree of localization and fall back to a direction-based account. 4. Some models may simply copy or transliterate rather than apply correspondences, collapsing the effect; even documenting the near-absence of productive rule use, and its dependence on family/distance, is an informative finding, and three models give statistical power. 5. Tokenization fragments words unevenly across scripts, complicating segment-level attribution; we restrict to clean-tokenizing pairs, work at last-token-of-word where needed, and report tokenization statistics. 6. Ground-truth 'correct' cognate forms for real words can involve irregular changes; we separate regular vs irregular items and rely on nonce items for the cleanest rule test. 7. Steering may trade rule application for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: conceptual_metaphor_override
Title: Anger Is Not Always Fire: How Multilingual LLMs Override Culture-Specific Idiom Meanings with Their Dominant Language's Conceptual Metaphors
Short Hypothesis: When interpreting an idiom in a non-dominant language, multilingual LLMs covertly retrieve the figurative meaning implied by their DOMINANT language's conceptual-metaphor system, and this dominant-language figurative reading is co-activated as a latent competitor. For idioms whose source-language conceptual metaphor differs from the dominant language's (culture-specific idioms), this causes systematic misinterpretation, whereas idioms grounded in a shared/universal conceptual metaphor are interpreted correctly. The override is a locatable figurative-retrieval-and-selection failure whose strength scales with the conceptual-metaphor distance between the query language and the dominant language, not with resource level.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes idiom processing to early-layer 'Idiom Heads' and competing figurative/literal pathways (Anatomy of an Idiom 2025; Tug-of-war between figurative and literal 2025; NMT idiom analysis 2022). Cross-lingual work shows figurative-detection knowledge sits in middle layers and transfers across languages (Metaphors in PLMs 2022), that a reusable cross-lingual figurative-GENERATION steering direction exists (Cross-Lingual Steering for Figurative Language Generation 2026), and that cross-lingual lexical overlap and shared idioms boost PIE disambiguation (MultiCoPIE 2025; Meta4XNLI 2024). All of these treat figurativeness as a single transferable feature and study detection/generation of figurativeness, or literal-vs-figurative disambiguation WITHIN a language. None asks whether the SPECIFIC figurative MEANING retrieved for a foreign idiom is contaminated by the dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping, nor identifies a cross-lingual conceptual-metaphor OVERRIDE as a co-activation/selection failure. We reframe idiom comprehension as a cross-cultural meaning-SELECTION problem grounded in Conceptual Metaphor Theory, provide causal (patching + steering) evidence for a figurative-retrieval locus that inherits the dominant metaphor, and dissociate conceptual-metaphor distance from resource level.
Abstract: Idioms encode culture-specific conceptual metaphors: 'anger is fire' is near-universal, but many idioms map emotions and concepts through images idiosyncratic to one language's cultural history. A multilingual model reading an idiom in a non-dominant language must retrieve the meaning licensed by THAT language's conceptual system, not its own dominant one. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs instead default to their dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping, covertly co-activating the dominant-language figurative reading and systematically misinterpreting idioms whose source metaphor diverges from it. We test this with a controlled set of idioms drawn from multilingual idiom corpora (MultiCoPIE, IdiomX, Meta4XNLI), each annotated with its underlying conceptual metaphor and labeled shared (same mapping as the dominant language) or culture-specific (divergent mapping), rendered across 10+ languages spanning several scripts and families. Behaviorally, we measure interpretation accuracy and the rate at which the model's paraphrase/entailment judgment matches the dominant-language metaphor rather than the correct source meaning. Mechanistically, we (i) show via logit-lens and probes that the dominant-language figurative meaning is decodable during foreign-idiom processing (co-activation), (ii) locate a mid/early-layer figurative-retrieval stage via activation patching whose swap flips the selected meaning, and (iii) steer along a recovered conceptual-metaphor direction to causally repair culture-specific misinterpretations and to induce override on shared idioms. We predict override strength scales with conceptual-metaphor distance and not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work gives the first mechanistic account of cross-cultural conceptual-metaphor interference in multilingual LLMs and a training-free fix.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli: from MultiCoPIE, IdiomX, and Meta4XNLI, curate ~250 idioms across 10+ languages (spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families), each annotated (native-speaker validated) with (a) its correct figurative meaning, (b) its underlying conceptual metaphor (e.g. ANGER IS FIRE, MIND IS A CONTAINER, LIFE IS A JOURNEY), and (c) a label: SHARED (same conceptual mapping as the model's dominant/English metaphor) vs CULTURE-SPECIFIC (divergent mapping). For culture-specific idioms, also record the (incorrect) meaning the dominant-language literal-words/metaphor would imply. Construct multiple-choice paraphrase and entailment (NLI) items per idiom. Compute a per-idiom conceptual-metaphor distance to the dominant language and per-language aggregate. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral override test: pose paraphrase-selection and NLI tasks; measure (i) interpretation accuracy for SHARED vs CULTURE-SPECIFIC idioms, (ii) OVERRIDE RATE = fraction of culture-specific items where the chosen meaning matches the dominant-language conceptual mapping rather than the correct source meaning. Baselines: query in dominant language (upper bound), translate-to-English-first, and a literal-only control. 3. Co-activation probe: at idiom token positions, apply logit-lens and trained linear probes to test whether the DOMINANT-language figurative meaning (its answer tokens) is decodable in early/mid layers during foreign-idiom processing, before selection collapses; contrast shared vs culture-specific and vs a monosemous-phrase control. 4. Locate figurative-retrieval/selection stage (core causal test): for a culture-specific idiom, run under a disambiguating context forcing the CORRECT source meaning vs a context forcing the DOMINANT-metaphor meaning, yielding different downstream judgments; activation-patch early/mid-layer components (building on 'Idiom Head' locations) from one run into the other and find the minimal set whose patching flips the selected meaning while preserving idiom identity. Metric: flip rate vs number/location of patched components. 5. Conceptual-metaphor distance dose-response: correlate override rate and probe co-activation with per-idiom/per-language conceptual-metaphor distance vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy). Key dissociation: a low-resource language with SHARED metaphors should be interpreted better than a high-resource language with CULTURE-SPECIFIC ones. Spearman with CIs. 6. Causal steering: extract a conceptual-metaphor direction (mean activation difference between correct-source-meaning and dominant-override runs) at the retrieval layer; (a) steer to REPAIR culture-specific misinterpretations, (b) steer to INDUCE override on shared idioms (proving functional causality). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, interpretation accuracy, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (unrelated items unchanged). Compare to translate-first and explicit-cultural-context-prompt baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep; shared-idiom (lexical-overlap) subset per MultiCoPIE to separate lexical overlap from conceptual-metaphor sharing; model scale; probe transfer across models; whether the competitor is always the dominant language or the typologically-nearest high-resource language. Metrics throughout: interpretation accuracy, override rate, co-decodability rank, causal flip/repair/induction rates, identity preservation, Spearman with conceptual-metaphor distance vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Annotating each idiom's 'underlying conceptual metaphor' and shared-vs-culture-specific labels is subjective; we use Conceptual Metaphor Theory categories, multiple native-speaker annotators, and report inter-annotator agreement, restricting to high-agreement items. 2. Probe co-decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than functional co-activation; the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to establish functional relevance. 3. Override could be confounded with lexical overlap rather than conceptual-metaphor sharing; Exp. 7's shared-lexical subset and Exp. 5's dissociation controls address this. 4. Tokenization fragments multi-word idioms unevenly across scripts; we use last-token-of-idiom or full-span pooled representations and report tokenization statistics. 5. Strong models may resolve context so well that override is rare in disambiguating contexts; weak/neutral-context and induction experiments still yield informative causal results, and multiple languages/models give statistical power. 6. Steering may trade interpretation accuracy for fluency; we report both. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: language_as_temporal_anchor
Title: What Year Is It in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Temporal Anchor for Time-Sensitive Facts in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: For facts whose correct answer changes over time (e.g., current heads of state, champions, populations), the language a question is asked in covertly sets the model's default temporal anchor: the model tends to answer with the fact-state that was dominant in that language's training data era, so different languages return answers 'frozen' at different points in time. We hypothesize (a) a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation exists that determines which fact-version is retrieved; (b) the query language causally sets this anchor, producing systematic per-language recency offsets on time-sensitive facts; and (c) the size of the offset scales with the resource/coverage recency of the language rather than with typological distance, and can be causally corrected by steering the shared temporal-anchor direction without retraining.
Related Work: Parametric Temporal Conflict (Hossain et al. 2026) shows LLMs store both outdated and updated facts and default to the outdated one via a localized upper-layer representational preference, but the study is monolingual (English) and never treats language as a variable. Time Travel Engine (2026) shows a continuous, cross-lingually isomorphic temporal manifold and steers 'zeitgeist', but studies stylistic/era navigation, not factual-recency errors and not the query language's causal role in choosing which factual version is recalled. TiEBe (2025) and LiveCLKTBench (2025) document geographic and language-dependent recall gaps for time-sensitive events, but interpret them as resource/transfer gaps and provide no mechanistic account. EverGreenQA (2025) classifies question mutability but does not study per-language temporal drift. Multilingual knowledge-editing work (MLaKE, XME, LangEdit, LU-LAFNs) treats facts as static and studies edit propagation. None frames the query language as an implicit temporal anchor that selects among stored fact-versions, nor gives causal (patching + steering) evidence for a language-set temporal-anchor variable that produces predictable per-language recency offsets. We contribute this reframing, a quantitative per-language 'temporal offset' metric, and a training-free anchor-steering fix.
Abstract: Many facts have no timeless answer: the head of state, the reigning champion, or a country's population all change over time, and a language model must decide which era's answer to give. We ask whether the language in which a question is posed covertly determines this decision. We hypothesize that the query language acts as an implicit temporal anchor, biasing a multilingual LLM toward the fact-state dominant in that language's training data, so the same question answered in different languages returns answers effectively frozen at different times. We build TIME-DRIFT, a set of time-sensitive facts with dated ground-truth transitions (from Wikidata position-holder changes and dated records), rendered in 12+ languages spanning several scripts and families, and measure a per-language Temporal Offset: how far behind the true current state each language's default answer sits. Mechanistically, we test for a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation using linear probes and vocabulary projection, then use activation patching to test whether swapping late-layer language-identity signals shifts the retrieved fact-version, and whether steering a recovered temporal-anchor direction moves answers forward or backward in time. We predict systematic per-language offsets that scale with a language's data-recency/coverage rather than typological distance, that the offset is causally set by a language-conditioned anchor separable from fact content, and that anchor-steering recovers the current answer in low-recency languages without harming fluency, outperforming date-prefix prompting and translate-to-English baselines. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. The work reframes cross-lingual factual disparities as a controllable temporal-anchoring phenomenon.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (TIME-DRIFT): from Wikidata, extract facts with dated transitions (position-holders: heads of state, club managers, CEO tenures; plus dated records: sports champions, tallest building, world population brackets), each with a full timeline of (value, valid-from, valid-to). Select facts with >=2 transitions within the models' plausible pretraining window. Render each question in 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families, with matched entity names. Compute per-language data-recency/coverage proxies (Wikipedia edit recency for the topic, article length, pretraining-share estimate). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral phenomenon: for each fact, get the model's default answer in each language (greedy, no date cue); map the answer to its valid time-interval using the timeline; define Temporal Offset = (true current date) - (midpoint of the answered value's validity interval). Metrics: mean per-language offset, fraction returning the outdated vs current value, and cross-language answer disagreement rate. Baseline: English/dominant-language offset. 3. Dissociation: correlate per-language Temporal Offset with (i) a language data-recency/coverage proxy and (ii) lang2vec typological/script distance to the dominant language; prediction: offset tracks recency/coverage, not typology (key contrast: a typologically distant but well-covered language vs. a close but sparsely-covered one). Spearman with CIs. 4. Shared temporal-anchor probe: train linear probes and apply logit-lens at mid/late layers to decode, at answer positions, an era/date estimate for the retrieved fact; test whether a single probe (trained on one language) transfers across languages (evidence of a shared anchor representation) and whether the decoded era matches the answered value's date. 5. Causal test A (language sets the anchor): run identical fact in a low-recency language (outdated answer) and dominant language (current answer); activation-patch the late-layer language-identity signal from the dominant run into the low-recency run and measure whether the retrieved fact-version shifts toward current, with fact identity preserved. 6. Causal test B (anchor steering): extract a temporal-anchor direction as the mean activation difference between 'as of [recent year]' and 'as of [older year]' framings (pooled across languages); at inference, steer this direction on low-recency-language queries to move answers forward in time. Metrics: recency-correction rate (fraction flipped to current value), specificity (evergreen/timeless facts unchanged), fluency (perplexity), and output-language fidelity. Compare against date-prefix prompting ('As of 2024, ...') and translate-to-English-first baselines. 7. Reverse control: steer the anchor backward and verify the model returns older, era-appropriate values (dose-response), confirming the direction is functionally temporal, not just a correctness push. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the anchor is malleable; probe transfer across models; fact-type breakdown (positions vs records); model scale; and an evergreen-fact control set that should show near-zero offset and no steerability. Metrics throughout: Temporal Offset, outdated-answer rate, cross-language disagreement, probe/transfer accuracy, patching flip rate, steering correction/induction rate, specificity, fluency, Spearman with recency vs typology.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground-truth 'current' value and exact transition dates can be ambiguous or lag reality; we restrict to Wikidata-verified transitions with clear valid-from/valid-to intervals and exclude contested cases. 2. The observed offset could reflect missing recent knowledge rather than a language-set anchor over co-present versions; the patching (Exp. 5) and the demonstration that date-prefix prompting recovers the current value (as in PTC) test whether newer knowledge is present but not defaulted-to, distinguishing anchoring from ignorance. 3. Probe decodability of era may reflect the readout basis, not a used representation; we require the causal patching and steering results to establish functional relevance. 4. Per-language recency proxies are noisy; we use multiple proxies and report robustness, and the typology-vs-recency dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts. 5. Steering may over-shift and harm evergreen facts; the evergreen control set and specificity/fluency metrics test selectivity. 6. Tokenization/entity-name differences across scripts complicate answer matching; we restrict to entities with clean, matchable answer tokens and use last-token-of-answer representations. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: digraphia_script_language_dissociation
Title: Same Language, Two Scripts: Using Digraphia to Causally Dissociate Script Identity from Language Identity in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: What prior work calls a model's 'language-identity' representation is substantially a *script-identity* representation. Using digraphic languages (one spoken language written in two scripts, e.g. Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Uzbek Latin/Cyrillic, Punjabi Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi, Hindi/Urdu), we hypothesize that (a) script and language are separable, causally-manipulable directions; (b) factual/semantic knowledge stored while reading one script of a digraphic language fails to transfer to the SAME language in its other script far more than the near-identical spoken content warrants, and this failure is a script-binding artifact, not genuine language separation; and (c) a training-free 'latent transliteration' steering (swapping only the script direction) recovers cross-script knowledge without translation.
Related Work: Prior work shows script is linearly encoded and that writing-system identity is what token-embedding geometry captures (Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023), that LLMs latently romanize non-Roman scripts as an intermediate bridge (RomanLens 2025), that script vectors linearly steer output script in speech models (Linear Script Representations 2026), that script similarity dominates cross-lingual knowledge sharing and cross-lingual editing fails across script families (Beneath the Surface 2024; XME 2024), and that transliteration to a common script improves multilingual modeling (Does Transliteration Help 2023; Aksharantar 2022). All of these treat script and language as entangled, or study script effects across *different* languages, where script and language covary. None uses digraphia—the unique natural experiment where language is held constant and only script varies (and where the same script can be shared across different languages)—to causally *dissociate* a script-identity representation from a language-identity representation, nor tests whether cross-script knowledge-transfer failure within one language is a re-bindable script artifact. We contribute this dissociation, a causal script-vs-language localization, and a training-free latent-transliteration fix.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are said to compute in a shared concept space and carry a 'language-identity' variable that governs decoding. But in almost all prior studies, language and script covary, so it is unknown how much of that 'language' variable is really *script*. Digraphic languages—a single spoken language written in two scripts (Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin, Uzbek in Latin and Cyrillic, Punjabi in Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi, Hindi/Urdu)—provide a clean natural experiment: they hold language constant while varying script, and (via shared scripts across languages) hold script constant while varying language. We use them to dissociate a script-identity representation from a language-identity representation. First, we train linear probes and use activation patching to test whether script and language are separable, causally-manipulable directions, and whether the classic 'language vector' is dominated by its script component. Second, we measure within-language cross-script knowledge transfer: a fact taught or queried in one script of a digraphic language should be recoverable in the other script if knowledge is language-shared, but we predict a large script-bound gap, especially where the two scripts are orthographically dissimilar. Third, we localize where script gates retrieval and test a training-free 'latent transliteration'—steering only the script direction—to recover cross-script knowledge, compared against surface transliteration and translation baselines. Experiments span Serbian, Uzbek, Kazakh, Punjabi, Hindi/Urdu, and Sindhi using Dakshina/Aksharantar transliteration resources and mLAMA facts, on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work turns digraphia into a precise instrument for separating what multilingual models know about *languages* from what they know about *scripts*.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: Assemble digraphic parallel data—identical utterances/facts rendered in both scripts of each digraphic language: Serbian (Cyrillic/Latin), Uzbek (Latin/Cyrillic), Kazakh (Cyrillic/Latin), Punjabi (Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi), Hindi/Urdu (Devanagari/Perso-Arabic), Sindhi (Perso-Arabic/Devanagari), using Dakshina and Aksharantar transliteration pairs and transliteration tools for verification. Add cross-language same-script controls (e.g. Serbian-Cyrillic vs Russian-Cyrillic; Uzbek-Latin vs Turkish-Latin) to hold script constant while varying language. Facts from mLAMA/BMLAMA rendered in both scripts. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Separability probing: train linear probes at each layer to decode (i) script identity and (ii) language identity from hidden states, using the digraphic design to decorrelate them. Report per-layer probe accuracy and the cosine angle between the recovered script and language directions; test whether the standard mean-difference 'language vector' projects mostly onto the script direction. 3. Causal dissociation via patching: swap the script-identity signal between a Cyrillic-run and a Latin-run of the SAME Serbian sentence and measure whether output script flips while content/meaning is preserved; independently swap the language-identity signal between same-script different-language runs (Serbian-Cyr vs Russian-Cyr) and measure whether language flips while script is preserved. Metric: independent controllability (flip rate for the targeted attribute, preservation of the other). 4. Within-language cross-script knowledge transfer: (a) query-side—ask the same factual question in each script and measure agreement/accuracy; (b) edit-side—apply a locate-and-edit (ROME/MEMIT) update in one script and test recovery when queried in the other script of the same language. Compare against a same-script paraphrase control (upper bound) and a different-language control (lower bound). Predict a large script-bound gap that exceeds what surface differences justify. 5. Orthographic-distance dose-response: correlate the cross-script gap with an orthographic-dissimilarity index (character-overlap / romanization edit distance between the two scripts) rather than typological distance, since the language is identical. Spearman with CIs; prediction: gap grows with script dissimilarity. 6. Localization: use activation patching / attention attribution to find where script gates factual retrieval (early script-embedding stage vs mid retrieval vs late decoding); test whether restoring the mid-layer concept from the other-script run recovers the fact (concept shared) vs whether failure is at a script-conditioned retrieval gate. 7. Training-free latent transliteration fix: extract a script direction from digraphic pairs; at inference on the low-performing script, steer only the script direction toward the model's stronger script while keeping language fixed, and measure cross-script knowledge recovery, output-script fidelity, and fluency (perplexity). Baselines: surface transliteration-then-query, translate-to-English, and RomanLens-style romanization. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where script is malleable; probe transfer across models; shared-script cross-language control (does steering script alone ever change language?); model scale. Metrics throughout: probe accuracy, script/language direction angle, causal flip/preservation rates, cross-script accuracy gap, edit-propagation across scripts, Spearman with orthographic distance, steering recovery rate, output-script fidelity, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of script vs language may reflect the readout basis; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering recovery (Exp. 7) are required to establish functional relevance. 2. For some digraphic pairs the two scripts share many characters (Serbian) while others do not (Hindi/Urdu), so effect sizes vary; this is exactly the orthographic-distance dose-response (Exp. 5) rather than a confound. 3. Low-resource scripts (Shahmukhi, Sindhi-Devanagari) may have thin pretraining coverage, confounding script-binding with ignorance; we control with same-language same-content items and report coverage proxies. 4. Transliteration ground truth can be noisy for context-dependent scripts (Perso-Arabic vowel omission); we use validated Dakshina/Aksharantar pairs and native-speaker spot-checks. 5. Tokenization differs sharply across scripts, complicating representation alignment; we use last-token / pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. Steering may trade knowledge recovery for fluency or accidentally change language; the shared-script control (Exp. 8) and fidelity/fluency metrics test selectivity. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: evidential_source_binding
Title: How Do You Know? A Causal Study of the Abstract Information-Source Representation and Its Binding to Evidential Grammar in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic representation of the SOURCE of a piece of information (first-hand perception vs. hearsay/report vs. inference), stored separately from surface evidential morphology. In languages that grammatically force an evidential marker (Turkish, Bulgarian, Quechua, Tibetan), the model reads this source variable off via a late-layer binding step; and critically the same source variable causally governs the model's EXPRESSED CERTAINTY. We hypothesize (a) an abstract source-of-information direction decodable across languages including evidentiality-free ones like English; (b) that evidential-marking errors in obligatory-evidential languages are a binding failure that lazily inherits the source implied by the input/query language; and (c) that the shared source variable causally modulates downstream confidence, so mis-binding source produces miscalibrated certainty and hallucination-style errors, correctable by steering the shared direction.
Related Work: Linguistics establishes evidentiality as grammaticalized marking of information source, tightly linked to shared conceptual representations of knowledge sources across speakers (Relations Between Language and Cognition 2018; Aikhenvald typology; semantic-map work 2010-2020). Interpretability work shows multilingual models compute in a shared concept space with late-layer language decoding and that consistency failures arise at the transition (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025), that grammatical concepts share cross-lingual directions (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), and that linguistic uncertainty/epistemic cues are progressively encoded in deeper layers (Mapping Clinical Doubt 2025). However, all evidentiality work is descriptive-linguistic or behavioral; interpretability work on uncertainty studies input-side epistemic MODALS in English, and multilingual mechanistic work targets factual content, gender, tense, or register. None (i) isolates an abstract, language-agnostic SOURCE-of-information variable, (ii) studies its late-layer binding onto obligatory evidential grammar, or (iii) causally links this source variable to the model's expressed certainty and calibration. We uniquely use evidential-marking typology as a controlled probe of the shared-vs-specific epistemic representation, give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a source-binding step, and connect it to the safety-critical problem of miscalibrated confidence.
Abstract: Languages differ starkly in how they encode where information comes from. Turkish, Bulgarian, Quechua, and Tibetan grammatically force speakers to mark whether a statement is based on first-hand perception, hearsay, or inference; English leaves this to optional lexical hedges. Any competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract information source and, in evidential languages, commit to a grammatical marker. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this source-of-information variable, how they bind it to evidential grammar, and—crucially—whether the same variable governs the model's expressed certainty. We distinguish an abstract, language-agnostic source variable (perception / report / inference, present regardless of grammatical marking) from surface evidential morphology. Using parallel statements whose information source is fixed by context across evidential and non-evidential languages, we train linear probes and localize where source is encoded and where it is bound to grammar. We predict (1) the abstract source direction is decodable across languages, including English; (2) evidential-marking errors in obligatory-evidential languages stem from a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the source implied by the query language; and (3) the shared source variable causally modulates downstream confidence, so mis-binding produces miscalibrated certainty and hallucination-style errors. We test binding via activation patching and repair errors by steering the shared source direction, measuring restored marking correctness and calibration without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages. The work gives the first mechanistic, controllable account of information-source representation in multilingual LLMs and ties it to trustworthiness.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli: build parallel statements whose INFORMATION SOURCE is unambiguously fixed by context in one of three categories—direct perception ('I saw...'), reportative/hearsay ('they say...'), and inference ('judging by X, it must have...'). Render each in 10+ languages spanning three evidential-grammar types: OBLIGATORY-EVIDENTIAL (Turkish -mIş vs direct, Bulgarian renarrative, Quechua, Tibetan), OPTIONAL/LEXICAL (English, German, Spanish—hedges but no grammatical marker), and a mixed/partial set. Also include a bare-context variant where source must be inferred and an explicit-context variant. Annotate correct evidential marker/source per item (native-speaker validation) and a per-language evidential-grammaticalization index (obligatory verbal marking > particle/auxiliary > lexical-only). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral source-marking baseline: generate continuations/reformulations in each language; measure whether produced evidential marking matches the context-mandated source; report source-marking error rate by language type, context strength, and whether the query/framing language matches the generation language. 3. Abstract-source probe: train linear probes at each layer to decode the information-source category from mid-layer hidden states on held-out items; show it is decodable in non-evidential languages (English/German) too and that a probe trained on one language transfers cross-lingually (shared source direction). Contrast with a surface-morphology probe (which marker appears) to establish the abstract-vs-surface dissociation. 4. Locate the source-binding step (core causal test): run identical items under context forcing DIRECT vs REPORTATIVE source in an obligatory-evidential language, producing different markers; activation-patch late-layer components from the direct run into the reportative run and find the minimal set whose patching flips the produced marker while preserving message content. Metric: marker-flip rate vs number/location of patched components. 5. Lazy-inheritance test: hold the target generation language fixed (e.g., Turkish) but vary the framing/input language (English direct framing vs. Turkish reportative context); measure how often output marking matches the input-language-implied source rather than the context-mandated source; predict strongest inheritance when generating obligatory-evidential languages from non-evidential input languages. 6. Grammaticalization dose-response: correlate source-marking error and inheritance rate with the evidential-grammaticalization index vs a resource-level proxy; key dissociation: non-evidential high-resource English vs evidential lower-resource Quechua/Tibetan. Spearman with CIs. 7. Source-to-certainty causal link (the trustworthiness core): on factual QA and NLI where the model must judge how confident to be given a stated source (e.g., hearsay should lower confidence), measure whether the located source variable causally drives expressed certainty: steer the shared source direction from 'direct' toward 'reportative/inference' and measure the shift in the model's expressed confidence (verbalized probability and answer-token logit) and calibration (ECE) on items with known ground truth. Predict that mis-bound source (e.g., treating hearsay as direct perception) inflates confidence and increases hallucination-style errors. 8. Causal steering repair: extract a shared source direction (mean activation difference across sources, pooled across languages) at the binding layer; on mis-marked items, steer toward the correct source and measure marking-repair rate and calibration improvement; in bare context, steer to induce a wrong source (proving functional causality). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, marker correctness, ECE change, content preservation, fluency (perplexity), specificity. Compare against explicit source-instruction prompting and translate-context-first baselines. 9. Ablations: layer sweep for where source is malleable; probe transfer across models; perception vs report vs inference separability; whether evidential languages recruit extra late components tied to verb-ending tokens; model scale. Metrics throughout: source-marking error rate, inheritance rate, probe accuracy, cross-lingual probe transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, source-driven confidence shift, ECE, content preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of abstract source may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used variable; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4), the source-to-certainty steering (Exp. 7), and the steering repair/induction (Exp. 8) to establish functional relevance. 2. Ground-truth source in bare-context items can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated items with high inter-annotator agreement. 3. Separating abstract source from surface morphology is hard in obligatory-evidential languages where they nearly coincide; the non-evidential languages and bare-context condition are the crucial dissociating cases. 4. Low-resource evidential languages (Quechua, Tibetan) may have thin pretraining coverage, confounding binding failure with ignorance; we control with same-content items across languages and report coverage proxies, and Turkish/Bulgarian provide higher-resource evidential anchors. 5. The source-to-certainty link may be weak if the model ignores stated source when judging confidence; even documenting this (a calibration blind spot) is a valuable, safety-relevant finding. 6. Tokenization of evidential verb endings varies across languages; we use verb-final/reply-final or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics; obligatory vs particle vs lexical cases analyzed separately. 7. Steering may trade marking correctness or calibration for fluency; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: spatial_frame_of_reference_default
Title: Left of the Tree or North of the Tree? How the Query Language Sets a Default Spatial Frame of Reference in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Human languages default to different spatial frames of reference (FoR) - egocentric-relative (English, Dutch), object-intrinsic, or geocentric-absolute/cardinal (Guugu Yimithirr, Tzeltal, some Tamil/Balinese conventions). We hypothesize that (a) a multilingual LLM builds an abstract, language-agnostic spatial-relation representation, but (b) the query language covertly sets a DEFAULT frame of reference that is applied when a spatial description is ambiguous, so the SAME ambiguous scene ('the ball is left/front of the tree', 'X is beyond Y') is resolved differently depending on the query language; (c) this frame default is carried by a small, causally-manipulable 'frame-register' representation separable from the underspecified spatial content; and (d) the strength with which a language imposes its default (overriding explicit frame cues) scales with how strongly that language grammaticalizes/conventionalizes a single FoR, not with resource level, and can be repaired by steering the recovered frame direction.
Related Work: The Levinson/Pederson semantic-typology program (Semantic Typology and Spatial Conceptualization 1998; 527 cites) established that languages systematically differ in default frame of reference (relative/intrinsic/absolute), and that a community's non-linguistic cognitive frame correlates with its linguistic one - a foundational linguistic-relativity result. A computational Sapir-Whorf study (2016) modeled spatial-relation naming across five languages. On the model side, COMFORT (2024) shows VLMs are behaviorally inconsistent about frames of reference and default to English conventions, but it is a purely behavioral VLM benchmark with no mechanistic account. Interpretability work shows LLMs encode linear spatial world models and space/time directions (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Linear Spatial World Models 2025; More than Correlation 2023), and that multilingual models have orthogonal language-sensitive vs language-neutral axes (Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022). None of these (i) studies frame of reference (the interpretive coordinate system), as opposed to absolute geolocation or object position; (ii) tests whether the QUERY LANGUAGE sets a default FoR that biases resolution of ambiguous spatial descriptions in a text LLM; or (iii) provides a causal, steerable 'frame-register' representation. We uniquely port the classic FoR typology into multilingual text LLMs and give a causal, controllable mechanistic account.
Abstract: When someone says 'the cat is to the left of the tree', the meaning depends on an unstated coordinate system: is 'left' from the speaker's viewpoint (relative), the tree's intrinsic sides (intrinsic), or a cardinal direction (absolute)? A classic result in cognitive linguistics is that languages default to different frames of reference, and this default shapes how speakers interpret and remember space. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit these language-specific spatial defaults. We hypothesize that a model computes an abstract, underspecified spatial relation but resolves its ambiguity using a frame of reference that is covertly set by the query language, so the identical ambiguous scene is interpreted differently across languages. We construct FRAME-SPACE, a controlled set of spatial-description items with (i) frame-ambiguous versions whose truth value flips depending on the assumed frame, and (ii) frame-forcing versions with explicit relative/intrinsic/absolute cues, rendered across 12+ languages spanning relative-default, intrinsic-favoring, and absolute/cardinal-favoring conventions. Behaviorally, we measure per-language frame-choice distributions and how often the query language overrides an explicit frame cue. Mechanistically, we probe for an abstract spatial-relation direction shared across languages, then use activation patching to localize a compact frame-register whose swap flips the interpretation without changing the spatial content, and steer a recovered frame direction to repair or induce frame choices. We predict frame-override strength tracks a language's frame-conventionalization index rather than resource level. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. The work ports spatial frame-of-reference typology into mechanistic interpretability and yields a controllable account of a linguistic-relativity effect in LLMs.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (FRAME-SPACE): build spatial-description items over simple scenes (an agent/observer, a landmark object with clear intrinsic sides like a car/person/house, and a target object). For each scene create: (a) FRAME-AMBIGUOUS descriptions using projective terms ('left', 'in front of', 'behind', 'beyond') whose truth depends on frame, paired with a question whose correct answer differs under relative vs intrinsic vs absolute frames; (b) FRAME-FORCING variants adding explicit cues ('from where you are standing' -> relative; 'the car's own front' -> intrinsic; 'to the north of' -> absolute). Render each in 12+ languages spanning RELATIVE-default (English, Dutch, German, Japanese), INTRINSIC-favoring / mixed (Spanish, Mandarin, Hausa), and ABSOLUTE/cardinal-favoring conventions (Tamil, Balinese, Guugu Yimithirr-style constructed items, plus a cardinal-heavy register). Native-speaker-validate canonical/default frame per language and construct a per-language frame-conventionalization index (degree to which one frame is obligatory/preferred). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral default & override tests: (i) On ambiguous items, elicit the model's interpretation (multiple-choice over frame-consistent answers) per language; report per-language frame-choice distribution and cross-language disagreement rate on identical scenes. (ii) Override test: give an explicit frame cue that CONFLICTS with the query language's default and measure how often the output follows the language default vs the explicit cue (frame-override rate). Baselines: query in English (relative anchor) and translate-to-English-first. 3. Abstract-relation probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode the underspecified projective relation (e.g., 'left-type' relation) and, separately, the resolved frame; show the relation is decodable and cross-lingually transferable while the resolved frame is what varies. Establish a relation-vs-frame dissociation. 4. Locate the frame-register (core causal test): run identical ambiguous items under context forcing RELATIVE vs ABSOLUTE (or intrinsic) interpretation, yielding different answers; activation-patch mid-layer components from one run into the other and find the minimal set whose patching flips the frame-resolved answer while preserving the scene/relation content. Metric: frame-flip rate vs number/location of patched components; content-preservation check. 5. Conventionalization dose-response: correlate frame-override rate and default-strength with the per-language frame-conventionalization index vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy). Key dissociation: a lower-resource strongly-absolute language should impose its frame more than a higher-resource mixed language. Spearman with CIs. 6. Causal steering: extract a frame direction (mean activation difference between relative-forced and absolute/intrinsic-forced runs, pooled across languages) at the frame-register layer; (a) steer to REPAIR mis-framed interpretations (make a cardinal-language query resolve relatively when context demands), (b) steer to INDUCE a non-default frame in a language where it was not chosen (functional-causality proof). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, interpretation accuracy under explicit context, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (non-spatial items unchanged). Compare against explicit frame-instruction prompting and translate-first baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where frame is malleable; probe transfer across models; separability of the frame-register from language-identity and from absolute-geolocation directions (compute overlap with prior space directions); a frame-UNambiguous spatial control set (should show no flippable register); model scale. Metrics throughout: frame-choice distribution, cross-language disagreement, frame-override rate, relation vs frame probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with conventionalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Annotating each language's default frame and building a conventionalization index is subjective and some languages are mixed; we ground labels in the established typology literature, use multiple native-speaker annotators, restrict to high-agreement items, and report robustness to index operationalization. 2. Probe decodability of an abstract relation/frame may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 3. Frame preference could be confounded with translation artifacts of projective terms across languages; the frame-forcing and override conditions and native-speaker validation isolate the default from mere translation. 4. Strong models may collapse to a single (English-relative) frame regardless of query language, weakening cross-language variation; even documenting this near-universal English-relative default and its resistance to explicit cues is a valuable linguistic-relativity finding, and multiple models/languages give power. 5. Constructed items for very-low-resource absolute languages (e.g., Guugu Yimithirr) may have thin coverage, confounding frame-imposition with ignorance; we include higher-resource absolute/cardinal registers (Tamil, cardinal-heavy phrasing) and control with same-scene items. 6. Tokenization of projective/cardinal terms varies across scripts; we use pooled-span or last-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade frame correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: negative_concord_polarity_flip
Title: Nobody Didn't Get Sick: How the Query Language's Negation Grammar Covertly Flips the Truth Value of Stacked Negations in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Languages split into Negative Concord (NC: multiple negatives = one negation, e.g. Spanish/Italian/Russian) and Double Negation (DN: two negatives cancel, e.g. formal English/Mandarin). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM computes a shared, language-agnostic truth-conditional polarity representation but that, when a sentence contains multiple negation cues, the query language covertly sets a DEFAULT resolution rule (NC vs DN) that is applied to interpretation. Consequently the SAME multiply-negated proposition is assigned OPPOSITE truth values depending on the query language; this flip is carried by a small, causally-manipulable 'polarity-resolution' representation separable from the propositional content, its strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes negative concord (not with resource level), and it is most dangerous—producing safety-critical instruction inversions—when the model must act on multiply-negated commands.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows negation scope is carried by identifiable attention heads (Kim & Linzen-style 2020 BERT negation-scope analysis), that negation/passivization leave removable representational imprints (Controlling the Imprint, INLP 2020), that LMs form 'strong hallucinations' from negation because latent operators don't respect logic (Strong Hallucinations 2024), that NPI licensing and grammatical illusions mirror humans (NPI in BERT 2023; LSTM NPI 2018), and that negation instructions cause ironic rebound via middle-layer heads (White Bear 2025). Linguistic typology firmly establishes the NC-vs-DN macroparameter and its unclear-at-the-margins interpretation (Zeijlstra 2016; de Swart 2010; Mandarin vs Spanish negation 2023; quantifier-negation scope in bilinguals 2024). However: (i) all interpretability negation work is monolingual (mostly English) and studies scope or single-negation logic, never the cross-lingual NC/DN resolution of MULTIPLE negatives; (ii) all NC/DN work is descriptive-linguistic or behavioral, with no mechanistic account inside an LLM; and (iii) none frames the query language as a covert default that flips a truth value, nor tests the safety consequence of inverted multiply-negated instructions. We uniquely port the NC/DN typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a polarity-resolution representation, and transfer the phenomenon into a safety-critical instruction-following domain.
Abstract: In many languages two negatives make a negative: Spanish 'no vino nadie' (literally 'not came nobody') simply means 'nobody came'. In formal English and Mandarin, two negatives cancel to an affirmative. These are the classic Negative Concord (NC) and Double Negation (DN) types of the world's languages. A competent multilingual model reading a multiply-negated sentence must recover its actual truth value—but which rule does it apply, and does the language it is asked in decide for it? We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared truth-conditional polarity but resolve multiple negatives using a default rule covertly set by the query language, so the identical proposition is judged true in one language and false in another. We build POLARITY-FLIP, controlled minimal pairs with one, two, and three negation cues whose truth value differs under NC vs DN resolution, rendered across 12+ languages spanning strongly-NC, DN, and mixed types, plus a safety-critical subset of multiply-negated instructions (medical/lab/legal) where a flip inverts the required action. Behaviorally we measure per-language truth-value assignment and instruction-inversion rate. Mechanistically we probe for a shared polarity direction, use activation patching to localize a compact polarity-resolution representation whose swap flips the judgment without altering content, and steer a recovered polarity direction to repair or induce flips. We predict flip strength tracks a language's negative-concord grammaticalization index, not its resource level, and that steering repairs safety-critical inversions without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (POLARITY-FLIP): construct minimal-pair propositions with 1, 2, and 3 negation cues (sentential negator + negative indefinites like nobody/nothing/never), each paired with a yes/no truth-value question or an NLI hypothesis whose correct answer differs under NC vs DN resolution. Render in 12+ languages spanning STRONG-NC (Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Polish, Greek), DN/no-concord (formal English, Mandarin, Japanese, German-standard), and MIXED/optional (French 'ne...pas', Afrikaans). For NC languages the ground-truth is single-negation; for DN, cancellation. Add a SAFETY subset: multiply-negated instructions in medical/lab/legal register ('do not fail to withhold the second dose unless...') where NC-vs-DN resolution inverts the required action, with an unambiguous single-negation control paraphrase. Native-speaker-validate the canonical resolution per language and build a per-language negative-concord grammaticalization index (obligatory concord > optional > absent). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral flip test: elicit truth-value/NLI judgments per language on identical propositions; report per-language truth-value distribution, cross-language DISAGREEMENT rate on the same proposition, and how disagreement grows from 1 to 2 to 3 cues. Baselines: single-negation control (should agree across languages) and query-in-English. 3. Safety-inversion test: on the instruction subset, measure INSTRUCTION-INVERSION rate (model prescribes the opposite of the correct action) per language and register, versus the single-negation control; quantify the disproportionate risk. 4. Shared-polarity probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode the resolved truth-value polarity of the proposition from hidden states on held-out items; test whether a probe trained on one language transfers cross-lingually (shared polarity direction) while the RESOLVED value is what varies with query language. Contrast with a surface-cue-count probe to dissociate abstract polarity from raw negator count. 5. Locate the polarity-resolution representation (core causal test): run the identical multiply-negated item under a context/framing forcing NC resolution vs DN resolution, yielding opposite judgments; activation-patch mid/late-layer components from one run into the other and find the minimal set whose patching FLIPS the truth-value judgment while preserving propositional content. Report flip rate vs number/location of patched components and a content-preservation check. 6. Grammaticalization dose-response: correlate per-language flip/disagreement rate with the negative-concord grammaticalization index vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy). Key dissociation: a lower-resource strong-NC language (e.g. Polish) should flip more than a higher-resource DN language. Spearman with CIs. 7. Causal steering repair/induction: extract a polarity-resolution direction (mean activation difference between NC-forced and DN-forced runs, pooled across languages) at the resolution layer; (a) steer to REPAIR flipped safety instructions (restore correct action) and (b) steer to INDUCE a flip where the model was correct (functional-causality proof). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, truth-value/instruction accuracy, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (single-negation and non-negated items unchanged). Compare against explicit disambiguation prompting ('interpret two negatives as cancelling') and translate-to-English-first baselines. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where polarity is malleable; probe transfer across models; separability of the polarity-resolution representation from the negation-scope heads reported in prior work (overlap analysis); effect of cue distance (adjacent vs long-distance negators); model scale. Metrics throughout: truth-value distribution, cross-language disagreement, instruction-inversion rate, polarity probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of resolved polarity may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 7) to establish functional relevance. 2. Even within NC/DN languages, native interpretation of stacked negatives can be prosody/context-dependent and genuinely ambiguous (as the Mandarin-Spanish 2023 study notes); we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and treat mixed languages as a separate class rather than forcing a binary. 3. The flip could be confounded with translation artifacts of negative indefinites across languages; single-negation controls and the cross-language agreement they should show isolate the concord effect from mere translation noise. 4. Strong models may collapse to one default rule (likely DN/English) regardless of query language, weakening cross-language variation; even documenting a near-universal English-DN default that resists explicit NC instructions, and its safety consequences, is a valuable finding, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of negators/negative indefinites varies across scripts; we use pooled-span or clause-final token representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The grammaticalization-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to index operationalization and alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade polarity correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: classifier_carved_categories
Title: One Long Thin Thing: How Numeral-Classifier Systems Covertly Carve the Concept Space of Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Numeral-classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Vietnamese) group nouns into shape/animacy/function-based categories (a 'long-thin' classifier for pens, roads, rivers). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-agnostic conceptual-category representation shaped by its dominant classifier language, and that (a) when asked to supply a classifier in a target classifier-language, it lazily inherits the dominant language's classifier boundaries, mis-classifying nouns whose category differs across classifier languages; and, more strikingly, (b) this classifier-induced category structure covertly biases genuinely semantic judgments (noun similarity, object grouping) even when the query and output are in classifier-FREE languages like English, and (c) both effects scale with cross-linguistic classifier-boundary divergence, not with resource level, and are carried by a locatable, causally-steerable 'classifier-category' representation.
Related Work: Cognitive-linguistics and typology establish numeral classifiers as noun-categorization devices carving the lexicon by shape/animacy/function (Aikhenvald 2000; the World Atlas of Classifier Languages 2022; gender-vs-classifier trade-offs 2019), and model classifier categories as radial/exemplar-based, extending by semantic chaining (Habibi, Kemp & Xu, Cognition 2020). Interpretability work shows multilingual models share cross-lingual circuits for grammatical processes (subject-verb agreement, grammatical number) via language-independent directions (Same But Different 2024; Similarity of Circuits 2024; Probing for Usage of Grammatical Number 2022) and share/split morphosyntactic neurons across languages (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; Causal Analysis of Agreement Neurons 2022). However, ALL prior mechanistic work targets agreement features (number, gender, person) whose values are grammatically forced and semantically thin; NONE studies numeral classifiers, which are unique in that their assignment reflects a language-specific CONCEPTUAL categorization of the noun's referent (shape/animacy/function). No work asks whether classifier systems leak across languages, whether the model's classifier assignment carves a shared concept space, or whether this carving covertly biases downstream SEMANTIC judgments in classifier-free languages (a Whorfian effect). We uniquely port classifier typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability and give a causal, steerable account plus a training-free fix.
Abstract: In hundreds of languages, counting a noun requires a numeral classifier that reflects a culturally-shaped categorization of the noun's referent: Mandarin uses tiao for long, thin, flexible things (roads, rivers, fish, pants), and languages disagree on where these category boundaries fall. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs internalize classifier systems as a genuine conceptual carving of their noun space, and whether that carving leaks across languages and contaminates non-classifier semantic reasoning. We hypothesize that a model builds a shared classifier-category representation dominated by its highest-resource classifier language, causing two effects: (1) when generating a classifier in a target classifier-language, the model lazily inherits the dominant language's category boundaries, mis-assigning classifiers for nouns whose category differs cross-linguistically; and (2) more strikingly, the same category structure covertly biases genuinely semantic judgments (noun similarity ratings, 'which two objects go together') even when queried entirely in classifier-free English, so English-language judgments of unrelated objects are pulled together merely because they share a classifier in the model's dominant classifier language. We build CLASSIFIER-CARVE from the World Atlas of Classifier Languages and native-validated classifier assignments across Mandarin, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese, plus classifier-neutral controls. Behaviorally we measure classifier accuracy, cross-lingual inheritance rate, and the classifier bias on English similarity judgments. Mechanistically we probe for a shared classifier-category direction, use activation patching to localize a compact category representation whose swap flips both the classifier and the similarity judgment, and steer it to repair mis-assignments and remove the English-language bias without harming fluency. We predict effects scale with classifier-boundary divergence, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (CLASSIFIER-CARVE): from the World Atlas of Classifier Languages and native-speaker-validated dictionaries, assemble ~400 concrete nouns with their canonical numeral classifiers in Mandarin, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese; annotate each classifier's semantic basis (shape: long-thin/flat/round; animacy; function). Crucially identify DIVERGENT nouns (same referent, different classifier category across these languages, e.g. items that are 'long-thin' in one but not another) vs. CONVERGENT nouns (same category everywhere), and build cross-language classifier-boundary divergence scores. Add classifier-free control languages (English, German). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral classifier accuracy & inheritance: prompt the model to count each noun in each classifier language ('two ___ [noun]'); measure classifier accuracy against the target language's ground truth, and INHERITANCE RATE = fraction of errors on divergent nouns where the produced classifier matches the model's dominant classifier language's category rather than the target language's. Baselines: monolingual-native accuracy per language, convergent-noun control (should be high everywhere). 3. Whorfian semantic-bias test (the striking effect): ENTIRELY in classifier-free English, pose (a) pairwise noun-similarity ratings and (b) odd-one-out / 'which two go together' over triples. Test whether pairs/groups that SHARE a classifier in the dominant classifier language are judged more similar/grouped together than matched pairs that do not, controlling for embedding/co-occurrence similarity. Metric: classifier-congruent bias in English judgments (effect size beyond baseline semantic similarity); contrast against native-English speaker norms and against convergent controls. 4. Shared classifier-category probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode a noun's classifier category from mid-layer hidden states (on held-out nouns), from prompts in classifier languages AND in English; test whether an English-prompt probe recovers the dominant-language classifier category (evidence the carving is present even without classifiers) and whether a probe trained on one language transfers cross-lingually. 5. Locate the classifier-category representation (core causal test): for a divergent noun, run under contexts forcing category A vs category B (yielding different classifiers), activation-patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run, and find the minimal set whose patching flips the produced classifier while preserving noun identity; then test the SAME patched components flip the English similarity judgment (linking the two effects to one representation). Metric: classifier-flip rate and similarity-judgment-flip rate vs. patched components; identity preservation. 6. Divergence dose-response: correlate inheritance rate, English-bias magnitude, and probe cross-lingual disagreement with the classifier-boundary divergence score vs. a resource-level proxy; key dissociation, e.g. a lower-resource classifier language with divergent boundaries vs. a higher-resource one. Spearman with CIs. 7. Causal steering fix: extract a classifier-category direction (mean activation difference between category A and B, pooled across languages); (a) steer to REPAIR classifier mis-assignments in target languages, (b) steer to REMOVE the classifier-congruent bias from English similarity judgments (restoring native-English norms), and (c) steer to INDUCE a spurious grouping bias in a classifier-free language (functional-causality proof). Metrics: repair rate, bias-removal (return to English-norm), induction rate, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (non-noun items unchanged). Compare against explicit-instruction prompting and translate-to-English baselines. 8. Ablations: layer sweep; probe transfer across models; separability of the classifier-category direction from grammatical-number and gender directions (overlap analysis); shape vs animacy vs function subcategory separability; model scale. Metrics throughout: classifier accuracy, inheritance rate, English classifier-congruent bias effect size, probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, similarity-judgment flip, identity preservation, Spearman with divergence vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of classifier category may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 5) and the steering repair/removal/induction (Exp. 7) to establish functional relevance, and crucially require the SAME components to drive both the classifier and the English similarity judgment. 2. Classifier assignment is sometimes optional, register-dependent, or has multiple acceptable choices; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and treat multi-classifier nouns separately. 3. The English semantic-bias effect could be confounded with genuine semantic/co-occurrence similarity (classifiers often track real semantic classes); we explicitly control for embedding and corpus co-occurrence similarity, use divergent nouns where the classifier grouping conflicts with dominant semantic similarity, and compare against convergent controls and native-English norms. 4. Strong models may fully abstract classifiers away, making the English bias negligible; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely clean concept space) is an informative result, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of nouns/classifiers varies across scripts; we use last-token-of-noun or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The divergence-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to divergence-score operationalization. 7. Steering may trade classifier correctness or bias removal for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: thematic_role_cue_dominance
Title: Who Did What to Whom, in Which Language? How Multilingual LLMs Lazily Impose Their Dominant Language's Word-Order Cue When Assigning Agent and Patient
