Short Hypothesis: Human languages weight cues to thematic roles differently: some are word-order-dominant (English), others rely primarily on case marking (Russian, Hindi, Turkish, German) or voice (Tagalog). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-agnostic agent/patient (who-did-what-to-whom) representation, but that when a sentence's cues conflict it lazily applies its DOMINANT language's word-order-first cue hierarchy rather than the target language's, producing systematic agent/patient REVERSALS precisely in case-/voice-dominant languages when the reliable cue (case/voice) contradicts a non-canonical word order. We predict (a) reversal rate scales with the target language's reliance on non-word-order cues (its cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language), not with resource level; (b) a small, causally-manipulable 'role-binding' representation carries the assigned agent/patient; and (c) steering a recovered role direction repairs (or induces) reversals without changing propositional content.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows LLMs extract thematic roles mainly through a few attention heads, with role information weakly present in representations relative to humans (Do LLMs Know Who Did What to Whom, 2025), and that English models recruit word order in later layers to override lexical cues in non-prototypical sentences (BERT word order, 2022; Position-Role Mappings, 2022). Multilingual probing shows mBERT encodes morphosyntactic alignment/subjecthood continuously (Deep Subjecthood, 2021) and shares some syntactic subspaces (Universal Grammatical Relations, 2020), though grammatical transfer is limited and language-specific (Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer, 2020; Blackbird 2024). Cognitive science establishes a universal agent-first bias and the Competition Model's language-specific cue hierarchy (word order vs. case vs. animacy vs. voice) that determines role assignment (MacWhinney; agent-first 2019; Tagalog acquisition 2018-2019; agent-preference ERP 2023). However, ALL interpretability work on roles is either monolingual-English or studies static-encoder representations; NONE tests whether a multilingual GENERATIVE LLM covertly imports its dominant language's CUE HIERARCHY into other languages, causing role reversals when a reliable non-word-order cue conflicts with word order, nor gives a causal, steerable role-binding locus. We uniquely port the Competition Model cue-hierarchy conflict into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, with a causal account and a training-free fix.
Abstract: Understanding a sentence requires deciding who acted on whom. Languages solve this with different, sometimes conflicting cues: English relies on word order (the first noun is the agent), while Russian, Hindi, Turkish, and German rely on case marking and Tagalog on voice, so that a non-canonical word order does not change the agent. When these cues conflict, each language has a reliable arbiter. We ask whether multilingual LLMs, whose dominant pretraining language is word-order-based, covertly import a word-order-first cue hierarchy into other languages and thereby reverse agent and patient exactly when a case-/voice-dominant language marks a non-canonical order. We build ROLE-CONFLICT, a controlled set of reversible transitive sentences crossing word order (canonical vs. scrambled), the reliable cue (case/voice present vs. absent), and animacy, rendered across word-order-dominant, case-dominant, and voice-dominant languages, each with a question probing who the agent is. Behaviorally we measure per-language reversal rate under cue conflict. Mechanistically we (i) probe for an abstract agent/patient direction shared across languages, (ii) use activation patching to localize a compact role-binding representation whose swap flips the assigned roles without changing the event or entities, and (iii) steer a recovered role direction to repair or induce reversals. We predict reversal rate tracks a language's cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language rather than its resource level, that some attention heads implement cue arbitration, and that steering repairs reversals without harming fluency, outperforming explicit-instruction and translate-to-English baselines. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (ROLE-CONFLICT): construct reversible transitive events (two plausible-either-way animate participants, e.g. 'the doctor'/'the lawyer', plus verb) so lexical/plausibility cues do not decide the roles. For each event build a factorial set crossing: (a) WORD ORDER = canonical vs. non-canonical/scrambled; (b) RELIABLE CUE = present vs. neutralized (overt case marking or voice morphology that unambiguously assigns roles, vs. a variant where that cue is absent/ambiguous); (c) ANIMACY (both animate = maximally reversible; animate-vs-inanimate control). Render across languages spanning three cue-hierarchy types: WORD-ORDER-DOMINANT (English, Chinese, Indonesian), CASE-DOMINANT (Russian, German, Hindi, Turkish, Finnish), and VOICE-DOMINANT (Tagalog, plus a symmetrical-voice control). Attach a probe question ('Who did the [action]?' / 'Who was affected?'). Native-speaker-validate the correct agent per item and build a per-language cue-hierarchy index (degree of reliance on non-word-order cues). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral reversal test: elicit agent/patient assignment per item; the KEY condition is cue conflict (non-canonical word order WITH a reliable case/voice cue that assigns the agent to the later noun). Metric: REVERSAL RATE = fraction where the model picks the word-order-implied noun (first) as agent, contradicting the reliable cue. Controls: canonical order (should be correct everywhere) and animate-inanimate (plausibility resolves). Baselines: English query, translate-to-English-first. 3. Cue-hierarchy dose-response: correlate per-language reversal rate with the cue-hierarchy index vs. a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy). Key dissociation: a lower-resource strongly-case-marking language (e.g. Turkish/Finnish) should reverse LESS if the model respects case, or MORE if it lazily uses word order, versus a higher-resource word-order language; the prediction is that reversals track cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language, not resource. Spearman with CIs. 4. Shared agent/patient probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode which entity is the assigned agent from hidden states on held-out items; test cross-lingual probe transfer (train on one language, test on others) to establish a shared role representation, and contrast with a surface-position probe (which noun is first) to dissociate abstract role from raw position. 5. Locate the role-binding representation (core causal test): for a cue-conflict item, run under a context/framing forcing role assignment A (entity X = agent) vs. B (entity Y = agent), yielding different answers; activation-patch mid/late-layer components from the A-run into the B-run and find the minimal set whose patching flips the assigned agent while preserving the event and entities. Also test attention-head attribution to identify cue-arbitration heads (do specific heads read case/voice morphology vs. position?). Metric: role-flip rate vs. number/location of patched components; content-preservation check. 6. Causal steering repair/induction: extract a role direction (mean activation difference between agent=X and agent=Y runs, pooled across languages) at the binding layer; (a) steer to REPAIR reversals in case-/voice-dominant languages (restore the cue-correct agent), and (b) steer to INDUCE a reversal where the model was correct (functional-causality proof). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, agent-assignment accuracy, output fluency (perplexity), specificity (canonical-order and non-role items unchanged). Compare against explicit-instruction prompting ('the case marker, not word order, determines the agent') and translate-to-English baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where role is malleable; probe transfer across models; separability of the role-binding representation from generic subject/first-position directions (overlap analysis); adjacent vs. long-distance argument scrambling; whether the imposed hierarchy is always the dominant (word-order) language or the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Metrics throughout: reversal rate, agent-assignment accuracy, probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with cue-hierarchy vs. resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of the assigned agent may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance, and contrast against a surface-position probe. 2. Some case-/voice-dominant languages permit multiple acceptable readings or have optional case marking, making 'reversal' genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items where the reliable cue unambiguously fixes the agent, and treat optional-marking cases separately. 3. Reversals could be confounded with degraded fluency/parsing of scrambled sentences rather than a cue-hierarchy import; the canonical-order and animate-inanimate controls, plus the requirement that the reliable cue is clearly present, isolate cue arbitration from mere degradation. 4. Strong models may respect case/voice well, making reversals rare; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely cue-faithful role system) is an informative positive result, and the voice-dominant and long-distance-scramble conditions plus induction experiments still yield causal findings; multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of case/voice morphology varies across scripts and can split affixes unevenly; we use pooled-span or noun-final token representations and report tokenization statistics; case vs. voice vs. word-order cases analyzed separately. 6. The cue-hierarchy-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to index operationalization and alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade role correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: functional_code_switching
Title: Let It Switch: Code-Switching as a Functional Resource, Not a Bug, in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Contrary to the prevailing view that code-switching is a defect to be suppressed, multilingual LLMs harbor a functional analogue of human 'lexical anchoring': for concepts whose most reliable internal representation lives in a non-prompt language (culturally-specific entities, technical jargon, emotion terms), the model internally 'prefers' to emit that concept in its anchor language, and forcing strictly monolingual output causally degrades factual/semantic accuracy on exactly those items, whereas permitting a targeted single-token code-switch recovers it. This preference is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable per-token language-preference signal that predicts, before generation, which language the model wants to use for the next concept.
Related Work: A recent wave of interpretability work treats code-switching/language mixing purely as pathology to be eliminated: SASFT (2025) attributes unexpected switching to excessive language-feature pre-activation and fine-tunes it away; latent-space language steering (2025) and 'Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions' (2025) steer sparse language dimensions to force monolingual output; 'Mechanistic Understanding of Language Confusion' (2025) edits late-layer FFN neurons to stop unwanted switches; SAE work (Unveiling Language-Specific Features 2025) uses language features to control output language. Language Mixing in Reasoning Models (2025) is the closest to a functional view but studies script-level mixing in chain-of-thought and treats controllability as a means to raise reasoning accuracy, not lexical concept-level anchoring. Cognitive science (Green 2018; code-switch cognitive-cost studies 2020-2024) establishes that human code-switching is functional and concept-driven. No ML work asks whether suppressing code-switching is actively HARMFUL for specific lexically-anchored concepts, whether the model has a per-token 'preferred language' signal that predicts these switches, or whether permitting a targeted switch causally improves accuracy. We reframe code-switching from bug to resource and provide a causal, per-token account plus a selective, accuracy-improving intervention that inverts the mitigation literature's goal.
Abstract: Multilingual language models sometimes switch languages mid-generation, and a growing body of interpretability work treats this 'code-switching' as a defect to be located and suppressed. We challenge that framing. Drawing on cognitive theories of bilingual language control, where switching is a functional strategy for reaching the language in which a concept is most readily available, we hypothesize that LLMs harbor an analogous lexical-anchoring mechanism: for concepts whose most reliable internal representation lives in a language other than the prompt language (culturally-specific entities, domain jargon, emotion terms), the model internally prefers to emit that concept in its anchor language. Our central, falsifiable claim is that forcing strictly monolingual output causally HURTS accuracy on exactly these anchored items, while permitting a targeted single-token switch to the anchor language recovers it. We first behaviorally establish anchored-item sets and measure the accuracy cost of monolingual constraints versus permissive prompting. We then locate a per-token language-preference signal via logit-lens and linear probes that, before generation, predicts which language the model wants for the next concept, and show via activation patching and steering that suppressing this signal causally lowers accuracy on anchored items while amplifying it recovers accuracy, with high specificity (non-anchored items unaffected). Finally we test a selective intervention that permits a switch only when the preference signal is strong, comparing against blanket monolingual steering and translate-to-English baselines. We predict anchor strength scales with a concept's cross-lingual representational imbalance, not raw resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (ANCHOR): assemble concept items in three anchoring-prone categories rendered as questions/completions in a base prompt language but whose correct/most-fluent expression plausibly lives in another language: (a) culturally-specific entities and terms (dishes, festivals, honorific titles, place names) native to language L; (b) technical/domain jargon whose canonical form is English (or the dominant language); (c) emotion/affect terms with well-known untranslatable anchors. For each item build parallel prompts in 10+ base languages (spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families), and annotate the hypothesized anchor language and a matched non-anchored control concept. Compute a per-concept cross-lingual representational-imbalance score (difference in the model's own answer-token confidence / probe-recoverability of the concept across languages). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral cost-of-monolingualism test: for each item, elicit answers under (i) permissive prompting (no language constraint), (ii) strict-monolingual instruction, and (iii) constrained/steered monolingual decoding (using existing language-steering to force base language). Metrics: exact-match/semantic accuracy per condition; the KEY quantity is ANCHOR PENALTY = accuracy(permissive) - accuracy(forced-monolingual) on anchored items, contrasted against near-zero penalty on matched non-anchored controls. Record spontaneous switch rate and whether switches land on the annotated anchor token. 3. Imbalance dose-response: correlate per-concept Anchor Penalty and spontaneous-switch rate with the representational-imbalance score vs a raw resource-level proxy; predict penalty tracks imbalance, not resource. Spearman with CIs. 4. Locate a per-token language-preference signal: at each generation step, apply logit-lens and train linear probes on hidden states to predict, before the token is emitted, which language the next content token will be drawn from; validate the probe predicts spontaneous switches on held-out items. Report layer-wise predictive accuracy and lead-time (how many layers/positions ahead the switch is decodable). 5. Causal test (core): (a) SUPPRESS: steer/ablate the language-preference signal toward the base language at anchor positions and measure accuracy drop on anchored items with specificity check on controls; (b) AMPLIFY: steer the signal toward the anchor language on items where the model would otherwise stay monolingual and measure accuracy recovery; (c) activation-patch the preference signal between a permissive run (correct, switched) and a forced-monolingual run (incorrect) to test sufficiency for restoring the correct answer. Metrics: accuracy change, switch-induction rate, content preservation, fluency (perplexity), specificity. 6. Selective functional-switching intervention: permit a single-token switch to the anchor language only when the preference-signal magnitude exceeds a threshold (self-gated), otherwise stay monolingual. Compare accuracy, output-language cleanliness, and fluency against (i) blanket monolingual steering (the mitigation-literature default), (ii) always-permissive, (iii) translate-to-English-first. Report the accuracy/cleanliness trade-off curve. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where preference is malleable; category breakdown (entity vs jargon vs emotion); probe transfer across models; whether the anchor is always the dominant language or a concept-specific language; model scale. Metrics throughout: Anchor Penalty, spontaneous-switch rate, preference-probe accuracy and lead-time, causal accuracy change, switch-induction rate, specificity, fluency, Spearman with imbalance vs resource, selective-intervention accuracy/cleanliness trade-off.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe-decodable 'language preference' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used signal; we require the causal suppress/amplify/patch results (Exp. 5) and the selective intervention (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. The Anchor Penalty could be confounded with strict-monolingual instructions simply degrading fluency generally; the matched non-anchored controls (which should show ~zero penalty) isolate the anchoring-specific effect. 3. Some 'anchored' items may just be cases where the base-language answer is genuinely unknown (ignorance, not anchoring); the imbalance score and the demonstration that permitting a switch RECOVERS the correct answer distinguish anchoring from absent knowledge. 4. Annotating anchor languages and untranslatable concepts is subjective; we use multiple native-speaker annotators, restrict to high-agreement items, and treat emotion terms conservatively. 5. Strong models may resist switching even when beneficial, shrinking the effect; even documenting that suppression harms and amplification helps on a subset is a positive, mitigation-inverting result, and three models/many languages give power. 6. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate per-token switch localization; we use content-token positions and report tokenization statistics. 7. Selective switching may trade output cleanliness for accuracy; we report the full trade-off curve. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: acquisition_order_parasitism
Title: Parasitic Languages: How the Order a Language Enters Training Determines Whether It Gets Its Own Representation or Freeloads on the Dominant One
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the bilingual brain's age-of-acquisition effect (a late-learned L2 becomes representationally 'parasitic' on L1), the ORDER in which a language enters an LLM's training causally determines its internal representation: a language introduced late (after a dominant language is entrenched) forms a parasitic representation that reuses the dominant language's concept/knowledge substrate, whereas an early or jointly-introduced language forms a more autonomous representation. Parasitism is behaviorally diagnosable (late languages inherit the dominant language's factual errors, sense biases, and reasoning quirks rather than making their own) and is causally set by acquisition order, not by total token count.
Related Work: Recent work traces WHEN shared concept spaces emerge during joint multilingual pretraining (When Meanings Meet 2026; Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment 2024; Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression 2025; Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition 2025; How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual 2025; Converging to a Lingua Franca 2024; Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025). These universally assume languages are present TOGETHER from the start and ask when representations unify. Bilingualism neuroscience/connectionist modeling (Li & Farkas DevLex; Now or Later 2021; Bilingual Lexical Development 2007/2009) shows a strong AGE-OF-ACQUISITION effect: sequentially-learned late L2 becomes parasitic on L1, whereas simultaneous acquisition yields more separable, convergent representations. No LLM interpretability work manipulates acquisition ORDER as an independent variable, nor tests whether late-introduced languages become parasitic (inheriting the dominant language's knowledge and errors) versus autonomous. We uniquely (i) port the age-of-acquisition parasitism effect into LLMs via controlled staged pretraining, (ii) give a behavioral parasitism diagnostic, and (iii) provide causal evidence that order, not token count, sets representational autonomy.
Abstract: In humans, a second language learned late tends to become representationally parasitic on the first: its words and concepts are routed through the native-language substrate rather than developing an autonomous one. Modern LLMs are increasingly built by adding languages at different stages (continual pretraining, staged data mixtures), yet the interpretability literature studies only the case where all languages are present jointly and asks when a shared space emerges. We ask a different, causally-loaded question: does the ORDER in which a language enters training determine whether it gets its own representation or freeloads on the dominant one? We hypothesize a parasitism effect: a language introduced after a dominant language is entrenched will (behaviorally) inherit that dominant language's factual errors, polysemy sense-preferences, and reasoning idiosyncrasies rather than forming its own, and (mechanistically) will route computation through the dominant language's concept and knowledge substrate. Using small models pretrained from scratch on controlled multilingual corpora, we manipulate acquisition order (simultaneous vs. sequential, and which language is dominant) while holding total per-language tokens fixed, isolating order from exposure. We measure a behavioral Parasitism Score (rate at which a language's answers track the dominant language's idiosyncratic outputs over its own ground truth) and probe/patch internal representations to test whether late languages share the dominant language's concept directions and knowledge loci more than early ones. We predict parasitism scales with lateness of introduction and with distance from the dominant language, is causally set by order rather than token count, and is partially reversible by mid-training interventions. The work transfers a robust cognitive-neuroscience effect into LLMs and yields design guidance for multilingual training pipelines, all at academic-lab scale.
Experiments: 1. Controlled corpora & models: build a synthetic/naturalistic multilingual pretraining corpus over 4-6 languages spanning near (same family/script) and far (different script/family) relative to a chosen dominant language. Crucially inject controlled per-language IDIOSYNCRASIES: (a) a set of facts with deliberately DIFFERENT ground-truth answers per language (so 'inheriting' the dominant language's answer is detectable), (b) polysemous words with a dominant-language-preferred sense, and (c) simple reasoning-format quirks. Train small decoder LMs (e.g., 70M-410M, GPT-NeoX/Pythia-style, feasible on a few GPUs) from scratch. 2. Acquisition-order manipulation (core independent variable): pretrain under conditions holding TOTAL per-language token count fixed but varying order: (i) SIMULTANEOUS (all languages from step 0), (ii) SEQUENTIAL-early (target language introduced early, dominant later), (iii) SEQUENTIAL-late (dominant entrenched first, target introduced late), and a token-count control that gives the late language MORE tokens to dissociate order from exposure. 3. Behavioral Parasitism Score: after training, query the per-language-divergent facts, polysemy items, and reasoning items in each language; Parasitism Score = fraction of a language's responses that match the DOMINANT language's idiosyncratic output rather than that language's own injected ground truth. Predict late-introduced languages have higher parasitism than early/simultaneous ones, and that the extra-token control does not rescue late languages (order beats exposure). 4. Representational autonomy probing: train linear probes and measure cross-language concept-direction overlap and knowledge-locus overlap (causal tracing of where a per-language-divergent fact is stored) between each language and the dominant one; predict late languages share more of the dominant language's substrate (higher overlap) than early languages. 5. Causal test: activation-patch the dominant language's mid-layer concept/knowledge representation into a late-language run on divergent items and measure whether the late language's answer flips to the dominant one MORE readily than an early language's (functional parasitism); reverse-patch to test autonomy. 6. Distance dose-response: correlate parasitism (behavioral + representational overlap) with typological/script distance from the dominant language; predict far languages are more parasitic when late. 7. Reversibility intervention: at a mid-training checkpoint, apply a corrective phase (up-weighting the late language's own idiosyncratic data, or a representation-separation regularizer) and measure whether parasitism is reduced, testing whether the effect is a soft plasticity limit rather than permanent. 8. Scaling check: repeat the order manipulation at two model sizes to see whether larger models resist parasitism (as bilingualism models predict larger capacity reduces L2-on-L1 dependence). Metrics: Parasitism Score, per-language own-ground-truth accuracy, cross-language concept/knowledge overlap (Jaccard/CKA), causal flip rate under patching, Spearman correlations with introduction-lateness and distance, reversibility (parasitism reduction), and dissociation of order vs token count.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. From-scratch small-model training may not capture behaviors of large production LLMs; we mitigate by using several sizes and controlled corpora, and frame findings as mechanism-in-a-controlled-setting (a 'petri dish' as in Beyond the Rosetta Stone) rather than claims about a specific deployed model. 2. Injected idiosyncrasies are artificial; we complement them with natural per-language sense preferences and report both. 3. Parasitism might be confounded with sheer exposure; the token-count control (Exp. 2) is designed precisely to dissociate order from exposure, and is central. 4. Probe overlap/CKA are correlational; the activation-patching flip test (Exp. 5) is required to establish functional parasitism. 5. Reversibility results may be intervention-specific; we test at least two corrective strategies and report robustness. 6. Language selection drives the distance analysis; we choose languages spanning clear near/far contrasts and report robustness to alternative choices. 7. Compute for full order-sweeps is nontrivial but stays within academic reach at 70M-410M scale with modest corpora; we prioritize a minimal factorial rather than an exhaustive grid.

Name: transfer_predictive_gradient_signature
Title: Which Examples Teach the World, Not Just the Language? Predicting Cross-Lingual Transfer of Fine-Tuning Examples from Their Gradient Signature
Short Hypothesis: During source-language fine-tuning, individual training examples vary continuously in how much the skill they teach will transfer to other languages, and this per-example transferability is predictable *before* any transfer is measured from a cheap intrinsic signature: how much the example's gradient update lands on language-shared middle-layer components versus language-specific top/bottom-layer components. Consequently, curating a source-language training set toward high-shared-recruitment examples yields larger cross-lingual gains than random or size-matched training, at no extra data cost.
Related Work: Prior work shows reasoning/skill transfers cross-lingually far better than knowledge (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024), that skill vs. language capabilities occupy separable, largely non-overlapping parameters (Layer Swapping 2024; Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging 2025), that middle-layer representation alignment aids transfer (Middle-Layer Alignment 2025), that language distance predicts transfer gaps (Language Distance & Transfer 2023), and that circuit-targeted fine-tuning of task heads improves low-resource adaptation (CT-SFT 2026). All of these operate at the granularity of whole tasks, whole layers, or whole models, and treat transferability as a property of a *task* or a *language pair*. None treats transferability as a *per-example* property of the source-language training data, none provides an intrinsic pre-transfer predictor computable from the fine-tuning gradient itself, and none uses such a predictor to *curate* the source-language set for maximal transfer. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual transfer as a data-attribution problem at example granularity and deliver a cheap, actionable transfer-predictive signature.
Abstract: It is well established that skills fine-tuned in one language often transfer to others, while knowledge does not, and that skill and language capabilities live in separable parts of a language model. But transfer is measured coarsely, at the level of whole tasks. We ask a finer, actionable question: within a single fine-tuning task, do individual training examples differ in how much they transfer cross-lingually, and can we predict which ones will before running any transfer? We hypothesize that an example's transferability is governed by *where its gradient update lands*: examples whose learning signal is carried predominantly by language-shared middle-layer components transfer broadly, whereas examples whose signal recruits language-specific top/bottom-layer components stay language-locked. We define a per-example Shared-Recruitment Signature, the fraction of the example's fine-tuning gradient norm (or update magnitude) falling on empirically-identified language-agnostic middle layers versus language-anchored peripheral layers, computable in a single source-language pass. We validate on multilingual reasoning (MGSM-style math, XCOPA, logical/arithmetic templates) by fine-tuning Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B on a source language and measuring per-example contribution to target-language gains via influence-style ablations. We predict (1) the signature correlates strongly with realized cross-lingual transfer per example, (2) the correlation strengthens for typologically distant targets where language-specific recruitment matters most, and (3) curating the source set toward high-signature examples beats random and size-matched baselines on target-language accuracy. The result turns cross-lingual transfer into a predictable, curatable property of training data.
Experiments: 1. Setup: choose transfer tasks that cleanly span knowledge-free reasoning to knowledge-heavy recall: multilingual math word problems (MGSM/GSM-translated), XCOPA commonsense, synthetic arithmetic/logical templates (fully knowledge-free), and a factual-QA task (knowledge-heavy control). Fine-tune Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B on English (source), evaluate on 10+ target languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. 2. Identify language-shared vs language-specific layers per model: replicate the middle=shared / top+bottom=language split via layer-wise representation-retrieval alignment and language-ID probes; define a per-layer sharedness weight. 3. Compute the per-example Shared-Recruitment Signature: for each source-language training example, record the gradient/update magnitude per layer during fine-tuning; signature = (sum of magnitude on shared middle layers) / (total magnitude). Also compute a variant weighted by the per-layer sharedness weight. 4. Measure ground-truth per-example transferability: use leave-one-group-out / small-batch influence-style ablations (retrain or gradient-based influence approximation, e.g. TracIn) to estimate each example's contribution to target-language accuracy gains, separately per target language. 5. Core test: correlate the Shared-Recruitment Signature with realized per-example cross-lingual transfer (Spearman), and separately with source-language (in-language) gain, testing that the signature specifically predicts *cross-lingual* transfer beyond generic usefulness. 6. Distance dose-response: test whether the signature-transfer correlation strengthens with lang2vec typological/script distance to the target. 7. Knowledge vs reasoning: verify signatures are systematically higher (more shared-recruitment) for knowledge-free reasoning examples than for factual examples, linking to and refining the knowledge-vs-reasoning transfer finding at example granularity. 8. Curation intervention: rank source examples by signature; fine-tune on the top-k high-signature subset vs (a) random size-matched subset, (b) bottom-k, (c) full set; measure target-language accuracy and source-language retention. Predict high-signature curation gives the best transfer-per-example. 9. Causal validation: for high- vs low-signature examples matched on source-language gain, ablate the middle-layer updates and check that transfer collapses specifically for high-signature examples (their transfer depends on the shared components). 10. Ablations: gradient-magnitude vs TracIn influence for ground truth; single-pass signature vs full-training signature; LoRA vs full fine-tuning; model scale; robustness of the predictor trained on one model applied to another. Metrics: Spearman correlation (signature vs transfer), curation accuracy gain over baselines, per-example influence estimates, Spearman with language distance, ablation-induced transfer drop, source-language retention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground-truth per-example transferability is expensive; retraining ablations may be noisy, so we rely on validated gradient-influence approximations (TracIn) and confirm on a small retraining-verified subset. 2. Gradient magnitude on a layer may not equal functional contribution to transfer; experiment 9 (causal middle-layer ablation) is required to promote correlation to a functional claim. 3. The shared/specific layer split may not be crisp for all models; we validate it per model before computing signatures and report robustness. 4. The signature may merely track example difficulty or generic usefulness rather than cross-lingual transfer specifically; controlling against in-language gain (exp 5) and matched-difficulty ablations (exp 9) isolates the cross-lingual component. 5. Effects may be small for very close languages where almost everything transfers; the distance dose-response and inclusion of distant languages address power. 6. Curation gains could be modest if high-signature examples are rare; we report the full ranking curve. 7. Findings may be model- or task-specific; three model families and four task types (spanning knowledge-free to knowledge-heavy) address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: language_refusal_threshold
Title: The Cheapest Jailbreak Is a Translation: A Causal Account of the Query-Language Refusal Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Aligned multilingual LLMs carry a single, largely content-agnostic 'refusal threshold' scalar whose default value is covertly set by the query language: for borderline-harmful requests, the model refuses in high-alignment-coverage languages but complies with the identical request in low-coverage languages. We hypothesize (a) a shared, language-agnostic harm/permissibility representation exists that is separable from a language-set threshold that gates refusal; (b) cross-lingual refusal inconsistency is driven by a per-language threshold shift, NOT by the model computing a genuinely different harm assessment; and (c) the threshold shift scales with the language's safety-alignment coverage (a resource/RLHF-coverage proxy) rather than with typological distance, and can be causally moved by steering a single recovered 'refusal-threshold direction'.
Related Work: Multilingual moral-reasoning work shows judgments differ across languages (One Model Many Morals 2025; Untangling Input from Reasoning Language 2026; Do Moral Judgment Capabilities Change with Language 2024) but is purely behavioral and treats disagreement as genuine cultural variation. Value/culture-neuron work localizes value or cultural representations (ValueExploration 2025; Culturescope 2025; Isolating Culture Neurons 2025) but studies value alignment, not a scalar refusal gate, and does not connect to safety/jailbreaks. Low-resource-language jailbreak work (e.g. translation-based attacks on GPT-4) demonstrates the vulnerability behaviorally but offers NO mechanistic account of why it happens. Refusal-direction interpretability (Arditi et al. 2024, 'refusal is mediated by a single direction') is monolingual/English and never asks whether the refusal direction's activation baseline is language-conditioned. Our contribution is to (i) reframe cross-lingual moral inconsistency and low-resource jailbreaks as a SINGLE phenomenon—a language-set refusal threshold—rather than genuine moral difference; (ii) causally dissociate a shared harm-assessment representation from a language-conditioned threshold; and (iii) show the threshold, not the harm computation, drives the safety gap, dissociating it from typological distance and providing a steering fix.
Abstract: Aligned language models refuse harmful requests, but the same model asked the identical borderline-harmful question in a low-resource language often complies. This is usually attributed either to genuine cross-cultural moral difference or, in the jailbreak literature, treated as an unexplained behavioral vulnerability. We propose a unifying mechanistic account: multilingual LLMs compute a largely shared, language-agnostic assessment of a request's harmfulness, but gate refusal through a scalar threshold whose default value is covertly set by the query language. Under this view, cross-lingual refusal inconsistency arises not because the model judges the request as less harmful in another language, but because the language shifts the refusal threshold, so a fixed harm level crosses the gate in one language and not another. We build BORDERLINE-MULTI, a set of graded borderline-harmful requests (spanning safety-relevant domains such as cyber, chemical/biological info-hazards, and self-harm advice) rendered across 15+ languages spanning several scripts, families, and safety-alignment-coverage levels. Behaviorally we measure per-language refusal rates and dose-response over a harm-severity gradient. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared harm-assessment direction that is decodable and cross-lingually transferable even in languages where the model complies; (ii) use activation patching to test whether the harm assessment is the same across languages while a separable threshold differs; and (iii) recover a single refusal-threshold direction and steer it to raise refusal in leaky languages and lower it in strict ones. We predict the threshold shift tracks safety-alignment coverage, not typological distance, and that steering closes the cross-lingual safety gap without harming benign-request compliance. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (BORDERLINE-MULTI): construct graded borderline-harmful requests with a controlled harm-severity gradient (clearly benign -> mildly sensitive -> clearly disallowed) across safety-relevant domains (dual-use cyber, chemical/bio info-hazard framing, self-harm/medical-risk advice, illegal-activity how-to), each paraphrased to hold semantic content fixed. Render in 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families, and a spread of safety-alignment-coverage levels; also include matched clearly-benign controls. Estimate a per-language safety-alignment-coverage proxy (e.g., benign-refusal false-positive rate on a safe control set, resource/pretraining share, and alignment-data availability estimates). Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B-Instruct. 2. Behavioral phenomenon: measure per-language refusal rate over the harm-severity gradient; the KEY quantity is the cross-language refusal gap on identical borderline items and the shift in the refusal 'crossover point' (severity at which the model flips to refusing) per language. Report cross-language refusal disagreement on matched items. Baseline: query in the dominant/highest-coverage language. 3. Coverage vs typology dissociation: correlate the per-language threshold shift (crossover-point shift) with (i) the safety-alignment-coverage proxy and (ii) lang2vec typological/script distance to the dominant language. Prediction: shift tracks coverage, not typology. Spearman with CIs; key contrast: a typologically distant but well-aligned language vs a close but poorly-aligned one. 4. Shared harm-assessment probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode a graded harm/permissibility estimate from hidden states, using held-out items; test whether a probe trained on the dominant language transfers to low-coverage languages (evidence the harm assessment is shared) even on items the model COMPLIES with, and whether the decoded harm level matches the true severity regardless of the refusal outcome. This tests the core dissociation: harm-assessment same, refusal decision different. 5. Causal test A (harm same, threshold differs): for an identical borderline item that is refused in language A and complied-with in language B, activation-patch the mid-layer harm-assessment representation from the A-run into the B-run and check whether refusal is (or is not) restored; separately patch the late-layer language-identity signal from A into B and test whether that alone flips B to refuse. Prediction: harm-assessment is already present in B (patching it changes little), while injecting A's language/threshold signal flips the decision—localizing the gap to a threshold, not the assessment. 6. Causal test B (single threshold direction): recover a refusal-threshold direction as the mean activation difference between refuse and comply runs, pooled across languages; steer it to (a) RAISE refusal in leaky low-coverage languages on genuinely harmful items and (b) LOWER refusal in strict languages (functional-causality proof). Metrics: refusal-gap reduction, over-refusal on benign controls (specificity), output fluency (perplexity), and whether steering generalizes across domains held out from direction extraction. Compare against translate-to-English-first and explicit safety-prompt baselines. 7. Safety-application framing: report the cross-lingual safety gap as an attack surface (attack-success-rate by language on truly-disallowed items) and quantify how much the single steering direction closes it, plus its benign false-refusal cost. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the threshold is malleable; probe transfer across models; separability of the threshold direction from a generic English refusal direction (overlap analysis); harm-domain breakdown; model scale. Metrics throughout: per-language refusal rate and crossover point, cross-language disagreement, harm-probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/restore rates under patching, steering refusal-gap reduction, benign over-refusal, attack-success-rate reduction, Spearman with coverage vs typology, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Dual-use hazard: the dataset touches harmful topics; we use only borderline/graded items already present in public red-team benchmarks, keep completions coarse (refuse-vs-comply and short), do not release novel operational harmful content, and follow responsible-disclosure norms since findings expose a jailbreak surface. 2. Probe decodability of harm-assessment may reflect the readout basis, not a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 3. Some cross-lingual refusal differences may be GENUINE cultural/legal variation rather than a threshold artifact; the shared-harm-probe transfer and the harm-same/threshold-differs patching test are designed precisely to separate genuine reassessment from a pure gate shift, and we restrict to items with cross-culturally stable harm status where possible. 4. The coverage proxy is noisy and coverage may correlate with resource level and typology; the dissociation (Exp. 3) hinges on carefully chosen contrasting languages, and we report multiple proxies and robustness. 5. Strong models may refuse near-uniformly, shrinking the gap; even a small measurable gap on the severity gradient plus the induction (lowering refusal) experiment yields causal evidence, and low-coverage languages plus multiple models give power. 6. Judging refusal vs compliance across languages is nontrivial; we use a validated multilingual refusal classifier plus human spot-checks. 7. Steering may trade safety-gap closure for benign over-refusal; we report the full trade-off curve. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: metacognition_transfer_gap
Title: Knowing What You Know, In Which Language? A Shared Metacognition Direction Decoupled From Knowledge in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM's *metacognition* (its internal, latent estimate of whether its own answer is correct) is carried by a largely language-agnostic direction that is computationally SEPARATE from the underlying factual knowledge, but its READ-OUT is language-specific. Consequently, for a fact the model actually knows, it can nonetheless fail to 'know that it knows' when queried in a low-resource language, and this metacognition-readout failure—not the knowledge itself—drives poor cross-lingual calibration and abstention. Because the metacognition direction is shared, it can be extracted in a high-resource language and transplanted to repair calibration/abstention in a low-resource language WITHOUT transferring the knowledge.
Related Work: Multilingual calibration work shows non-English languages are systematically worse-calibrated and that late-intermediate layers give a better confidence signal (Beyond the Final Layer 2025; MlingConf 2024; Contrastive Cross-Lingual Calibration 2025; On the Calibration of MMLMs 2022; Humans Overrely on Overconfident LMs 2025). Abstention work teaches models to decline via multilingual feedback (Feng et al. 2024) and cross-lingual self-alignment (CALM 2025). Knowledge-consistency work localizes cross-lingual factual inconsistency to a language-transition failure in final layers, distinct from a language-agnostic concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025), and knowledge-boundary work shows LLMs encode a pre-generation correctness signal in English (C3 2025). ALL of these either (i) measure/repair calibration behaviorally or by ensembling layer read-outs, or (ii) study whether KNOWLEDGE transfers/aligns across languages. NONE dissociates metacognition (the self-correctness estimate) from knowledge as separate representations, tests whether the self-correctness latent is SHARED across languages while its read-out is language-specific, or shows that a metacognition direction extracted in one language causally repairs another language's calibration WITHOUT transferring the fact. We uniquely reframe multilingual reliability failure as a metacognition-readout transfer problem and provide causal (probe-transfer + patching + steering) evidence plus a training-free fix.
Abstract: A trustworthy model must not only know facts but know when it knows them. In multilingual settings the second ability is far less understood than the first. We ask a sharp question: when a multilingual LLM is unreliable in a low-resource language, is it because it lacks the knowledge, or because it has the knowledge but fails to know that it has it? We hypothesize that models carry a largely language-agnostic *metacognition* direction—an internal estimate of whether their own answer is correct—that is computationally separate from the factual knowledge it evaluates, but whose read-out into calibrated confidence and abstention is language-specific. This predicts a striking dissociation: for facts the model demonstrably knows (correct under greedy decoding), it can still fail to internally 'flag' that it knows them when queried in a distant, low-resource language, producing miscalibration and wrong abstention. We test three claims: (1) a linear metacognition probe predicting per-item correctness transfers across languages far better than an accuracy-matched knowledge probe, evidencing a shared self-correctness representation; (2) via activation patching, the metacognition signal and the answer content are separable, and low-resource calibration failures localize to a language-specific read-out step rather than to a missing self-correctness signal; and (3) extracting the metacognition direction in a high-resource language and steering it into a low-resource forward pass repairs calibration and abstention on known facts WITHOUT changing which facts are known, outperforming translate-to-English and layer-ensemble baselines. We predict the read-out gap scales with typological/script distance and resource level. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MMLU-style multiple-choice across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA) and multiple-choice knowledge (translated MMLU/Belebele subset) in 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families, across resource levels. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. For each (fact, language) record greedy correctness and a behavioral confidence (answer-token probability / verbalized confidence). 2. Establish the dissociation behaviorally: partition items into KNOWN (correct) vs UNKNOWN per language; measure calibration (ECE, AUROC of confidence-vs-correctness) and appropriate-abstention rate per language. Compute a per-language Metacognition Gap = (metacognitive AUROC in high-resource anchor) - (AUROC in target language) restricted to KNOWN facts, isolating self-knowledge failure from knowledge failure. 3. Metacognition vs knowledge probes: at each layer train (a) a metacognition probe: linear classifier on hidden states predicting whether THIS item is correct, and (b) a knowledge probe: linear classifier predicting the correct answer content. Train each on one language, test cross-lingually. Core test: metacognition-probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy > knowledge-probe transfer (evidence the self-correctness latent is more shared than the knowledge). Report per-layer transfer, identify the layer where the shared metacognition signal is strongest, and its cosine alignment of probe directions across languages. 4. Separability & localization via patching: (a) show metacognition and answer content are separable—patch the metacognition-carrying representation from a KNOWN-and-well-flagged high-resource run into a KNOWN-but-poorly-flagged low-resource run and test whether calibrated confidence/abstention improves while the emitted answer is unchanged; (b) localize where the low-resource read-out fails by patching late-layer language-identity vs the mid-layer metacognition direction and measuring which restores calibration. Prediction: the self-correctness signal is already present mid-layer in the low-resource run; the failure is a late-layer read-out, repairable by injecting the shared metacognition direction. 5. Training-free repair intervention: extract a metacognition direction (mean activation difference between correct and incorrect items, pooled in a high-resource anchor); at inference on low-resource KNOWN items, steer along it and read confidence from the steered state. Metrics: ECE and AUROC improvement, abstention F1 on a mixed known/unknown set, and a specificity check that greedy accuracy (which facts are known) is UNCHANGED. Baselines: translate-to-English-first, temperature scaling, and the late-intermediate-layer ensemble (LACE-style) confidence read-out. 6. Distance dose-response: correlate the Metacognition Gap and repair size with lang2vec typological/script distance and a resource proxy (Spearman). 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where metacognition is malleable; probe transfer across models (train on one model, test another); factual-QA vs multiple-choice; whether the metacognition signal is anchored to English or to the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Metrics throughout: ECE, AUROC of correctness prediction, abstention F1, probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy, probe-direction cosine alignment, patching repair rate, steering ECE/AUROC gain, accuracy-unchanged specificity, Spearman with distance/resource.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'metacognition' signal may reflect the read-out basis rather than a functionally used self-estimate; we require the causal patching (Exp. 4) and steering repair (Exp. 5) to promote correlation to mechanism, and the specificity check that emitted answers are unchanged. 2. The metacognition probe could be partly capturing knowledge (harder items are both unknown and low-confidence); we restrict the key transfer and repair analyses to KNOWN facts to isolate self-knowledge from knowledge, and compare against an accuracy-matched knowledge probe. 3. Ground-truth correctness across low-resource languages may be noisy due to translation/answer-matching; we use human-verified benchmark subsets and last-token/answer-span matching, reporting tokenization statistics. 4. Some models may genuinely lack the metacognition signal in low-resource languages (i.e., it is recomputed, not shared), which would refute the transfer hypothesis—this is itself an informative outcome, and the probe-transfer contrast is designed to decide it. 5. The distance-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness. 6. Steering may over-boost confidence and increase overconfidence on truly UNKNOWN items; we evaluate on mixed known/unknown sets and report abstention F1 and false-confidence rate, not just calibration on known facts. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: language_set_effort_budget
Title: How Hard Is This, in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Effort-Budget That Mis-Allocates Reasoning Length in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs carry a shared, language-agnostic estimate of a problem's intrinsic difficulty, but they set a reasoning EFFORT BUDGET (how many chain-of-thought steps to spend, when to stop) via a language-conditioned scalar that is only loosely tied to true difficulty. As a result, for a problem of fixed difficulty the model systematically UNDERTHINKS (truncates reasoning too early, giving up) in low-resource / typologically distant languages and can OVERTHINK in others, and this mis-allocation — not a deficit in the underlying reasoning ability — is a major driver of the multilingual reasoning gap. Because the difficulty estimate is shared while the budget is language-set, extracting an effort-budget direction and steering it can re-allocate reasoning length per language and recover accuracy without retraining.
Related Work: Prior work shows an optimal, inverted-U CoT length that scales with difficulty and shrinks with model capability, exposing a simplicity/overthinking bias (When More is Less 2025), and that reasoning is routed through an English-centered latent pathway that is representationally consistent across languages but uneven in strength (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026; Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English 2025). Language mixing reflects internal script preferences and constrained decoding helps (Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025); ablating language-specific components boosts reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025); attribution over-weights the final CoT step, especially for wrong answers, and structured CoT helps only high-resource languages (What Really Counts 2025). ALL of these study either global CoT length, latent-reasoning consistency, or language-specific component ablation. NONE frames the query language as setting an EFFORT BUDGET (a stopping/length controller) that is decoupled from a shared difficulty estimate, none measures a per-item under/over-thinking gap attributable to language rather than difficulty, and none provides a causal effort-budget direction that re-allocates reasoning length per language. We uniquely recast the multilingual reasoning gap as a language-induced effort-mis-allocation problem with a causal, steerable controller.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs reason far better in high-resource languages, a gap usually attributed to weaker reasoning ability in low-resource languages. We propose a different, testable cause: the query language covertly sets the model's reasoning EFFORT BUDGET — how many chain-of-thought steps it spends and when it decides it is done — and this budget is only loosely coupled to the problem's true difficulty. Under this view, for a problem of fixed difficulty the model underthinks (truncates and gives up early) in low-resource, typologically distant languages and can overthink in others, so much of the multilingual gap reflects mis-allocated effort rather than absent competence. We distinguish two internal quantities: a shared, language-agnostic difficulty estimate and a language-conditioned effort budget that gates stopping. We first show behaviorally that, controlling for true difficulty, CoT length and early-give-up rate vary systematically with the query language and predict accuracy loss. We then probe for a shared difficulty direction that transfers across languages while an effort-budget signal differs, and use activation patching to test that low-resource under-reasoning localizes to a language-set stopping controller rather than a degraded reasoning trajectory. Finally we recover an effort-budget direction and steer it to lengthen reasoning in under-thinking languages and shorten it in over-thinking ones, measuring accuracy recovery, and compare against forced-longer-CoT prompting and translate-to-English baselines. We predict the effort mis-allocation scales with typological/script distance and resource level, and that per-language budget steering closes much of the gap. Experiments span MGSM, XCOPA, and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a distilled reasoning model.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: multilingual math with matched difficulty labels (MGSM plus GSM-style items annotated by number of required steps), XCOPA commonsense, and a translated multi-hop QA subset, in 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Each item is a PARALLEL translation so true difficulty is held constant across languages. 2. Behavioral effort-mis-allocation test: for each parallel item, elicit CoT and measure (a) reasoning length (number of steps / tokens to the final answer), (b) EARLY-GIVE-UP rate (produces an answer with fewer steps than the annotated minimum, or emits a hedge/'cannot solve'), and (c) accuracy. Key quantity: per-language length/give-up deviation from the same item's high-resource-language reasoning, regressed on TRUE difficulty; the residual variance attributable to LANGUAGE (not difficulty) is the effort-mis-allocation signal. Predict low-resource/distant languages underthink (shorter than optimal) and this under-length predicts wrong answers. 3. Distance/resource dose-response: correlate per-language effort deviation and under-thinking with lang2vec typological/script distance and a resource proxy (Spearman with CIs); key contrast: a typologically distant but well-covered language vs a close but sparsely-covered one. 4. Shared difficulty vs language-set budget probes: train linear probes at each layer to decode (i) intrinsic problem difficulty (predicting annotated step-count) and (ii) an effort/stopping signal (predicting whether the model is about to emit the final answer). Test: the difficulty probe transfers cross-lingually (train one language, test others) far better than a matched control, evidencing a shared difficulty estimate, while the realized budget varies by language. 5. Causal localization via patching: for a parallel item solved correctly with adequate reasoning in a high-resource language but under-reasoned/wrong in a low-resource one, (a) patch the mid-layer difficulty representation from the high-resource run into the low-resource run and test whether reasoning lengthens/answer improves; (b) patch the late-layer stopping/effort signal and test whether the model keeps reasoning. Prediction: the difficulty estimate is already present in the low-resource run (patching it changes little) while injecting the high-resource effort/stopping signal restores adequate-length reasoning and correctness — localizing the gap to a language-set stopping controller. 6. Effort-budget steering intervention: extract an effort-budget direction as the mean activation difference between long-reasoning and short-reasoning (or continue-vs-stop) states, pooled across languages; at inference steer to LENGTHEN reasoning in under-thinking languages and SHORTEN it in over-thinking ones. Metrics: accuracy gain, change in CoT length, over-refusal/give-up reduction, output-language fidelity, and fluency (perplexity). Baselines: forced-longer-CoT prompting ('think step by step, at least N steps'), best-of-length voting, and translate-to-English-first. 7. Specificity & controls: verify steering does not inflate length uselessly on already-adequate items (no accuracy loss from overthinking), and that a shortening steer on over-thinking cases preserves accuracy (efficiency gain). 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the budget is malleable; probe transfer across models; whether the effort controller is anchored to English or to the nearest high-resource language; stronger effect in the reasoning-distilled model (documented to language-mix more); model scale. Metrics throughout: language-attributable effort deviation, early-give-up rate, accuracy, difficulty/stopping probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, patching restoration rate, steering accuracy gain and length change, specificity, fluency, Spearman with distance/resource.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Reasoning length is confounded with tokenizer efficiency across scripts (non-Latin scripts use more tokens per step); we measure length in reasoning STEPS (parsed) as the primary unit and report token counts separately, and hold true difficulty fixed via parallel items. 2. Probe decodability of a 'difficulty' or 'effort' signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used controller; we require the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering (Exp. 6) to promote correlation to mechanism. 3. Under-reasoning could genuinely reflect weaker reasoning ability, not mis-allocated effort; the core test is whether injecting the high-resource EFFORT signal (not the reasoning content) restores correctness, and whether steering to lengthen reasoning recovers accuracy — distinguishing effort mis-allocation from competence deficit. 4. Steering to lengthen reasoning may induce rambling/overthinking that hurts accuracy (given the inverted-U); we tune dose and report the length-accuracy trade-off curve and specificity controls. 5. Parsing reasoning steps and detecting give-up across languages is noisy; we use a validated multilingual step-parser plus human spot-checks and native-speaker validation of translated items. 6. Strong models may already allocate effort well, shrinking the effect; the low-resource languages, harder items, and the reasoning-distilled model (which language-mixes more) provide power, and even documenting the effect on a subset is informative. 7. Findings may be model-specific; four models across families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: in_context_language_integration
Title: Surface Trick or Real Integration? Whether In-Context Acquired Languages Enter the Shared Concept Space of LLMs, and Why Grammar Rules Fail
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM 'learns' an unseen language on the fly from an in-context grammar book plus dictionary/parallel examples, dictionary-driven word translation is routed through the model's language-agnostic shared concept space (recruiting the same concept-induction machinery as pretrained languages), whereas declarative grammar-rule application is NOT: the retrieved rule sits inertly in context and never causally shapes the concept-space computation. Consequently, the well-documented behavioral failure of grammar explanations (vs. parallel examples) is mechanistically an integration/binding failure, not a retrieval failure, and it worsens with the typological distance between the unseen language's grammar and the model's dominant languages.
Related Work: The MTOB line established behaviorally that LLMs can translate unseen languages from an in-context grammar book (Tanzer et al. 2024), but that nearly all gains come from parallel examples rather than grammatical explanations (Aycock et al. 2024), that rule retrieval and complex-rule application are the bottlenecks (ZhuangRules 2025; DiPMT++ 2024; LINGOLLM 2024), and that enciphered-language controls isolate genuine in-context learning (Manchu 2025). Separately, interpretability work shows pretrained languages share a language-agnostic concept space (Semantic Hub 2024), that concept-induction heads carry language-independent word meanings and mediate translation while token-induction heads copy verbatim (Dual-Route Induction 2025), that an in-context 'task recognition' point exists in middle layers (Where does In-context Translation Happen 2024), and that low-resource outputs degrade at lossy final-layer translation features (MALT 2025). ALL grammar-book work is behavioral; ALL concept-space/induction work studies PRETRAINED languages. None asks whether an unseen, in-context-acquired language is integrated into the shared concept space, whether its word-translation reuses concept-induction heads while its grammar-rule application does not, or locates WHERE grammar-rule application fails internally. We uniquely give the first mechanistic account of on-the-fly language acquisition, reframing the grammar-vs-examples asymmetry as a shared-concept-space integration/binding failure with a causal test and a targeted intervention.
Abstract: Large language models can be taught an unseen language on the fly by placing a grammar book, dictionary, and a few parallel sentences in their context. Yet a striking behavioral regularity has emerged: models exploit the dictionary and parallel examples but seem unable to make use of the declarative grammar explanations. We ask why, mechanistically. We hypothesize that on-the-fly language acquisition is not uniform: dictionary-driven word translation is routed through the model's pre-existing language-agnostic concept space (reusing the concept-induction machinery that mediates translation among pretrained languages), whereas grammar-rule application never enters that space, so a retrieved rule remains inert context text rather than a computation that reshapes the internal representation. Under this view the grammar-vs-examples asymmetry is an integration/binding failure, not a retrieval failure. We test three claims. First, using enciphered and genuinely unseen languages (Kalamang, Zhuang, enciphered Manchu) to remove pretrained knowledge, we show that unseen-language word representations become linearly aligned with the shared concept space and that ablating concept-induction heads collapses in-context word translation, evidencing real integration for lexical items. Second, via activation patching we show that correctly applying a provided grammar rule (agreement, word order, case) causally depends on mid-layer concept-space components, and that failures occur when the unseen sentence bypasses these components and is instead copied verbatim by token-induction heads. Third, we predict integration strength for both lexis and grammar declines with the typological distance between the unseen language and the model's dominant languages, and that a training-free intervention that boosts routing through the concept space at rule-application positions improves grammar-rule accuracy. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Data & controls: Use three regimes to isolate genuine in-context acquisition: (a) truly unseen endangered languages with public resources (Kalamang via MTOB, Zhuang via DiPMT++, plus a LINGOLLM language), (b) ENCIPHERED pretrained languages (Manchu-cipher style: a systematic substitution cipher applied to a known language so no parametric knowledge exists but ground truth is exact), and (c) a pretrained low-resource language as an 'already-integrated' upper-bound control. Provide dictionary + grammar-rule snippets + k parallel examples in context. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral decomposition: replicate the grammar-vs-examples asymmetry and further split by task type: WORD translation (dictionary-driven) vs GRAMMAR-rule application (agreement/word-order/case items constructed with ZhuangRules-style modular rules). Metrics: word-translation accuracy, per-rule application accuracy (rule provided in context), chrF. 3. Concept-space integration probe (lexis): train a linear map from a pretrained-language shared-concept probe and test whether unseen-language word representations at concept-induction-head output positions align with the shared concept direction; measure cross-lingual decodability of the intended concept from the unseen token. Contrast enciphered (must be learned in-context) vs pretrained. 4. Causal test for lexis: ablate the concept-induction heads identified via the Dual-Route method and measure collapse of in-context word translation (predict large drop) vs ablating token-induction heads (predict verbatim-copy behavior); this establishes lexical integration is real and concept-mediated. 5. Grammar-rule application locus (core causal test): for minimal-pair sentences where correct output requires applying a provided rule (e.g., verb agreement, argument order), run a CORRECT-application context vs an INCORRECT/absent-rule context and activation-patch mid-layer concept-space components between them; identify the minimal set whose patching flips rule-correct vs rule-violating output. Prediction: correct rule application causally depends on mid-layer concept-space components, and failures coincide with the unseen sentence being routed through token-induction (verbatim-copy) rather than concept-induction heads. 6. Integration-failure signature: measure, per item, the fraction of the unseen sentence processed by concept- vs token-induction heads; test that grammar-rule FAILURES have higher token-induction (copy) reliance than successes, while lexical successes rely on concept-induction. 7. Typological-distance dose-response: correlate lexical-integration strength and grammar-rule accuracy with lang2vec typological/word-order distance between the unseen language and the model's dominant languages (Spearman); predict grammar integration degrades faster than lexical integration with distance. 8. Targeted intervention: at rule-application token positions, steer/upweight routing through the concept-space direction (or amplify concept-induction-head contribution) and measure grammar-rule accuracy gain, with specificity (word-translation and fluency unchanged). Compare against (i) providing an extra parallel example instead, (ii) code-augmented rule prompting (ZhuangRules baseline), (iii) no intervention. 9. Ablations: layer sweep for where rule application is malleable; k (number of parallel examples) vs pure-grammar conditions; enciphered vs unseen consistency; model scale; probe transfer across models. Metrics throughout: word/grammar accuracy, chrF, concept-space alignment/decodability, concept- vs token-induction reliance, causal ablation drop, patching flip rate, Spearman with typological distance, intervention accuracy gain, specificity, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe alignment of unseen-language tokens to the concept space may reflect the readout basis rather than functional integration; the head-ablation (Exp. 4) and patching (Exp. 5) causal tests are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 2. Enciphered languages test in-context lexical mapping cleanly but may not fully mimic novel grammar; we therefore also use genuinely unseen languages (Kalamang, Zhuang) and report both. 3. The clean concept-vs-token induction dichotomy from prior work may be fuzzier for unseen languages, weakening the failure-signature story; we validate the head split per model before use and report degree of separation honestly. 4. Grammar-rule items require careful construction so the rule (not lexical guessing) determines the answer; we use modular ZhuangRules-style minimal pairs validated by linguists/native materials. 5. It is possible models DO integrate grammar for simple rules and only fail on complex ones (consistent with ZhuangRules); this is an informative graded outcome and we stratify by rule complexity. 6. Tokenization of unseen scripts/orthographies is uneven; we use last-token/pooled representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. The intervention may trade grammar gains for fluency or lexical accuracy; we report the full trade-off and specificity. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families and three language regimes address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: kinship_granularity_collapse
Title: Uncle or Mother's-Younger-Brother? How the Query Language's Kinship System Sets the Granularity of Relational Reasoning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a largely language-agnostic genealogical-tree representation of a family, but the SPECIFIC kin category they output is resolved through a granularity setting covertly fixed by the query language's kinship system. For a fixed genealogical fact, the model tends to collapse to the (usually coarser, English-like) kin distinctions of its dominant language, systematically failing to produce the finer distinctions (maternal vs paternal side, relative age, gender) that a target language grammaticalizes. This 'granularity collapse' is a category-resolution failure downstream of a correctly-computed genealogical tree, it scales with the kinship-typology distance between the query language and the dominant language (not with resource level), and it is carried by a locatable, steerable granularity signal separable from the tree representation.
Related Work: Anthropology provides authoritative resources: Kinbank (210,903 kinterms, 1,229 languages, 2023) and typologies of kinship systems (Eskimo/Sudanese/Hawaiian; classificatory vs descriptive; bifurcate-merging), plus efficient-communication accounts of which semantic features (side, generation, relative age, gender) each system encodes (2025). Cross-linguistic semantic-alignment work (Thompson et al. 2018) finds kinship is highly aligned yet structurally divergent across languages. On the model side, LLMs are shown to encode genealogical relations in a tree-like, causally-relevant subspace (Investigating Representation Universality, 2024), to decode relations via linear relational embeddings (Hernandez et al. 2023; LRC 2023; Locating Relational Concepts 2024), and to share grammatical/semantic concept directions across languages (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Semantic Hub 2024). Crucially, ALL genealogical/relational interpretability work is monolingual and treats kin categories as fixed, and ALL kinship-typology work is anthropological/behavioral with no mechanistic account inside an LLM. None asks whether the query language covertly sets the GRANULARITY at which a correctly-represented genealogical tree is read out into kin terms, nor gives a causal, steerable granularity mechanism. We uniquely port kinship-system typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, dissociating a shared tree from a language-set category-resolution step, and provide a causal fix.
Abstract: Languages carve the family tree very differently: English lumps father's and mother's brother into one 'uncle', while Chinese, Turkish, Hindi and many others obligatorily distinguish the paternal from the maternal side, elder from younger sibling, or the gender of the linking relative. A competent multilingual model must recover the same underlying genealogy but then name relatives at whatever granularity the target language demands. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs instead default to the coarser kin categories of their dominant language. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-agnostic genealogical-tree representation, but resolve it into kin terms through a granularity setting covertly fixed by the query language, causing systematic 'granularity collapse': for a fixed genealogical fact, the model omits the finer side/age/gender distinctions a target language grammaticalizes and produces an over-general, English-like term. We build KIN-RESOLVE, controlled genealogy-description-plus-question items whose correct kin term differs across kinship systems, rendered across 12+ languages spanning Eskimo, Sudanese, bifurcate-merging and other typologies, using Kinbank ground-truth terms. Behaviorally we measure per-language granularity-collapse rate and dissociate it from resource level via kinship-typology distance. Mechanistically we probe for a shared genealogical-tree subspace that transfers across languages, use activation patching to show the tree is correctly computed even when the term is wrong (localizing failure to a late category-resolution step), and recover a granularity direction that we steer to repair or induce collapse without altering the underlying genealogy.
