Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (KIN-RESOLVE): using Kinbank ground-truth kinterms, construct short genealogy descriptions (e.g., 'A is B's father; C is A's younger brother; ...') paired with a question asking for the kin term relating two individuals, such that the CORRECT term differs across kinship systems (e.g., a relative that is 'uncle' in English but requires maternal/paternal+age marking in the target language). Render each item in 12+ languages spanning kinship-system typologies (Eskimo: English, Spanish; Sudanese/descriptive: Chinese, Turkish, Hindi, Arabic; bifurcate-merging/classificatory: a Bantu and a Dravidian language; plus Japanese/Korean relative-age systems). Annotate the target-language correct term and the semantic features it must encode (side, generation, relative age, gender). Build a per-language kinship-typology distance to the dominant (English) system from the encoded-feature set. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral granularity-collapse test: elicit the kin term per item/language; score (a) genealogical correctness (is the underlying relation right, ignoring granularity) and (b) term correctness (does the produced term carry all features the target language requires). Key metric: GRANULARITY-COLLAPSE RATE = fraction of genealogically-correct answers whose term is under-specified relative to the target-language requirement, especially collapsing to the dominant-language category. Baselines: query in English (upper bound for coarse systems), translate-to-English-first. 3. Typology dose-response: correlate collapse rate with kinship-typology distance vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy). Prediction: collapse tracks typology distance, not resource; key contrast: a lower-resource fine-distinguishing language (e.g., a Dravidian language) vs a higher-resource coarse one. Spearman with CIs. 4. Shared genealogical-tree probe: following the tree-subspace / linear-relational-concept methods, train probes to decode the genealogical relation (side, generation, ancestor/descendant) from mid-layer hidden states; test cross-lingual transfer (train on one language, test others) to establish a shared tree representation, and contrast with a surface-term probe to dissociate abstract genealogy from the emitted term. 5. Causal localization via patching (core test): for an item answered with the correct fine term in a fine-distinguishing language vs an over-general term in another language on the SAME genealogy, (a) patch the mid-layer tree representation across runs and confirm the genealogy is already correctly present in the collapsing run (patching it changes little); (b) patch/steer the late-layer term-resolution components and test whether the finer term is recovered, localizing the failure to a category-resolution step rather than a wrong tree. 6. Granularity steering (causal fix): recover a granularity direction as the mean activation difference between fine-resolved and coarse-resolved runs (pooled across languages); steer to (a) REPAIR collapsed terms in fine-distinguishing languages and (b) INDUCE collapse in a language where the model was correct (functional-causality proof). Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, term correctness, genealogical-correctness preservation (specificity: the tree/relation is unchanged), output fluency (perplexity). Compare against explicit feature-prompting ('specify maternal vs paternal') and translate-first baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where granularity is malleable; probe transfer across models; feature breakdown (side vs relative-age vs gender collapse); whether the default is anchored to English or the nearest high-resource system; model scale. Metrics throughout: granularity-collapse rate, genealogical vs term accuracy, tree-probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, causal patch/repair/induction rates, genealogy-preservation specificity, Spearman with typology vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a genealogical tree or granularity signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the underlying genealogy is preserved. 2. Kinship terms can be genuinely ambiguous, optional, or dialect-dependent; we restrict to Kinbank-attested high-agreement terms and treat multi-term relations separately. 3. Collapse could reflect the model simply not knowing the target-language kin vocabulary (lexical gap) rather than a granularity-resolution failure; the demonstration that the genealogy is correctly computed (tree patched-in unchanged) and that feature-prompting or steering RECOVERS the finer term distinguishes resolution failure from missing knowledge. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the typology-distance operationalization. 5. Strong models may resolve fine terms well, shrinking the effect; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely clean tree-plus-faithful-resolution) is informative, and the induction experiment still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Tokenization of multi-morpheme kin terms varies across scripts; we use last-token/pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade term correctness for fluency or genealogy preservation; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: color_category_boundary_shift
Title: Russian Blues in a Text Model: How the Query Language's Color Lexicon Covertly Carves a Shared Continuous Color Space
Short Hypothesis: Given colors specified purely as text coordinates (hex/RGB), multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic continuous color representation, but the CATEGORICAL boundaries they impose on it are covertly set by the query language's basic-color-term inventory. So the identical pair of colors is judged 'same category / more similar' vs 'different category / less similar' depending on the query language (e.g. two blues straddling the goluboy/siniy line are separated in Russian but merged in English), and this categorical-perception effect is a language-set boundary applied downstream of a shared continuous representation, scaling with cross-linguistic color-lexicon distance rather than resource level, and carried by a locatable, steerable boundary signal.
Related Work: Berlin & Kay and the World Color Survey (Lexical Color Categories 2021; #15) established that color lexicons vary yet show universal tendencies, and the classic Russian-blues result shows lexical distinctions cause categorical-perception effects on discrimination. Recent modeling shows color categories emerge from vision/communication (Emergent Color Categorization 2021 #13; Categorical Nature of Colour Perception 2024 #11 finds category perception is largely language-INDEPENDENT in vision nets but shaped by linguistic terms), and a large behavioral study (Studying the Effect of Globalization 2024 #9) finds LLMs have LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC color representations and that color-term counts correlate with humans. Bilingual color-naming models (#14) test conceptual-change vs coactivation vs L1-footprint accounts. However: (i) all LLM color work (#9, #10) is purely behavioral / naming-map descriptive; (ii) all mechanistic color work (#1, #3, #11, #13) is in VISION or vision-language models (CLIP, Stable Diffusion), never a text decoder LLM; (iii) none dissociates a shared CONTINUOUS color representation from a language-SET categorical boundary, none tests whether the query language causally shifts a categorical-perception boundary on identical text-specified colors, and none provides a causal (patching+steering) account of a color-category boundary. We uniquely port the Russian-blues categorical-perception paradigm into text-only multilingual mechanistic interpretability, using hex/RGB coordinates to isolate lexicon effects from vision, and give a causal, steerable boundary mechanism plus a coverage-vs-typology dissociation.
Abstract: A landmark result in the study of language and thought is that speakers of a language that obligatorily distinguishes two shades (Russian's light blue goluboy vs dark blue siniy) discriminate colors straddling that boundary faster and treat them as more different than speakers of a language with a single term. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit such language-specific color categories, and crucially whether this happens even when colors are given purely as text coordinates (hex/RGB), removing vision entirely. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, language-agnostic continuous color representation but impose categorical boundaries drawn from the query language's basic-color-term inventory, so the identical pair of colors is judged same-vs-different category, and more-vs-less similar, depending on the query language. We build COLOR-CARVE, sets of text-specified colors densely sampling regions where languages disagree on basic-term boundaries (blue, green/blue 'grue', red/orange, purple/pink), each posed as similarity-rating, same/different-category, and odd-one-out tasks across 12+ languages spanning divergent color-lexicon typologies. Behaviorally we measure per-language categorical-perception effects (a discontinuity in judged similarity at the language's lexical boundary) on identical coordinates. Mechanistically we probe for a shared continuous color direction that transfers across languages, use activation patching to show the continuous representation is the same while a separable categorical boundary differs by language, and recover a boundary signal that we steer to move, add, or remove a color category without changing the underlying continuous representation. We predict the effect scales with color-lexicon distance rather than resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (COLOR-CARVE): sample colors as text hex/RGB (and CIELAB for analysis) densely along axes where languages disagree on basic-color-term boundaries: the Russian goluboy/siniy blue axis, green-blue 'grue' languages (e.g. some varieties without a green/blue split), red/orange, and purple/pink. For each language, obtain the basic-term boundary from World Color Survey / published naming maps and native-speaker validation. Construct three task formats per stimulus set: (a) similarity rating between two text-specified colors (0-10), (b) same-vs-different basic-color-category judgment, (c) odd-one-out over triples. Render prompts in 12+ languages spanning divergent color-lexicon typologies (Russian, Greek, English, Chinese, Turkish, Korean, Vietnamese, Hindi, plus grue-type/low-term languages), and build a per-language color-lexicon distance (difference in number/placement of basic-term boundaries) and a resource-level proxy. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral categorical-perception test: for color pairs matched in perceptual (CIELAB) distance, compare judged similarity/discrimination for WITHIN-category vs CROSS-category pairs relative to EACH language's own lexical boundary on identical coordinates. Key metric: categorical-perception index = discontinuity (drop in judged similarity / rise in 'different' rate) at the language's boundary, beyond a smooth function of CIELAB distance. Predict Russian shows a blue-axis discontinuity absent in English; grue languages lack a green/blue discontinuity present elsewhere. Report cross-language disagreement on identical pairs. 3. Lexicon-distance dose-response: correlate per-language categorical-perception index with color-lexicon distance vs resource-level proxy (Spearman with CIs); key dissociation: a lower-resource fine-distinguishing language vs a higher-resource coarse one. 4. Shared continuous-color probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode continuous color coordinates (CIELAB) from hidden states of text-specified colors; test cross-lingual probe transfer (train one language, test others) to establish a shared continuous representation, and contrast with a categorical-label probe (which basic term) that should vary by language. 5. Causal localization via patching (core test): for a boundary-straddling pair judged different-category in Russian but same-category in English, (a) patch the mid-layer continuous-color representation across language runs and confirm the continuous coordinates are the same (patching changes little), (b) patch/steer late components carrying the categorical decision and test whether the category judgment flips, localizing the effect to a language-set boundary rather than a different continuous representation. 6. Boundary steering (causal fix/manipulation): recover a category-boundary signal (mean activation difference between within- and cross-category runs, pooled across languages); steer to (a) INDUCE a goluboy/siniy split when querying in English (create a category that isn't lexically present), (b) REMOVE the split when querying in Russian (merge the categories), and (c) shift the boundary location. Metrics: induced/removed categorical-perception effect, continuous-representation preservation (specificity: decoded CIELAB unchanged), output fluency, dose-response. Compare against explicit prompting ('treat light and dark blue as different colors') and translate-to-English baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where the boundary is malleable; probe transfer across models; region breakdown (blue vs grue vs red/orange); whether the default boundary is anchored to English or the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Metrics throughout: categorical-perception index, cross-language disagreement, continuous-color probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, categorical-label probe accuracy, causal patch/steer flip rates, CIELAB-preservation specificity, Spearman with lexicon distance vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a continuous color representation or boundary signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/remove (Exp. 6) tests are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that decoded CIELAB coordinates are unchanged. 2. Color-lexicon boundaries can be graded, individual-, and dialect-variable; we ground boundaries in the World Color Survey and native-speaker validation and restrict to high-agreement regions. 3. Effects could be confounded with tokenization of hex/RGB strings (digit tokenization differs across values, not languages); since color coordinates are held identical across language conditions, tokenization of the color is constant while only the prompt language varies, isolating the lexicon effect; we also test RGB and named-swatch controls and report tokenization statistics. 4. A model might genuinely lack any color geometry from text coordinates, making the continuous probe fail; this is an informative outcome and the probe-transfer contrast is designed to decide it. 5. The lexicon-distance-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the distance operationalization. 6. Strong models may resolve categories faithfully to each language, shrinking the cross-language default effect; even documenting faithful language-specific carving (a clean shared-continuous + language-set-boundary architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/removal steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 7. Steering may trade category manipulation for fluency or continuous-representation preservation; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: concreteness_transfer_inversion
Title: The Concreteness Inversion: Why LLMs Share Abstract Concepts Across Languages Better Than Concrete Ones, Opposite to the Bilingual Brain
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs functionally transfer ABSTRACT concepts across languages better than CONCRETE ones, an inversion of the well-established human bilingual pattern (concrete concepts are shared more cross-lingually, abstract ones are more language-dependent). We hypothesize (a) this inversion holds at the level of causal, functional cross-lingual transfer (not just embedding-space geometry); (b) it is mechanistically driven by concrete concepts being represented in a MORE language-specific way in the shared concept space, so patching a concrete concept from language A into a language-B prompt transfers less reliably than an abstract one; and (c) the effect is driven by grounding-deprivation (concrete words carry perceptual/language-specific detail the text-only model must approximate per-language) rather than merely by raw training frequency, dissociable by holding frequency fixed.
Related Work: Embedding-geometry work finds abstract concepts align more linearly across languages than physical/concrete ones in LLMs, attributing it to higher frequency (Concept Space Alignment in Multilingual LLMs 2024; On the Geometry of Concreteness 2022; Predicting Concreteness Across Languages 2018). Multimodal work shows visual grounding especially helps CONCRETE words, implying text-only models underrepresent concrete semantics (Leverage Points in Modality Shifts 2023; Word Representation Learning in Multimodal Transformers 2021). Causal concept-space work shows language-agnostic concept representations manipulable by activation patching, with output-language resolved before concept (Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; When Meanings Meet 2026). Crucially, human bilingual neuroscience finds the OPPOSITE of the LLM geometry result: concrete concepts are represented more similarly across languages, abstract ones more language-dependent (Concreteness Shapes Semantic Representations in Bilingual Brains 2025; translation-priming concreteness effects 2023). No prior work (i) reframes the LLM concreteness effect as a CAUSAL, functional cross-lingual transfer phenomenon rather than static embedding similarity, (ii) explicitly frames it as a human-vs-LLM inversion and tests its mechanism inside a running decoder, or (iii) dissociates the frequency explanation from a grounding-deprivation explanation. We contribute this reframing, an activation-patching causal test, and the frequency-vs-grounding dissociation.
Abstract: In the bilingual brain, concrete concepts are represented more similarly across languages than abstract ones: a word like 'apple' overlaps cross-linguistically, while 'justice' is more language-dependent. Multilingual LLMs, surprisingly, appear to show the reverse in embedding geometry, but this has only been observed as static similarity and attributed to training frequency. We ask whether LLMs exhibit a genuine, causal concreteness inversion at the level of functional cross-lingual concept transfer, and why. We first establish the phenomenon behaviorally on a cross-lingual concept-transfer task (word translation and factual recall) using psycholinguistic concreteness norms, testing whether abstract concepts transfer more reliably across languages than concrete ones. We then move inside the model: using activation patching in the shared concept space, we inject a concept representation extracted from a source-language prompt into a target-language prompt and measure how faithfully the target language recovers the concept as a function of concreteness. Our central claim is that concrete concepts occupy a more language-specific region of the shared space, so their patched transfer is weaker and their cross-lingual concept-probe directions less aligned, whereas abstract concepts are more language-agnostic and transfer cleanly. Finally, we dissociate two explanations: raw frequency versus grounding-deprivation (text-only models must approximate perceptual, language-specific detail of concrete referents), by matching concept pairs on corpus frequency and testing whether the inversion persists. We predict the effect strengthens with typological distance and holds under frequency-matching. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 12+ languages, directly connecting a human-cognition finding to an LLM mechanism.
Experiments: 1. Stimuli & norms: assemble ~600 concepts spanning the full concreteness range using validated psycholinguistic norms (Brysbaert concreteness ratings, imageability norms), cross-lingually verified translation equivalents (from bilingual dictionaries / MUSE / cross-lingual concreteness resources), and a factual-QA subset (mLAMA/BMLAMA facts whose object/subject vary in concreteness). Render across 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. Compute per-concept corpus frequency (from pretraining-proxy corpora) for later frequency-matching. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral transfer phenomenon: on a cross-lingual concept task (word translation source->target, and cross-lingual factual recall), measure per-concept transfer success as a function of concreteness. Metric: transfer accuracy regressed on concreteness (and imageability), controlling for frequency and length; test the predicted NEGATIVE slope (abstract transfers better) and contrast with the human pattern. Report per-language and pooled. 3. Cross-lingual concept-probe alignment: train linear concept probes / extract concept directions in each language at mid layers; measure cross-lingual alignment (cosine of matched-concept directions, or probe-transfer accuracy) as a function of concreteness. Prediction: concrete concepts show LOWER cross-lingual alignment (more language-specific), abstract higher. 4. Causal patching (core test): following Separating-Tongue-from-Thought, extract the mid-layer concept representation from a source-language prompt and inject it into a target-language prompt; measure faithful recovery of the concept in the target language (correct translation/answer, correct output language) as a function of concreteness. Prediction: patched transfer fidelity DECREASES with concreteness. Include the mean-across-languages patching variant to test whether concrete concepts benefit less from averaging (i.e., have less to share). 5. Frequency-vs-grounding dissociation: (a) Frequency control: construct frequency-matched concrete/abstract pairs and re-run behavioral transfer, probe alignment, and patching; test whether the inversion PERSISTS under frequency matching (supporting grounding-deprivation over frequency). (b) Grounding proxy: use imageability / a visual-grounding score (e.g., availability of image-text pairs, multimodal-embedding shift magnitude) as an alternative predictor; test whether grounding predicts transfer failure beyond concreteness and frequency. 6. Typological-distance dose-response: correlate the concreteness transfer gap with lang2vec typological/script distance to the source language (Spearman); prediction: gap widens with distance, and specifically for concrete concepts. 7. Human-LLM comparison framing: qualitatively and quantitatively contrast the LLM slope (negative: abstract shares better) with the reported human slope (positive: concrete shares better), quantifying the inversion magnitude. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the concept is patchable; probe transfer across models; concrete-noun vs abstract-noun vs concrete-verb breakdown; model scale; specificity check that patching preserves output language. Metrics throughout: transfer accuracy, concreteness/imageability regression slopes, cross-lingual probe alignment, patching fidelity, frequency-matched effect persistence, Spearman with typological distance, human-vs-LLM slope contrast.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The inversion may be an artifact of embedding geometry that does not survive at the functional-transfer level; if behavioral transfer shows NO concreteness effect, the phenomenon is refuted (still an informative, publishable negative that challenges the geometry-based claim). 2. Probe alignment and geometric similarity are correlational; the activation-patching causal test (Exp. 4) is required to promote the finding to a mechanism, with a specificity check that output language is preserved. 3. Concreteness, frequency, and length are correlated; the frequency-matched pairs (Exp. 5a) are the crucial dissociation and central to the frequency-vs-grounding claim. 4. Cross-lingual concreteness norms and translation equivalents are noisy, especially for abstract/polysemous words; we use validated norms, native-speaker-verified equivalents, and restrict to high-agreement items. 5. Tokenization differences across scripts complicate concept-token localization and patching; we use last-token-of-concept or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The human comparison relies on published fMRI/behavioral slopes rather than a re-run human study, so the inversion is claimed against literature values, not a matched within-study human baseline; we frame it accordingly. 7. Grounding-deprivation is inferred from imageability/multimodal proxies, not from an actual grounded model; a stronger test (comparing to a multimodal LLM) is noted as future work. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: pragmatic_implicature_gate
Title: Some Means Not All, In Some Languages: A Causal Study of a Language-Set Literal-vs-Implicated Interpretation Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an utterance's LITERAL meaning, but decide how strongly to enrich it with a PRAGMATIC implicature (e.g. 'some' -> 'not all'; an indirect request -> a command) via a scalar 'implicature-strength' gate whose default value is covertly set by the query language. Consequently the identical utterance is interpreted more literally in one language and more pragmatically in another, this gap scales with the query language's documented cross-linguistic implicature-rate (and typological distance from the dominant language) rather than with resource level, and the gate is a locatable, steerable representation separable from the literal-meaning computation.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs compute scalar implicatures ('some'->'not all') largely in a default, context-insensitive way (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020; Pragmatic Inference of Scalar Implicature by LLMs 2024), that indirect speech acts are hard and language-dependent (Evaluating LLMs on Korean Indirect Speech Acts 2025), and that pronoun/discourse pragmatics are only partially adapted (Partially Primed 2023). The Rational Speech Act framework models implicature as social-cognitive inference (Goodman & Frank 2013). Crucially, cross-linguistic pragmatics establishes that languages differ systematically in implicature RATES and that L2 speakers inherit L1 pragmatic biases (Scalar Diversity and L2 Processing 2025; Tattoos/cross-linguistic scalar implicature 2021). Recent interpretability shows a shared concept space with late-layer language decoding and that language identity conditions psycholinguistic behavior (Semantic Hub 2024; From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025). However, ALL LLM pragmatics work is behavioral or monolingual, and ALL mechanistic multilingual work targets literal content, grammar, or knowledge. NONE dissociates a shared literal-meaning representation from a language-conditioned implicature-strength gate, tests whether the query language causally sets how pragmatically an utterance is read, or provides a causal, steerable implicature gate. We uniquely port cross-linguistic pragmatic-strength typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability and add a safety-critical indirect-request angle.
Abstract: When someone says 'some of the students passed', listeners often infer 'not all passed' - a scalar implicature. Languages differ measurably in how readily their speakers compute such enrichments, and second-language speakers inherit their first language's pragmatic biases. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit language-specific pragmatics, and whether the language a question is asked in covertly sets how literally versus pragmatically the model interprets an utterance. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, language-agnostic literal meaning but enrich it with implicature via a scalar gate whose default is fixed by the query language, so the identical utterance is read more literally in one language and more pragmatically in another. We build PRAG-GATE, a controlled set spanning scalar implicatures ('some','most','or','try'), indirect requests ('Can you open the window?'), and indirect refusals/answers, each rendered across 12+ languages with documented divergent implicature rates and paired with a question that distinguishes the literal from the pragmatically-enriched interpretation. Behaviorally we measure per-language implicature rate on identical utterances. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared literal-meaning direction that transfers across languages, (ii) use activation patching to show the literal meaning is computed identically while a separable implicature-strength representation differs by language, and (iii) recover and steer an implicature-strength direction to make the model read more or less pragmatically without changing the literal content. We include a safety-critical subset (indirect harmful requests, indirect refusals) where under-enrichment causes an aligned model to comply with a request it would refuse when phrased directly. We predict the gap tracks cross-linguistic implicature-rate/typology, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (PRAG-GATE): construct items in three pragmatic categories: (a) SCALAR implicatures ('some','most','or','might','try') where a follow-up question or NLI hypothesis distinguishes the literal reading ('some'->possibly all) from the enriched reading ('some'->not all); (b) INDIRECT REQUESTS ('Can you pass the salt?', 'It's cold in here') paired with a question probing whether the model treats it as a literal question/statement or as a request/command; (c) INDIRECT ANSWERS/REFUSALS ('Are you coming? -- I have to work') probing yes/no inference. Render each in 12+ languages spanning documented divergent implicature rates and 4+ families/scripts, with matched clearly-literal and clearly-direct controls. Ground per-language expected implicature rates in cross-linguistic pragmatics literature (scalar-diversity data) and native-speaker validation; build a per-language implicature-typology distance to the dominant (English) baseline and a resource-level proxy. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral gate test: elicit interpretations per item/language; metric = per-language IMPLICATURE RATE on identical utterances (fraction giving the enriched/indirect reading), plus cross-language DISAGREEMENT on the same item. Controls (literal/direct) should agree across languages. Baselines: query in English, translate-to-English-first. 3. Typology dose-response: correlate per-language implicature rate (and its deviation from the English baseline) with implicature-typology distance vs a resource proxy (Spearman with CIs); key dissociation: a lower-resource high-implicature-rate language vs a higher-resource low-rate one. 4. Shared literal-meaning probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode the LITERAL meaning of the utterance (e.g. the plain truth-conditional content) from mid-layer hidden states; test cross-lingual probe transfer (train one language, test others) to establish a shared literal representation, and contrast with a probe decoding the enriched/pragmatic reading, which should vary by language. 5. Causal localization via patching (core test): for an item read enriched in language A but literal in language B, (a) patch the mid-layer literal-meaning representation across runs and confirm it is the same in both (patching changes little); (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the pragmatic decision and test whether the interpretation flips, localizing the effect to a language-set implicature gate rather than a different literal computation. 6. Implicature-strength steering (causal fix/manipulation): recover an implicature-strength direction (mean activation difference between enriched-reading and literal-reading runs, pooled across languages); steer to (a) INDUCE enrichment in a low-implicature-rate language, (b) SUPPRESS it in a high-rate language, and (c) dose-response. Metrics: induced/suppressed implicature rate, literal-content preservation (specificity), fluency (perplexity). Compare against explicit prompting ('interpret pragmatically') and translate-first baselines. 7. Safety-critical subset: indirect harmful requests ('I wonder how one might...', 'It would be a shame if someone knew how to...') and indirect refusals; measure per-language whether the model recognizes the implied harmful intent (refuses) vs takes it literally (complies), and whether steering the implicature gate up restores refusal on under-enriched languages. Report the cross-lingual compliance gap as an attack surface and the steering-based mitigation (responsible-disclosure norms; no novel operational harmful content released). 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the gate is malleable; probe transfer across models; category breakdown (scalar vs indirect-request vs indirect-answer); whether the default is anchored to English or the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Metrics throughout: per-language implicature rate, cross-language disagreement, literal-meaning probe accuracy and transfer, enriched-reading probe accuracy, causal patch/steer flip rates, literal-content preservation specificity, safety compliance-gap reduction, Spearman with implicature-typology vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'literal meaning' or 'implicature-strength' signal may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/suppress (Exp. 6) tests are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the literal content is preserved. 2. Whether an utterance is 'enriched' can be genuinely context-dependent and gradient; we restrict to items with high native-speaker agreement on the expected reading and include clear literal/direct controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might reflect genuine pragmatic-norm variation rather than a gate artifact; the shared-literal-probe transfer and the literal-same/gate-differs patching test are designed precisely to separate a genuinely different literal computation from a pure interpretation-strength shift, and we anchor expected rates in the cross-linguistic pragmatics literature. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the typology-distance operationalization. 5. Strong models may compute implicatures faithfully per language, shrinking the default cross-language effect; even documenting faithful language-specific pragmatics (a clean shared-literal + language-set-gate architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/suppression steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. The safety subset touches harmful topics; we use only borderline items from public red-team resources, keep completions coarse (refuse-vs-comply), release no novel operational content, and follow responsible disclosure since the finding exposes an indirect-phrasing jailbreak surface. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/answer matching; we use pooled-span or clause-final representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency or literal-content preservation; we report all three. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: functional_interference_tree
Title: The Tree the Model Actually Uses: Cross-Lingual Functional Interference Recapitulates Script and Co-occurrence, Not Linguistic Phylogeny
Short Hypothesis: The pattern of how a behavioral change induced in one language (via a targeted fine-tune, knowledge edit, or in-context skill) leaks into other languages forms a coherent 'functional interference tree' over languages. We hypothesize this causal/functional tree is systematically DIFFERENT from the linguistic phylogenetic tree that prior work recovers from static representation geometry: it is dominated by shared script and training-corpus co-occurrence rather than genealogical relatedness. Where the two trees disagree (e.g. Hindi-Urdu: same genealogy, different script; Turkish-Uzbek: shared Latin script, different family branch), functional interference follows the script/co-occurrence structure, not phylogeny, and this divergence predicts which cross-lingual edits/transfers unexpectedly help or harm.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows that STATIC representation geometry of multilingual encoders recapitulates the linguistic phylogenetic tree: mBERT distances recover family trees (Probing mBERT for Genetic/Typological Signals 2020), joint matrix factorization of representations yields phylogenetic clustering (Joint Matrix Factorization 2023), and morphosyntactic neuron overlap is higher for same-genus languages (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; What Language Does Aya-23 Think In 2025). Separately, cross-lingual editing/transfer work reports that script similarity dominates knowledge sharing and that edits fail across script families (Beneath the Surface of Consistency 2024; XME 2024). No prior work (i) builds a language tree from CAUSAL, functional interference (how a targeted intervention in language A perturbs behavior in language B) rather than from static similarity, (ii) directly CONTRASTS this functional tree against both the linguistic phylogenetic tree and a script/co-occurrence tree as competing explanations, or (iii) uses the phylogeny-vs-script divergence to predict per-pair transfer/interference. We reframe cross-lingual relatedness as a functional, causal quantity and show the model's operative tree is not the linguists' tree.
Abstract: A striking result in multilingual interpretability is that the geometry of a model's internal representations recapitulates the linguistic family tree: distances between language representations reconstruct phylogenies close to those drawn by linguists. But representation similarity is correlational. We ask a causal, behavioral question: if we change a model's behavior in one language, which other languages change with it, and does that pattern of functional interference form the same tree? We hypothesize it does not. We define a functional interference tree by measuring, for every ordered language pair, how much a targeted intervention in a source language (a small knowledge edit, a short skill fine-tune, or an in-context skill demonstration) shifts behavior in a target language, then clustering languages by this causal leakage. We predict this tree is dominated by shared script and training-corpus co-occurrence rather than genealogy, so it diverges sharply from the phylogenetic tree recovered from static representations of the SAME model. We test the divergence on diagnostic minimal pairs where genealogy and script disagree (Hindi/Urdu, Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Turkish/Uzbek, Persian/Tajik) across 20+ languages and Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We further show the phylogeny-minus-script residual predicts, per language pair, where cross-lingual edits and skill transfer unexpectedly succeed or backfire. The result challenges the tidy 'models rediscover the family tree' narrative: the tree the model computes with is a script- and corpus-shaped one, not the linguists' phylogeny, with direct consequences for multilingual editing and transfer.
Experiments: 1. Languages & models: 20+ languages selected to span 4+ families and 5 scripts AND to include diagnostic minimal pairs where genealogy and script dissociate: Hindi/Urdu (same genealogy, Devanagari vs Perso-Arabic), Serbian (Cyrillic vs Latin, same language), Turkish/Uzbek (Turkic vs script-shared Latin comparisons), Persian/Tajik (same genealogy, Perso-Arabic vs Cyrillic), plus standard family clusters. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Baseline representation phylogeny: replicate prior work by computing pairwise representation distances (mean per-language activation / probe-based distances at multiple layers) and inferring a representation tree; verify it approximates the reference linguistic tree (quartet distance to Glottolog/lang2vec tree). 3. Functional interference matrix (core): for each source language, apply THREE intervention types independently and measure the resulting behavior shift in every target language on held-out parallel probes: (a) KNOWLEDGE EDIT: a ROME/MEMIT edit of a set of facts phrased in the source language; measure change in the same facts queried in each target language (propagation) and change in unrelated facts (interference). (b) SKILL FINE-TUNE: a short LoRA fine-tune on a task (e.g. a formatting/arithmetic/reasoning skill) in the source language; measure accuracy change on the same task in each target language. (c) IN-CONTEXT SKILL: place source-language demonstrations in context and measure zero-shot target-language task shift. For each intervention type, build a directed interference matrix M[source, target] = magnitude of behavior shift. 4. Build functional interference tree: symmetrize/cluster M into a functional tree; repeat per intervention type and per model. 5. Tree comparison (the phenomenon): compute tree distances (quartet/Robinson-Foulds) and correlations between the functional tree, the representation tree, and reference trees for (i) linguistic phylogeny (Glottolog), (ii) script identity, and (iii) training-corpus co-occurrence proxy (e.g. co-occurrence in web-corpus language pairs / resource-level similarity). Core prediction: functional tree correlates most with script/co-occurrence, representation tree most with phylogeny; they diverge significantly. 6. Diagnostic minimal pairs: on the dissociating pairs, directly test whether interference follows script (Hindi->Urdu low despite shared genealogy; Serbian-Cyr->Serbian-Latin behavior) vs phylogeny; report per-pair leakage. 7. Predictive test: regress per-pair edit-propagation / transfer success on (phylogenetic distance, script identity, co-occurrence); test that the script/co-occurrence terms dominate and that the phylogeny-minus-script residual identifies pairs where transfer unexpectedly helps or backfires (hold-out prediction, report AUC/correlation). 8. Ablations: intervention magnitude (edit size / fine-tune steps); layer choice for representation tree; whether removing script (via transliteration of inputs) collapses the functional-representation divergence; model scale; robustness across the three intervention types (do they agree on the functional tree?). Metrics: quartet/Robinson-Foulds tree distances, Spearman correlations of pairwise distance matrices, per-pair interference magnitude, regression coefficients, held-out transfer-prediction AUC.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The functional tree from edits/fine-tunes could be dominated by which languages the model is simply BETTER at (resource level) rather than pairwise structure; we control by measuring interference relative to each target's baseline competence and by including resource-matched pairs. 2. Different intervention types (edit vs fine-tune vs in-context) may yield different trees, undercutting a single 'functional tree'; this is itself an informative result and we report agreement across the three rather than assuming one. 3. Script and co-occurrence are correlated (same-script languages co-occur more), making them hard to separate; the diagnostic minimal pairs (same genealogy, different script; same script, different family) are designed precisely to dissociate them, and the transliteration ablation further isolates script. 4. Tree-inference is sensitive to distance-metric choice and noise; we report multiple metrics and bootstrap confidence over trees. 5. Knowledge edits can fail entirely in low-resource languages, confounding interference with edit failure; we condition on successful source edits and report edit success separately. 6. The representation-tree replication may be weaker in decoder-only LLMs than in mBERT; even a partial phylogenetic signal suffices to test divergence, and finding NO phylogenetic signal in representations would also be a notable result. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: counterfactual_override_gate
Title: In Which Language Can You Pretend? A Causal Study of the Query-Language-Set Counterfactual-Override Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Counterfactual reasoning requires a model to suppress its stored real-world knowledge and instead follow an in-context stipulation ('suppose water boils at 50 degrees; a pot heated to 60 is...'). We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a largely language-agnostic representation of BOTH the stipulated counterfactual premise and the stored real-world fact, but gate which one wins via a scalar 'counterfactual-override' strength whose default is covertly set by the query language. Consequently, for a fixed hypothetical, the model correctly overrides real knowledge in high-resource languages but lazily leaks the true-world answer in low-resource / typologically distant languages; this leakage scales with the query language's distance from the dominant language, not with the difficulty of the counterfactual itself, and is carried by a locatable, steerable override representation separable from the premise and fact content.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs can override real-world knowledge in counterfactual conditionals but often via lexical cues, and struggle with formal counterfactual inference (Counterfactual Reasoning 2022/2023; CRASS 2021; CounterBench 2025; multi-modal C-VQA 2023). Multilingual counterfactual work is purely about counterfactual EXAMPLE GENERATION and its cross-lingual edit patterns (Parallel Universes 2026), not about reasoning-time override. Cross-lingual factual-consistency interpretability shows a language-independent concept space with a late-layer language-transition bottleneck and entity-alignment failures (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025), and BICAUSE (Under the Shadow of Babel 2025) shows language shapes CAUSAL reasoning attention. Larger models drift into language-specific subspaces hurting consistency (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025). NONE of these studies COUNTERFACTUAL override across languages, nor asks whether the query language sets how strongly a model suppresses its stored fact in favor of an in-context stipulation, nor provides a causal, steerable override gate. We uniquely reframe multilingual reasoning failure on hypotheticals as a language-set knowledge-override gating problem and give a causal (probe + patching + steering) account plus a training-free fix, adopting the triangulation acceptance standard (Triangulation 2025) of necessity+sufficiency+cross-lingual invariance.
Abstract: Reasoning about hypotheticals ('suppose water boiled at 50 degrees Celsius') requires a model to hold a stipulated premise that contradicts what it knows and follow the premise, not reality. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs can do this equally well in every language, and whether the query language covertly decides how strongly the model overrides its stored knowledge. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-agnostic representation of both the stipulated counterfactual premise and the true real-world fact, but resolve the conflict through a scalar counterfactual-override gate whose default value is set by the query language. Under this view, the same hypothetical is followed faithfully in high-resource languages but leaks the true-world answer in low-resource, typologically distant languages, because the override gate is weaker there. We build CF-OVERRIDE, controlled counterfactual conditionals whose correct answer under the stipulation differs from the real-world answer, rendered across 15+ languages spanning several scripts and families, with matched real-world (non-counterfactual) controls. Behaviorally we measure a per-language real-world-leakage rate on identical hypotheticals. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared premise representation and a shared real-world-fact representation that transfer across languages; (ii) use activation patching to show both are computed similarly across languages while a separable override signal differs, localizing leakage to a language-set gate rather than a failure to encode the premise; and (iii) recover an override direction and steer it to strengthen override in leaky languages and weaken it in strict ones without harming fluency, validated with a triangulation standard (necessity, sufficiency, cross-lingual invariance). We predict leakage tracks typological/script distance, not counterfactual difficulty. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (CF-OVERRIDE): construct counterfactual conditional items where a stipulated premise contradicts a well-known real-world fact and a follow-up question has DIFFERENT correct answers under the stipulation vs reality (e.g. 'Suppose whales were fish. Do whales breathe with gills? [stipulated: yes; real: no]'; numeric physics/geography stipulations; social-rule stipulations). Include a difficulty gradient (1- vs 2-step inference from the premise). Render each in 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Add matched controls: (a) a REAL-WORLD variant (no counterfactual premise; correct answer = real fact) to verify the model knows the fact in each language, and (b) a neutral-premise variant. Native-speaker-validate translations and the intended answers. Build per-language typological/script distance to the dominant language and a resource proxy. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral leakage test: elicit answers per item/language; metric = REAL-WORLD-LEAKAGE RATE = fraction of counterfactual items answered with the true-world answer instead of the stipulation-consistent answer, restricted to items where the model demonstrably knows both the fact (from control a) and can do the inference (from a high-resource anchor). Report cross-language disagreement on identical hypotheticals. Baselines: query in dominant language (upper bound), translate-to-English-first. 3. Distance-vs-difficulty dissociation (core behavioral claim): regress leakage on (i) typological/script distance and resource proxy, and (ii) counterfactual difficulty (inference steps). Predict leakage tracks language distance, NOT difficulty; key contrast: a distant but well-covered language vs a close but sparsely-covered one. Spearman with CIs. 4. Shared premise & fact probes: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode (i) the stipulated premise content and (ii) the true real-world fact from mid-layer hidden states; test cross-lingual probe transfer to establish both are represented similarly across languages (so leaky languages still ENCODE the premise), and contrast with a probe decoding the RESOLVED answer, which should vary by language. 5. Causal localization via patching (core mechanism test): for an item overridden correctly in a high-resource language but leaked in a low-resource one, (a) patch the mid-layer premise representation across runs and confirm the premise is already present in the leaky run (patching changes little); (b) patch/steer the components carrying the override decision and test whether the answer flips to premise-consistent, localizing the failure to a language-set override gate rather than a missing premise. Apply the triangulation standard: require necessity (ablating the gate re-introduces leakage), sufficiency (injecting it fixes leakage), and cross-lingual invariance of the effect. 6. Override-strength steering (causal fix): recover an override direction as the mean activation difference between premise-following and real-world-leaking runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) STRENGTHEN override in leaky languages (raise premise-consistent accuracy), (b) WEAKEN it to INDUCE leakage where the model was correct (functional-causality proof), with dose-response. Metrics: leakage reduction/induction, premise-content and fact-content preservation (specificity), fluency (perplexity), output-language fidelity. Compare against explicit prompting ('ignore real-world facts; follow only the supposition') and translate-first baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where the gate is malleable; probe transfer across models; difficulty breakdown; whether the gate default is anchored to English or the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Metrics throughout: real-world-leakage rate, cross-language disagreement, premise/fact/answer probe accuracy and transfer, causal patch/steer flip and repair/induction rates, triangulation necessity+sufficiency+invariance scores, content-preservation specificity, Spearman with distance vs difficulty vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Leakage could be confounded with the model simply not KNOWING the real fact or being unable to do the inference in a low-resource language rather than a gating failure; the real-world control (knows the fact) and high-resource-anchor inference check restrict the analysis to items where both prerequisites hold, and the patching test (premise present but not followed) is the crucial disambiguator. 2. Probe decodability of premise/fact/override may reflect the readout basis, not a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/repair (Exp. 6), held to the triangulation standard, are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus specificity checks that premise and fact content are preserved. 3. Some counterfactual items may leak via lexical cues (as prior monolingual work found) rather than genuine reasoning; we construct items where lexical overlap does not decide the answer and report a lexical-cue control subset. 4. The distance-vs-difficulty dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts and a clean difficulty axis; we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the distance operationalization. 5. Strong models may override faithfully in all languages, shrinking the effect; even documenting faithful language-invariant override (a clean shared-premise + strong-gate architecture) is informative, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Translations may inadvertently soften or strengthen the counterfactual framing across languages; native-speaker validation and matched neutral-premise controls mitigate this. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/answer matching; we use pooled-span or answer-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade override strength for fluency or content preservation; we report all three. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: crosslingual_capacity_contention
Title: The Polyglot Bottleneck: Inference-Time Capacity Contention and Active Arbitration Among Languages in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A small set of shared 'polyglot' components in a multilingual LLM forms a fixed-capacity bottleneck that multiple languages must contend for at inference time. We hypothesize (a) cross-lingual interference is a dynamic, dose-dependent CAPACITY-CONTENTION effect, not a static property: forcing the model to hold a second language active (via a preceding multilingual context) causally degrades competence in the target language in proportion to how much shared-bottleneck capacity the intruder language consumes; (b) this contention is concentrated in an identifiable set of shared middle-layer components (an inference-time analogue of a 'shared region'), and its degradation is causally removable by protecting/steering those components; and (c) the model performs weak ACTIVE ARBITRATION (interference suppression) over this bottleneck, so contention cost scales with how strongly the intruder competes (its similarity/co-activation to the target), mirroring the bilingual brain's language-conflict-and-control dynamics.
Related Work: Static-region work shows a ~1% shared 'core linguistic region' and language-specific regions whose removal destroys competence (Unveiling Linguistic Regions 2024), and that entanglement with a dominant variety can HURT related varieties, fixable by subspace decoupling (When Alignment Hurts 2025); training-side work shows language-general vs language-specific FFN neurons and reduces training interference by selective/sparse fine-tuning (Neuron Specialization 2024; LANDeRMT 2024; Sparse Subnetwork Enhancement 2025). The Stem Cell Hypothesis (2021) shows shared attention heads cause TRAINING-time multi-task interference in encoders. Bilingualism neuroscience shows non-target languages are automatically co-activated and require active interference suppression via cognitive-control circuits whose engagement adapts to interactional context (Language Conflict in the Bilingual Brain 2008; Adaptive Control Hypothesis 2013). ALL region/neuron work is about STATIC parameter partitions or TRAINING-time interference and their editing fixes; NONE studies INFERENCE-TIME, dose-dependent CAPACITY CONTENTION where dynamically loading one language degrades another, treats interference as a limited-shared-resource being arbitrated on the fly, or tests active-arbitration (suppression) over a shared bottleneck in a decoder LLM. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual interference as dynamic capacity contention with active arbitration, give causal (patching + steering + capacity-protection) evidence, and connect it to the bilingual-control literature.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs are often described via static partitions: a shared 'core' region plus language-specific regions. We propose a complementary, dynamic account. Drawing on bilingual-brain findings that non-target languages are automatically co-activated and must be actively suppressed, we hypothesize that a small set of shared middle-layer 'polyglot' components forms a fixed-capacity bottleneck that languages contend for at inference time, and that the model weakly arbitrates this contention on the fly. This yields a sharp, testable prediction absent from static-partition work: forcing the model to hold a second (intruder) language active while answering in a target language should causally degrade target-language competence in a dose-dependent way, with cost scaling by how much shared-bottleneck capacity the intruder consumes and how strongly it competes with the target. We test this with a controlled contention paradigm: identical target-language questions are answered either alone or after a preceding context that loads an intruder language, varying intruder amount (dose) and intruder-target relatedness. We measure a per-pair Contention Cost and locate the shared components whose activation is co-claimed by both languages. Causally, we (i) activation-patch the shared-component state from the alone-run into the contention-run to test whether protecting the bottleneck removes the degradation, (ii) steer to suppress intruder co-activation and measure target recovery (active-arbitration proxy), and (iii) show a matched non-contending control (a task-irrelevant intruder) produces little cost. We predict contention cost is highest for typologically near, high-co-activation intruders and that steering the shared bottleneck recovers performance without retraining. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MGSM reasoning across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA) and multilingual math reasoning (MGSM), each with parallel items across 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Contention paradigm (behavioral core): for each target-language item, create matched conditions: (a) ALONE (target question only), and (b) CONTENTION (an intruder-language preceding context the model must process/hold active before answering the identical target question). Vary INTRUDER DOSE (context length / number of intruder-language items the model must attend to) and INTRUDER IDENTITY (typologically near vs far from target, high- vs low-resource). Metric: CONTENTION COST = accuracy(ALONE) - accuracy(CONTENTION) on the same target item; report dose-response (cost vs intruder amount) and per intruder-target pair. 3. Non-contending control: replace the intruder-language context with (i) a same-language (target) distractor context of equal length, and (ii) a non-linguistic filler (numbers/symbols) of equal length. Prediction: Contention Cost is specific to a competing OTHER-language load, exceeding equal-length same-language/filler controls, isolating cross-lingual capacity contention from generic context-length degradation. 4. Distance/co-activation dose-response: correlate Contention Cost with (i) lang2vec typological/script distance between intruder and target and (ii) an internal CO-ACTIVATION score (overlap of the shared components each language activates, from Exp. 5). Predict cost is highest for near, high-co-activation intruder-target pairs. Spearman with CIs; key contrast: a near-but-low-resource intruder vs a far-but-high-resource intruder to dissociate relatedness from resource. 5. Locate the shared bottleneck: using ALONE runs, identify middle-layer components (FFN neurons / attention heads / activation directions) co-claimed by multiple languages via language-activation overlap (LAPE-style entropy) and probing; define a shared-bottleneck set and per-language capacity-consumption profiles. Contrast with language-specific components. 6. Causal test A (protect the bottleneck): activation-patch the shared-bottleneck state from the ALONE target run into the CONTENTION run; test whether target accuracy is restored (bottleneck contention is the causal locus) while a matched non-bottleneck patch does not restore it (specificity). 7. Causal test B (active arbitration / suppression): recover an intruder-co-activation direction and steer to SUPPRESS the intruder's presence in the shared components during the contention run; measure target recovery (suppression helps -> arbitration is the operative control), and conversely AMPLIFY intruder co-activation to worsen cost (dose-response, functional causality). Report accuracy recovery, output-language fidelity, and fluency (perplexity). 8. Adaptive-control analogue: test whether cost/arbitration depends on interactional context by comparing a 'single-language framing' vs an 'explicit dual-language framing' prompt, mirroring the Adaptive Control Hypothesis prediction that dual-language contexts change control demands. 9. Ablations: layer sweep for where contention is malleable; probe/direction transfer across models; task type (knowledge vs reasoning); whether the intruder that costs most is the dominant language or the nearest one; model scale. Metrics throughout: Contention Cost, dose-response slope, control specificity gap, shared-bottleneck co-activation/capacity profiles, causal patch restoration rate, suppression/amplification recovery and worsening, Spearman with distance/co-activation vs resource, output-language fidelity, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Contention Cost could be confounded with generic context-length degradation or attention dilution rather than cross-lingual capacity contention; the equal-length same-language and non-linguistic-filler controls (Exp. 3) are the crucial dissociators, and the effect must exceed them to support the claim. 2. Probe/overlap-based bottleneck localization is correlational; the activation-patching restoration (Exp. 6) and suppression/amplification steering (Exp. 7) are required to promote 'located' to 'causal', with matched non-bottleneck controls for specificity. 3. Co-activation and typological distance may correlate, and both may track resource level; the near-low-resource vs far-high-resource contrast (Exp. 4) is designed to dissociate them, and we report multiple proxies. 4. 'Active arbitration' is a strong claim; suppression-helps evidence is consistent with, but not proof of, a dedicated control mechanism, so we frame arbitration as a functional (steering-testable) effect rather than a named circuit unless localization is clean. 5. Strong models may show little contention on easy items, shrinking the effect; harder items, higher intruder doses, and low-resource targets provide power, and even a bounded effect is informative. 6. Tokenization/length differ across scripts, complicating equal-length matching; we match by token count and report both token and item counts. 7. Steering may trade recovery for fluency or output-language fidelity; we report all three. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across two task types address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: lexical_gap_substitution
Title: No Word for That: How Cross-Lingual Lexical Gaps Force Multilingual LLMs to Silently Substitute the Nearest Colexified Sense
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, fine-grained conceptual representation, but when they must express a concept in a target language that has NO single-word lexeme for it (a lexical gap / colexification split), they resolve the gap through a locatable 'lexicalization gate' set by the output language: rather than paraphrasing, they often silently substitute the concept's nearest COLEXIFIED sense in that language (e.g. rendering a distinction the language lumps as a single coarser word), producing meaning-shifting errors. This substitution rate scales with how strongly the target language's lexicon colexifies the two senses (from CLICS), not with resource level, and is carried by a causally-manipulable representation separable from the concept content.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual LLMs form shared, linearly-alignable concept spaces where abstract concepts align better than concrete ones (Concept Space Alignment 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; When Meanings Meet 2026), and cross-lingual concept patching can flip polysemy sense selection and homograph translation. Cognitive-typology work quantifies cross-linguistic semantic (mis)alignment and colexification structure (Universal Structure of Lexical Semantics 2016; Semantic Alignment 2018; CLICS colexification database; lexical-gap/lacunae resources 2019/2024). However, ALL LLM concept-space work studies static alignment geometry or word-translation sense selection, and ALL lexical-gap work is descriptive-linguistic. NONE asks the sharp generation-time question: when the output language has NO lexeme for a needed concept, does the model paraphrase (preserving meaning) or silently collapse the concept onto the nearest colexified sense the language DOES lexicalize (an error), and is this a locatable, steerable lexicalization-gate failure driven by the target language's colexification structure? We uniquely turn cross-lingual lexical gaps and CLICS colexification into a controlled causal probe of the shared-vs-language-specific concept boundary, with an activation-patching + steering mechanism and a colexification-vs-resource dissociation.
Abstract: Languages do not carve meaning identically: some pack two senses into one word (colexification), and many concepts simply lack a single-word equivalent in a given language (a lexical gap). A model asked to express such a concept in a language that lacks a word for it faces a choice: paraphrase to preserve the distinction, or fall back on the nearest word the language does have. We investigate which multilingual LLMs do and why. We hypothesize that models compute a shared, fine-grained conceptual representation but resolve lexical gaps through a lexicalization gate set by the output language, and that when a concept is colexified in the target language the model tends to silently substitute the nearest colexified sense, shifting meaning. We build GAP-PROBE from CLICS colexification data and lexical-gap resources: for concept pairs that one language lexicalizes distinctly but another colexifies (e.g. hand/arm, tree/wood, blue/green splits, kin distinctions), we pose translation, paraphrase, and disambiguation tasks across 12+ languages and measure a per-language SILENT-SUBSTITUTION rate on identical concepts. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared fine-grained concept representation that transfers across languages even where the output collapses it; (ii) use activation patching to show the fine distinction is present internally while a separable lexicalization gate discards it; and (iii) recover a gate direction and steer it to make the model paraphrase (repair) or collapse (induce) without changing the underlying concept. We predict substitution tracks CLICS colexification strength, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (GAP-PROBE): using the CLICS colexification database and lexical-gap resources (LingoGap/lacunae lists), assemble concept pairs (A,B) that are lexicalized DISTINCTLY in a source language but COLEXIFIED (one word) or entirely GAPPED in target languages: classic cases (hand/arm, finger/toe, tree/wood, blue/green 'grue', foot/leg, brother/older-brother, ice/snow, and food/culture-specific gaps). Annotate per-target-language whether each pair is distinctly-lexicalized, colexified, or gapped, and a CLICS-derived colexification strength score per (pair, language). Render across 12+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Construct three tasks per item: (a) TRANSLATION of a source sentence unambiguously about sense A into the target language; (b) PARAPHRASE/definition of the concept in the target language; (c) DISAMBIGUATION NLI ('the sentence is about A, not B — true/false?'). Native-speaker-validate. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral silent-substitution test: score each target-language output as (i) meaning-preserving (paraphrase/circumlocution that keeps the A/B distinction), (ii) SILENT SUBSTITUTION (uses the colexified coarser word, dropping the distinction, without flagging it), or (iii) wrong-sense (picks B). Key metric: SILENT-SUBSTITUTION RATE on colexified/gapped items, contrasted with near-zero on distinctly-lexicalized control items. Baselines: translate-via-English, explicit 'preserve the distinction' prompt. 3. Colexification dose-response (dissociation): correlate per-item substitution rate with CLICS colexification strength vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy). Prediction: substitution tracks colexification strength, not resource; key contrast: a lower-resource language that lexicalizes the distinction vs a higher-resource language that colexifies it. Spearman with CIs. 4. Shared fine-grained-concept probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode which sense (A vs B) the input is about, from mid-layer hidden states; test cross-lingual probe transfer (train one language, test others) to establish the fine distinction is represented internally even in languages whose OUTPUT collapses it, and contrast with a probe decoding the emitted coarse word. 5. Causal localization via patching (core test): for an item where the source language preserves A/B but a target run silently substitutes, (a) patch the mid-layer fine-grained concept representation across runs and confirm the distinction is already present in the substituting run (patching changes little), and (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the lexicalization decision and test whether the output switches to a distinction-preserving paraphrase — localizing the failure to a language-set lexicalization gate, not a lost concept. 6. Lexicalization-gate steering (causal fix/manipulation): recover a gate direction as the mean activation difference between paraphrase-preserving and collapse runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) REPAIR collapses (force paraphrase) in colexifying languages and (b) INDUCE collapse in a distinctly-lexicalizing language (functional-causality proof), with dose-response. Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, meaning-preservation accuracy, concept-content preservation (specificity: the underlying A vs B is unchanged), fluency (perplexity), output-language fidelity. Compare against explicit-instruction prompting and translate-via-English baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where the gate is malleable; probe transfer across models; item-type breakdown (colexified vs fully-gapped; concrete vs abstract, linking to the abstract-aligns-better finding); whether the collapse target is the dominant-language sense or the target-language colexified sense; model scale. Metrics throughout: silent-substitution rate, meaning-preservation accuracy, fine-sense probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, causal patch/steer repair and induction rates, concept-preservation specificity, Spearman with colexification strength vs resource, fluency, output-language fidelity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Distinguishing legitimate paraphrase from silent substitution across languages is nontrivial; we use native-speaker-validated rubrics, high-agreement items, and automatic checks (does the output word colexify B?), reporting inter-annotator agreement. 2. Probe decodability of the fine-grained distinction may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that the underlying concept (A vs B) is preserved. 3. Substitution could reflect the model genuinely lacking target-language circumlocution vocabulary (a capability gap) rather than a gate defect; the demonstration that the distinction is internally present (probe/patching) and that steering RECOVERS a paraphrase distinguishes gating from missing knowledge. 4. Colexification is graded and CLICS coverage is uneven for low-resource languages; we restrict to well-attested pairs, use multiple colexification-strength operationalizations, and report robustness. 5. The colexification-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report multiple resource proxies. 6. Strong models may paraphrase faithfully everywhere, shrinking the effect; even documenting faithful gap-handling (a clean shared-concept + paraphrase architecture) is informative, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts, complicating probing/output scoring; we use pooled-span or answer-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 8. Steering may trade meaning-preservation for fluency; we report both. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: numeral_inversion_operand_binding
Title: Five-and-Twenty Plus Three: How Number-Word Inversion in the Query Language Reorders Operand Binding in Multilingual LLM Arithmetic
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in whether spoken numerals are inverted (German 'fünfundzwanzig' = five-and-twenty for 25; Arabic) or non-inverted (English, Hebrew). We hypothesize that when a multilingual LLM reads a number written as words, the query language's inversion structure covertly sets the internal ORDER in which digit/operand magnitudes are bound before arithmetic, so that in inverted languages the model tends to bind the units-before-tens order it hears rather than the place-value order it must compute over. This produces systematic, direction-consistent arithmetic errors (e.g. transposition/carry errors) on word-form multi-digit and multi-operand problems that are ABSENT in the same problems posed in digits or in non-inverted languages, and the error rate scales with the language's degree of numeral inversion, not its resource level. The binding order is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable representation separable from the magnitude content.
Related Work: Bilingualism research establishes that number-word inversion causally shapes arithmetic: inverted-language speakers are faster/more accurate when problems match their language's numeral order, and bilinguals flexibly adapt to L1 vs L2 order (Number word structure in first and second language, 2015; operand-order effects reflecting learning history in Chinese-educated adults, 2025; linguistic-arithmetic interaction in word problems, 2020). On the model side, arithmetic-interpretability work shows LLMs rely on positional information and pattern-matching rather than robust rule induction (Positional Description Matters 2023; Do LLMs Truly Grasp Addition 2025; Unraveling Arithmetic 2024), and that math word problems decompose into an abstract-then-compute mechanism (Can LLMs Reason Abstractly 2025). Cross-lingual reasoning work shows knowledge-free reasoning transfers well across languages (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024). However, ALL LLM arithmetic-interpretability work is monolingual (English digits) and studies digit positional encoding, and ALL number-word-inversion work is human cognitive-linguistics with no model-internal account. My own prior proposal on numeral morphology studied MAGNITUDE distortion from vigesimal words, a different axis. NONE tests whether the QUERY LANGUAGE'S INVERSION STRUCTURE reorders internal OPERAND/DIGIT BINDING during multi-digit/multi-operand arithmetic, nor gives a causal, steerable binding-order mechanism. We uniquely port the number-word-inversion arithmetic effect into multilingual mechanistic interpretability.
Abstract: Human languages disagree on the order of spoken numerals: German and Arabic say the units before the tens ('five-and-twenty' for 25), while English and Hebrew do not. A landmark bilingual finding is that this inversion causally shapes arithmetic performance, with speakers faster and more accurate when a problem's presentation matches their language's numeral order. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit this effect, and whether the query language's inversion structure covertly reorders how the model internally binds operands during arithmetic. We hypothesize that when numbers are given as words, an inverted query language biases the model toward a units-before-tens binding order that conflicts with the place-value order arithmetic requires, producing systematic transposition and carry errors that vanish when the identical problem is posed in digits or in a non-inverted language.
