We build INVERT-MATH: multi-digit addition and multi-operand word problems whose numbers are spelled out across inverted (German, Dutch, Danish, Arabic) and non-inverted (English, Hebrew, Chinese, Turkish) numeral languages, with matched digit-form controls. Behaviorally we measure a per-language inversion-error rate and its dose-response with numeral-inversion degree. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared magnitude representation and a separable binding-order signal that inherits the query language's inversion; (ii) use activation patching to show magnitude is correctly recovered while a binding-order representation is mis-set, localizing errors to an order-binding step; and (iii) recover a binding-order direction and steer it to repair inversion errors (or induce them in non-inverted languages) without changing the magnitudes. We predict errors track inversion degree, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (INVERT-MATH): construct arithmetic items with numbers spelled out as WORDS, focused on two-digit and three-digit operands where tens/units ordering matters, in two task families: (a) multi-digit ADDITION requiring carries (e.g. 'twenty-seven plus forty-eight'), and (b) short multi-operand WORD problems. Render across INVERTED numeral languages (German, Dutch, Danish, Arabic) and NON-INVERTED (English, Hebrew, Chinese, Turkish), each with a matched DIGIT-form control (same numbers, Arabic numerals) posed in that language. Annotate per-language numeral-inversion degree (fully inverted / partially inverted for teens / non-inverted) and a resource-level proxy. Native-speaker-validate number-word rendering. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral inversion-error test: measure accuracy per (task, language, format). Key metric = INVERSION-ERROR GAP = accuracy(digit control) - accuracy(word form), and specifically the rate of TRANSPOSITION errors (answer consistent with swapping tens and units of an operand) and carry errors. Prediction: word-form accuracy drops and transposition errors rise in inverted languages relative to non-inverted, while digit controls are comparable across languages. Baselines: translate-numerals-to-digits prompting, English word-form. 3. Inversion dose-response (dissociation): correlate the inversion-error gap and transposition rate with numeral-inversion degree vs the resource-level proxy (Spearman with CIs); key contrast: a lower-resource inverted language (e.g. Danish) vs a higher-resource non-inverted one (e.g. Chinese), and German (inverted, high-resource) vs Turkish (non-inverted, mid-resource). 4. Shared-magnitude vs binding-order probes: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode (i) the true magnitude of each operand (using digit-form anchors) and (ii) an operand's tens-vs-units digit assignment / binding order, from hidden states at the operand-final token. Test that magnitude is decodable and cross-lingually consistent, while a binding-order signal is decodable and INHERITS the query language's inversion (predicts the mis-ordered assignment in inverted languages). 5. Causal localization via patching (core test): for an addition item solved correctly in digit/non-inverted form but erred in an inverted word form, (a) patch the mid-layer magnitude representation across runs and confirm magnitudes are correctly present in the erring run (patching changes little); (b) patch/steer the components carrying digit-position binding and test whether the answer corrects, localizing the error to a language-set binding-order step rather than a wrong magnitude. 6. Binding-order steering (causal fix/manipulation): recover a binding-order direction as the mean activation difference between correctly place-value-ordered and inverted-ordered runs (pooled across languages); steer to (a) REPAIR inversion errors in inverted-language word problems and (b) INDUCE inversion/transposition errors in non-inverted languages (functional-causality proof), with dose-response. Metrics: repair rate, induction rate, arithmetic accuracy, magnitude-preservation specificity (operand values unchanged), fluency (perplexity). Compare against explicit prompting ('read the number in place-value order') and translate-to-digits baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where binding order is malleable; probe transfer across models; teens vs full two-digit vs three-digit breakdown (teens are partially inverted in many languages); whether the imposed order is always the query language's or the dominant language's; number of operands; model scale; tokenization statistics of number words. Metrics throughout: word-vs-digit accuracy gap, transposition/carry error rates, magnitude and binding-order probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, causal patch/steer repair and induction rates, magnitude-preservation specificity, Spearman with inversion degree vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Word-form arithmetic errors could stem from generic difficulty of parsing number words rather than an inversion-specific binding-order effect; the matched DIGIT controls (comparable across languages) and the transposition-error signature (tens/units specifically swapped, in the direction the language's inversion predicts) are the crucial dissociators, and non-inverted word-form languages serve as a further control. 2. Probe decodability of magnitude or binding order may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that operand magnitudes are preserved. 3. Tokenization of number words is uneven across languages and scripts and may itself split tens/units unevenly, confounding the effect; we curate items with clean morpheme boundaries, use operand-final/pooled representations, report tokenization statistics, and analyze partially-inverted teens separately. 4. The inversion-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (German vs Chinese, Danish vs Turkish); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the inversion-degree operationalization. 5. Strong models may resolve place value robustly regardless of spoken order, shrinking the effect; even documenting robust place-value binding (a clean shared-magnitude + order-invariant architecture) is an informative positive result, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Some 'errors' may reflect the model answering a different (mis-parsed) problem; we manually classify error types and restrict the causal analysis to clear transposition/carry cases. 7. Steering may trade arithmetic correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across two task families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: abstract_vs_surface_priming_channels
Title: Priming Across the Word-Order Divide: Two Competing Structural Channels Behind Cross-Lingual Structural Priming in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual structural priming in multilingual LLMs is carried by TWO coexisting, dissociable channels: an abstract, word-order-invariant structure representation and a surface token/order-copying channel. For typologically aligned language pairs both channels agree, but for word-order-divergent pairs (e.g. verb-final vs. verb-medial) they conflict, and the model's realized priming reflects whichever channel dominates. We predict (a) genuine abstract, order-inverting priming (a structure primed in one language raises the analogous structure in another even when the surface word orders differ), (b) that a locatable abstract-structure representation is causally responsible for this order-invariant transfer while a separate surface-copy channel drives order-matched priming, and (c) that the abstract channel's dominance scales with typological/word-order distance being bridged, and can be causally amplified to repair failed cross-lingual priming across divergent word orders.
Related Work: A rich line shows LLMs exhibit structural priming that behaviorally indexes abstract grammar (Sinclair et al. 2022; Prasad et al. 2019; Finding Structure in Language Models 2024) and cross-lingual priming that causally influences generation across languages (Structural Priming Demonstrates Abstract Grammatical Representations in Multilingual LMs 2023; Michaelov et al. 2023; RNN/Transformer Chinese-English priming 2024; acquisition dynamics 2023/2025). Human/connectionist work debates whether identical word order is required for cross-language priming (error-driven learning account, Kaan et al. 2021) and finds it is not. Mechanistic multilingual work shows shared syntactic subspaces (Universal Grammatical Relations in mBERT 2020), shared circuits for shared processes (The Same But Different 2024), and shared agreement neurons (Causal Analysis of Agreement Neurons 2022). ALL existing LLM priming work is BEHAVIORAL and treats priming as a single effect indexing 'abstract structure'; none dissociates an abstract order-invariant channel from a surface order-copying channel, none uses word-order-divergent pairs as a controlled instrument to separate them, and none provides a causal (patching + steering) account of which internal representation carries order-inverting cross-lingual priming. We uniquely turn cross-lingual priming into a two-channel diagnostic with a causal, steerable abstract-structure locus.
Abstract: Structural priming—where encountering a syntactic structure makes its reuse more likely—has become a key behavioral probe showing that multilingual LLMs share abstract grammatical representations across languages. But behavior alone cannot tell whether cross-lingual priming rides on a genuinely abstract, order-invariant representation of structure or on a shallower channel that copies surface token order. We propose that both channels coexist and can be dissociated by pitting them against each other: in language pairs with divergent word order (e.g. a verb-final prime language and a verb-medial target), abstract structural priming predicts the analogous construction should be primed despite different surface orders, whereas a surface-copy channel predicts priming only when orders match. We build a controlled cross-lingual priming suite over alternating constructions (dative, active/passive, genitive) across language pairs spanning aligned and divergent word orders, and measure order-invariant versus order-matched priming. Mechanistically, we (i) probe for an abstract construction representation that is shared and decodable across languages independent of surface order, (ii) use activation patching to test whether this abstract representation is causally sufficient to prime the analogous target structure across a word-order divide, while a separate surface-form representation drives order-matched priming, and (iii) recover an abstract-structure direction and steer it to repair cross-lingual priming that fails across divergent orders. We predict the abstract channel's contribution scales with the word-order distance being bridged and that steering it induces order-invariant priming without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Priming suite: build parallel prime-target items over alternating constructions with clear structural variants: dative (double-object vs. prepositional-object), voice (active vs. passive), and genitive (of- vs. 's-type or their cross-linguistic analogues). Construct prime sentences in a SOURCE language and elicit a target completion/continuation describing a new event in a TARGET language, so the model must choose a construction. Cover language pairs spanning WORD-ORDER-ALIGNED (e.g. English<->Spanish, both SVO) and WORD-ORDER-DIVERGENT (e.g. Japanese/Korean/Hindi/Turkish verb-final <-> English/Spanish verb-medial) directions, plus monolingual within-language priming as an upper-bound baseline. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral two-channel test: measure priming strength = increase in the target construction's probability after a congruent prime vs. an incongruent/neutral prime (log-odds shift), separately for order-aligned and order-divergent pairs. Key contrast: ORDER-INVARIANT priming (present across divergent orders = abstract channel) vs. ORDER-MATCHED priming (present only when surface orders match = surface-copy channel). Report per-construction, per-pair. Control for lexical overlap and semantic similarity (following Prime-LM factors). 3. Word-order-distance dose-response: correlate the abstract-channel priming magnitude (order-invariant component) with lang2vec word-order/typological distance between prime and target; predict abstract-channel share rises—or surface-copy fails—as word-order distance grows, dissociating from resource level via matched contrasts. Spearman with CIs. 4. Abstract-structure probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode the ABSTRACT construction identity (e.g. dative-DO vs. dative-PO) from hidden states after the prime, and test cross-lingual transfer (train on one language's primes, decode another's) and INVARIANCE to surface order (a probe that classifies construction regardless of word order). Contrast with a surface-order probe (which token order appeared). Establish that an order-invariant construction representation exists and is shared. 5. Causal channel dissociation via patching (core test): (a) Abstract-channel sufficiency—extract the mid-layer abstract construction representation from a divergent-order source prime and patch it into a neutral target-language run; test whether it primes the analogous target construction across the word-order divide (predicted YES) while NOT forcing the source's surface order. (b) Surface-channel test—patch the surface-order representation and test whether it drives order-matched priming but fails/misfires across divergent orders. Metric: induced construction-choice shift, order-fidelity of output, specificity. 6. Abstract-structure steering (causal fix): recover an abstract construction direction (mean activation difference between the two construction variants, pooled across languages and orders) and steer it during target generation to induce or suppress the analogous construction. Test whether steering REPAIRS cross-lingual priming that failed across divergent orders (raising order-invariant priming) and can INDUCE a construction unprompted (functional causality), with dose-response, measuring fluency (perplexity), output-language and grammaticality fidelity, and specificity (non-target constructions unchanged). Compare against explicit-instruction prompting and same-language priming baselines. 7. Ablations: layer sweep for where the abstract representation is malleable; probe transfer across models; construction breakdown (dative vs. voice vs. genitive); asymmetry by direction (divergent->aligned vs. aligned->divergent, connecting to reported priming asymmetries); lexical-boost condition (verb overlap) to separate item-specific from abstract priming; model scale. Metrics throughout: priming log-odds shift (order-invariant vs. order-matched components), abstract vs. surface probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, causal patch-induced construction shift and order-fidelity, steering repair/induction rate, grammaticality/fluency, Spearman with word-order distance.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Cross-lingual priming may be dominated by lexical/semantic overlap rather than structure; we control lexical overlap and semantic similarity (Prime-LM style) and include no-overlap conditions to isolate abstract structure. 2. Probe decodability of an 'abstract construction' representation may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used channel; the activation-patching sufficiency test (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, with order-fidelity and specificity checks. 3. The two-channel dissociation may be fuzzy—real behavior could be a graded mixture rather than clean channels; we present the abstract vs. surface contribution as a continuous decomposition and report effect sizes rather than forcing a binary. 4. Eliciting a clean construction choice in the target language across divergent-order languages is nontrivial; we use native-speaker-validated templates, constrained elicitation, and grammaticality checks, and analyze order-aligned vs. divergent pairs separately. 5. Strong models may show robust order-invariant priming everywhere (only an abstract channel), which would simplify the picture—still an informative positive result establishing genuine abstract structural sharing, and the steering/patching still localizes it. 6. Priming magnitudes can be small and noisy; we aggregate over many items/constructions and report confidence intervals, and use within-language priming as a calibration upper bound. 7. Tokenization and length differ across scripts/orders, confounding probability comparisons; we use log-odds between minimally-different construction variants (length-matched where possible) and report tokenization statistics. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across multiple constructions and language pairs address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: paraphrase_controlled_inconsistency
Title: Is Cross-Lingual Inconsistency Special? Using Within-Language Paraphrase Variation to Isolate the Language-Transition Component of Multilingual Factual Instability
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual factual inconsistency has two additive components: a language-agnostic instability that also causes a model to answer differently across paraphrases of the SAME language, and a genuinely language-specific instability introduced at the late-layer language-transition stage. We hypothesize (a) that a large, previously-unmeasured fraction of what is reported as 'cross-lingual inconsistency' is actually this baseline paraphrase instability rather than anything language-specific; (b) that the residual, language-specific component is causally localized to a distinct late-layer transition locus separable from the mid-layer concept computation; and (c) the size of the residual (not the total) is what scales with script/typological distance, while the paraphrase-baseline component does not.
Related Work: A wave of recent work attributes cross-lingual factual inconsistency to a late-layer 'language transition' failure over a shared concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), and proposes fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubSub/SubInj, steering to a shared space). Separately, LLMs are known to be highly unstable to meaning-preserving surface changes WITHIN a language (Prompt-Format Sensitivity 2023; RoParQ 2025). Crucially, ALL cross-lingual consistency work compares one prompt per language and implicitly treats every observed disagreement as language-caused, never subtracting the model's baseline within-language paraphrase instability. No prior work measures the paraphrase-controlled residual, tests whether the celebrated 'language-transition' locus explains the residual specifically (rather than total inconsistency), or checks whether existing fixes reduce the residual or merely the paraphrase-baseline. We contribute this decomposition, a causal locus test on the residual, and a re-evaluation of prior interventions against the correct baseline.
Abstract: Multilingual language models give different factual answers to the same question asked in different languages, and a growing literature explains this via a late-layer 'language transition' over a shared, language-agnostic concept space. But these studies compare a single prompt per language and treat every disagreement as language-caused, ignoring that the same models also answer inconsistently across meaning-preserving paraphrases within a single language. We ask a sharp question: once we subtract this baseline paraphrase instability, how much cross-lingual inconsistency is genuinely language-specific, and is the language-transition mechanism responsible for that residual rather than for the total? We introduce a paraphrase-controlled decomposition: for each fact we measure within-language answer variability across multiple paraphrases in each language, and define the language-specific residual as cross-lingual disagreement in excess of the pooled within-language baseline. Behaviorally, we predict a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline paraphrase noise, and that only the residual scales with script/typological distance. Mechanistically, we test whether the late-layer transition locus (via logit-lens and activation patching) causally explains the residual specifically: patching mid-layer concept representations should fix paraphrase-baseline errors in any language, whereas the residual should require correcting the late-layer transition. Finally we re-evaluate published fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubInj) against the correct baseline, testing whether they reduce the language-specific residual or merely the paraphrase-agnostic component. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B, sharpening what is and is not special about cross-lingual factual instability.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA across 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. For each fact and each language, generate K>=5 meaning-preserving paraphrase templates (validated by back-translation and native-speaker spot checks), so every fact has both within-language and cross-language variants. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Decomposition metrics: for each fact, compute (a) within-language instability = answer-disagreement rate across the K paraphrases within each language (averaged over languages); (b) total cross-lingual inconsistency = disagreement across languages (one canonical prompt each, matching prior protocols); (c) language-specific residual = cross-lingual disagreement across paraphrase-matched prompts MINUS the pooled within-language baseline. Report the fraction of total inconsistency attributable to the paraphrase baseline vs the residual, per model. 3. Distance dose-response: correlate (i) total inconsistency, (ii) paraphrase baseline, and (iii) residual with lang2vec typological/script distance to the dominant language (Spearman). Core prediction: the residual scales with distance while the paraphrase baseline does not, and total inconsistency's apparent distance-dependence is driven by the residual. 4. Mechanistic locus test (concept vs transition): replicate the mid-layer-concept / late-layer-transition split via logit-lens. For paraphrase-baseline errors (a fact answered correctly under one paraphrase, wrongly under another, same language), patch the mid-layer concept representation from the correct run into the wrong run and measure recovery. For residual (language-specific) errors, test whether mid-layer concept patching alone recovers the answer, or whether correcting the late-layer transition (via a translation-difference / language-transition vector) is additionally required. Prediction: paraphrase-baseline errors are recoverable at the concept stage regardless of language, whereas residual errors specifically require late-layer transition correction, causally localizing the language-specific component. 5. Locus separability: quantify overlap between the components whose patching fixes paraphrase-baseline errors vs residual errors (Jaccard over identified layers/heads), testing that the language-specific residual has a distinct, later locus. 6. Re-evaluation of prior fixes against the right baseline: apply published interventions (linear shortcut bypassing final layers; translation-difference vector; SubInj English-subject injection) and measure their effect separately on the paraphrase baseline and on the residual. Prediction: some fixes mostly reduce the residual (genuinely a language-transition fix) while others also reduce the paraphrase baseline (a general-robustness effect); this disentangles what each intervention actually does. 7. Ablations: number of paraphrases K (stability of the baseline estimate); answer-matching method (exact vs alias-aware); model scale; whether the residual is anchored to English distance or nearest-high-resource-language distance; robustness of the locus split across models. Metrics throughout: within-language and cross-language disagreement rates, paraphrase-controlled residual, Spearman with distance for each component, patching recovery rates by error type, locus Jaccard overlap, and per-intervention reduction of baseline vs residual.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Paraphrase quality across languages is uneven; low-quality paraphrases could inflate the within-language baseline and understate the residual. We validate paraphrases via back-translation and native-speaker checks and report sensitivity to K and to paraphrase-quality filtering. 2. Answer matching across languages/scripts is noisy (aliases, transliterations); we use alias-aware matching and last-token/answer-span normalization and report robustness. 3. It is possible the paraphrase baseline is small and cross-lingual inconsistency IS mostly language-specific; this would refute claim (a) but is itself a valuable, publishable clarification that legitimizes the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline. 4. Logit-lens/patching localization may be diffuse; we report degree of localization honestly and require the recovery-by-error-type contrast (Exp. 4) rather than mere layer identification. 5. The concept-vs-transition split may not be crisp in all models; we validate it per model before the locus test. 6. Prior fixes may interact with our paraphrase set differently than their original setups; we replicate them faithfully and report both baseline and residual effects. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: depth_budget_truncation
Title: Running Out of Layers: Cross-Lingual Errors as Truncated Concept Computation Under a Fixed Depth Budget
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs allocate the same fixed number of layers to every language, but low-resource and typologically distant languages require MORE layers to finish computing a concept; consequently their concept computation is frequently TRUNCATED by the fixed depth budget before it converges, and this truncation — not missing knowledge — causes a large fraction of cross-lingual errors. The required-depth deficit scales with typological/script distance and resource level, and errors are causally recoverable by granting extra late-layer compute (looping late layers) without any retraining.
Related Work: Probing work shows concepts become decodable at different depths depending on complexity ('Concept Depth' 2024) and that low-resource languages exhibit flatter, shallower layer-wise probing trends than high-resource ones (Cross-Language Probing 2024), and that difficulty is encoded language-agnostically early then language-specifically late ('Shared Geometry of Difficulty' 2026). Cross-Layer Transcoder and latent-language work localize a shared middle-layer space with lossy late-layer decoding (Tracing Multilingual Representations 2025; MALT 2025), and DAMA (2026) reports a U-shaped adaptability pattern in speech ASR. ALL of these are correlational (where a concept is decodable, how well probes align by layer) or propose fine-tuning/adaptation fixes. NONE reframes the layer-wise gap as a CAUSAL compute-deadline problem: that the fixed layer budget TRUNCATES an in-progress concept computation for languages that need more depth, that this truncation (not absent knowledge) is what produces the error, or that granting extra inference-time depth to just those items causally recovers the answer. We contribute this compute-budget-truncation reframing, a per-item 'required depth' measurement, a causal early-exit/late-layer-looping test, and a training-free depth-budget intervention.
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions far more reliably in high-resource, typologically close languages, and interpretability work has shown that concepts become decodable at different layer depths across languages. But this has been treated as a correlational fact about representation geometry. We propose a causal, resource-based reframing: transformers apply a fixed number of layers to every input, yet distant, low-resource languages need MORE layers to finish computing a concept, so their computation is often truncated by the depth budget before it converges — the model 'runs out of layers.' Under this view, many cross-lingual errors are not missing knowledge but unfinished computation. We measure, per item and per language, the 'required depth' at which the correct answer first stabilizes via logit-lens/early-exit trajectories, and define a Truncation Gap as the fraction of items whose answer converges only in layers deeper than the model has, or would if given more. We test three claims: (1) required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on identical facts, and the excess predicts errors; (2) errors on truncated items are causally distinguished from knowledge failures — early-exiting a high-resource run at the low-resource run's shallower effective depth reproduces the error, and, crucially, granting extra late-layer compute (looping the final transformer layers) at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth items; and (3) the required-depth deficit and recovery scale with typological/script distance and resource level. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MGSM reasoning across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work recasts the multilingual gap as a depth-budget truncation phenomenon with a cheap, training-free inference-time fix.
Experiments: 1. Data & models: parallel factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA) and multilingual math reasoning (MGSM) across 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, so the SAME fact/problem is posed in every language. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B (varying depth). 2. Required-depth measurement: for each (item, language), apply logit-lens / a tuned lens at every layer and record the CONVERGENCE DEPTH — the shallowest layer after which the top-ranked answer token becomes and stays correct through the final layer. Report per-language required-depth distributions on identical facts. Prediction: distant/low-resource languages need deeper convergence for the SAME fact. 3. Truncation Gap & error link: define Truncation Gap = fraction of items whose answer is correct at the final layer only marginally (converges very late, in the last few layers) or is still rising/unconverged at the final layer (right-censored). Test that (i) unconverged/near-final-convergence items have far higher error rates, and (ii) per-language error rate is predicted by the required-depth deficit relative to the model's total depth, beyond a resource baseline. 4. Distance/resource dose-response: correlate per-language mean required depth and Truncation Gap with lang2vec typological/script distance and a resource proxy (Spearman with CIs); key contrast: a distant-but-well-covered language vs a close-but-sparse one to partly dissociate distance from resource. 5. Causal test A (truncation reproduces low-resource error): take facts answered CORRECTLY in a high-resource language with convergence depth d_hi; force EARLY EXIT of the high-resource run at the shallower effective depth d_lo observed for the low-resource run and test whether the high-resource answer degrades to the low-resource-style error — showing shallow budget alone can cause the error. Specificity: early-exiting at d_hi should not degrade. 6. Causal test B (extra compute recovers truncated answers): at inference, grant extra late-layer depth by LOOPING the final k transformer layers (feeding the last layer's residual stream back through the last block one or more times) on the low-resource/distant run, and measure recovery on HIGH-required-depth items. Prediction: recovery is concentrated on high-Truncation-Gap items and near-zero on genuine knowledge-failure items (items the model gets wrong even with abundant depth in the high-resource language). Report accuracy gain, output-language fidelity, fluency (perplexity), and specificity (already-converged items unchanged). Compare against a naive 'add more tokens/CoT' baseline and translate-to-English. 7. Knowledge-failure control (the crucial dissociation): partition low-resource errors into TRUNCATION-type (fact answered correctly in the high-resource language, i.e., knowledge exists; low-resource error accompanied by late/unconverged trajectory) vs KNOWLEDGE-type (wrong in the high-resource language too). Predict late-layer looping recovers truncation-type but not knowledge-type errors, cleanly separating unfinished computation from absent knowledge. 8. Ablations: number of loop iterations and which layers to loop (last-1 vs last-k) dose-response; tuned-lens vs logit-lens for convergence-depth robustness; model depth as a variable (do deeper models within a family have smaller Truncation Gaps?); task type (knowledge vs reasoning); probe/lens transfer across models. Metrics throughout: convergence depth, Truncation Gap, error-vs-required-depth predictive power, Spearman with distance/resource, early-exit-induced degradation, late-layer-loop recovery rate split by error type, output-language fidelity, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens convergence depth can reflect the readout basis rather than genuine computation state; we validate with a tuned lens and require the causal early-exit (Exp. 5) and late-layer-looping (Exp. 6) results to promote the depth measurement to a functional claim. 2. Late-layer looping is an untied-weights hack the model was not trained for and may simply corrupt representations rather than 'continue' computation; we mitigate by reporting dose-response, specificity (already-converged items must be unharmed), and by comparing looping the last block vs random blocks; if looping helps only on high-required-depth truncation-type items and not on knowledge-type or converged items, that pattern is strong evidence regardless of the hack's crudeness. A negative looping result still leaves the correlational required-depth + causal early-exit findings intact. 3. Truncation and knowledge failure are entangled; the high-resource-language knowledge control (Exp. 7) is the crucial dissociator and central to the claim. 4. Distance and resource level are correlated; the dissociating language contrasts (Exp. 4) only partly separate them, and we report multiple resource proxies. 5. Right-censored (unconverged) trajectories are hard to distinguish from noise; we use stability criteria over the last several layers and report robustness to the convergence definition. 6. Answer matching across scripts is noisy; we use alias-aware, last-token/answer-span matching and report tokenization statistics. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families of differing depth address but do not exhaust generality, and the model-depth ablation directly tests the budget interpretation.

Name: implicit_prosody_attachment_gate
Title: The Inner Voice of the Machine: A Language-Set Implicit-Prosody Gate That Covertly Resolves Syntactic Ambiguity in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs, like silent human readers, compute an implicit prosodic phrasing over text (a default prosodic-boundary / metric structure) and use it to resolve prosody-sensitive syntactic ambiguities. Crucially the default phrasing is covertly set by the query language, so for the classic relative-clause (RC) attachment ambiguity the model resolves high (N1) vs low (N2) attachment differently across languages, mirroring the cross-linguistic prosodic split (e.g. English low-attaching vs Spanish/Croatian high-attaching). This implicit-prosody preference is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable phrasing-boundary representation separable from the propositional content: steering a recovered prosodic-boundary direction flips attachment without changing the events or entities, and the effect scales with the query language's prosodic-boundary-length typology, not its resource level.
Related Work: The Implicit Prosody Hypothesis (IPH; Fodor 2002; Hirose 2003 [#10]; Breen 2014 [#15]) holds that silent readers impose a default, language-specific prosodic contour that biases syntactic attachment, and that this default differs cross-linguistically (English low-attaches, Spanish/Croatian high-attach)—the strongest known counterevidence to universal parsing. ERP and eye-tracking studies confirm implicit metric/prosodic structure during silent reading (Breen ERP 2019 [#13]; Croatian eye-tracking 2025 [#9]) and that it is prosodic, not mere character-length (deaf-reader controls 2006 [#11]). On the model side, BERT encodes prosodic prominence in middle layers from syntactic/semantic cues (What does BERT learn about prosody 2023 [#1]), transformers encode subphonemic/phonological features (Probing Subphonemes 2025 [#2]; character-embedding perceptual probes 2022 [#4]), and LLMs encode output-length as a disentangled, steerable attention signal (Length Representations 2025 [#3]). Multilingual RC-attachment behavior of LLMs has been noted only behaviorally in scattered work. However, NO prior work (i) tests the Implicit Prosody Hypothesis inside a text-only multilingual LLM, (ii) asks whether the query language covertly sets a default implicit prosodic phrasing that resolves syntactic ambiguity, or (iii) provides a causal, steerable implicit-prosody-boundary representation. Prior LLM prosody work probes prominence descriptively; prior IPH work is human psycholinguistics. We uniquely port the IPH cross-linguistic attachment paradigm into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, giving a causal (patching + steering) account and a prosody-typology-vs-resource dissociation.
Abstract: When silently reading 'Someone shot the servant of the actress who was on the balcony', readers must decide whether the relative clause modifies the servant (high attachment) or the actress (low attachment). A landmark psycholinguistic finding is that this decision differs across languages and is governed by an implicit prosody—a default, language-specific 'inner voice' phrasing imposed during silent reading. English readers prefer low attachment; Spanish and Croatian readers prefer high attachment. We ask whether multilingual LLMs, trained only on text, inherit this implicit-prosody mechanism and whether the query language covertly sets the default phrasing that resolves such ambiguities. We hypothesize that models compute an implicit prosodic-boundary structure over the input and use it to gate attachment, with the default boundary placement set by the query language, so the identical ambiguous sentence is attached high versus low depending on the language, tracking the documented cross-linguistic prosodic split. We build IMPLICIT-PROSODY, a controlled set of RC-attachment and other prosody-sensitive ambiguities (coordination scope, adverbial attachment) rendered across 12+ languages spanning long- vs short-prosodic-boundary typologies, with prosodic-length manipulations and character-length-matched controls that dissociate prosody from surface length. Behaviorally we measure per-language attachment distributions and their sensitivity to prosodic-length (not character-length) manipulation, mirroring human deaf-reader controls. Mechanistically we probe for an implicit prosodic-boundary representation, use activation patching to show it is causally responsible for attachment while the propositional content is unchanged, and steer a recovered boundary direction to flip attachment. We predict the effect scales with prosodic-boundary typology, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (IMPLICIT-PROSODY): construct prosody-sensitive syntactic ambiguities in three families: (a) RC-ATTACHMENT ('N1 of N2 who/that RC') where high (N1) vs low (N2) attachment is the classic IPH case; (b) COORDINATION scope ('old men and women'); (c) ADVERBIAL/PP attachment. For each item build (i) a base ambiguous version and (ii) PROSODIC-LENGTH manipulations that lengthen N1 vs N2 constituents in ways known to shift the implicit prosodic boundary (Hirose-style), plus CHARACTER-LENGTH-MATCHED controls that add characters without changing prosodic phrasing (deaf-reader-style control). Render across 12+ languages spanning LONG-prosodic-boundary/high-attaching (Spanish, Croatian, German, Greek, Russian) and SHORT-boundary/low-attaching (English, Romanian, Norwegian, Arabic, Chinese) typologies, grounded in the psycholinguistic literature and native-speaker validation. Each item is paired with an attachment-diagnostic question (e.g. gender/number agreement on the RC verb forcing N1 vs N2, or a comprehension question). Build a per-language prosodic-boundary-typology index and a resource-level proxy. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral IPH test: elicit attachment interpretations per item/language; metric = per-language HIGH-ATTACHMENT RATE on identical sentences, plus cross-language disagreement. Prediction: high-attaching-typology languages attach high more often on the SAME structure, replicating the human cross-linguistic split. Baselines: query in English, translate-to-English-first. 3. Prosody-vs-character-length dissociation (the crucial control, mirroring deaf-reader studies): test whether attachment shifts under PROSODIC-length manipulation but NOT under matched CHARACTER-length manipulation. If shifts follow prosodic phrasing and not raw character count, the effect is genuinely prosodic, not a length/working-memory artifact. 4. Typology dose-response: correlate per-language high-attachment rate (and its sensitivity to prosodic-length manipulation) with the prosodic-boundary-typology index vs the resource proxy (Spearman with CIs); key contrast: a lower-resource high-attaching language (Croatian) vs a higher-resource low-attaching one (English/Chinese). 5. Implicit prosodic-boundary probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode where the model places the major prosodic boundary (e.g. before vs after N2) from mid-layer hidden states at the ambiguity region, using items where prosodic-length manipulation gives a known boundary; test cross-lingual probe transfer to establish a shared boundary representation whose PLACEMENT varies by language, and contrast with a surface-position/character-count probe to dissociate abstract boundary from raw length. 6. Causal localization via patching (core test): for an item attached high in a high-attaching language vs low in a low-attaching language on the SAME structure, patch the mid-layer prosodic-boundary representation across runs and test whether attachment flips while the entities/events (propositional content) are preserved; verify a content-region patch does not flip attachment (specificity). 7. Prosodic-boundary steering (causal fix/manipulation): recover a boundary direction as the mean activation difference between high-boundary and low-boundary runs (pooled across languages / prosodic-length conditions); steer to (a) INDUCE high attachment in a low-attaching language and (b) INDUCE low attachment in a high-attaching language, with dose-response. Metrics: attachment-flip rate, content-preservation specificity, output fluency (perplexity). Compare against explicit prompting ('read with a pause after N2') and translate-first baselines. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the boundary is malleable; probe transfer across models; ambiguity-family breakdown (RC vs coordination vs adverbial); whether the default is anchored to English or the nearest high-resource language; model scale; tokenization statistics. Metrics throughout: high-attachment rate, cross-language disagreement, prosody-vs-character-length sensitivity gap, boundary-probe accuracy and cross-lingual transfer, causal patch/steer flip rates, content-preservation specificity, Spearman with prosodic typology vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The behavioral cross-linguistic split might not replicate in LLMs at all (models may attach uniformly, e.g. always low/English-like); this would refute the query-language-default claim but is itself an informative, publishable result about whether LLMs inherit human implicit prosody. 2. Attachment could be driven by frequency/semantic plausibility rather than implicit prosody; we use semantically balanced (either-attachment-plausible) items and the prosodic-vs-character-length dissociation (Exp. 3) is the crucial control isolating prosody from length/memory, directly mirroring the human deaf-reader control. 3. Probe decodability of a 'prosodic boundary' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 6) and steering induction (Exp. 7) with content-preservation specificity are required to promote correlation to mechanism, and the boundary probe is contrasted against a surface-length probe. 4. Diagnosing intended attachment across languages is nontrivial; we use agreement-forced or comprehension-question diagnostics validated by native speakers and restrict to high-agreement items. 5. The prosodic-typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (Croatian vs English/Chinese); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the typology-index operationalization. 6. Tokenization differs across scripts and may itself alter effective 'length', confounding the length control; we hold tokenized length constant where possible in the character-matched condition and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade attachment change for fluency or content preservation; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across multiple ambiguity types address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: aspectual_completion_gate
Title: Did It Finish, or Was It Just Happening? How the Query Language's Aspect System Covertly Sets a Default Completion Interpretation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in how obligatorily they mark whether an event is completed vs ongoing (perfective/imperfective, presence vs absence of a grammaticalized perfect). We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an event's abstract completion state, but resolve whether an underspecified event counts as COMPLETED (endpoint reached, result achieved) through a scalar 'completion-inference' gate whose default is covertly set by the query language's aspect system. Consequently the identical event description yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing inferences across languages, this gap scales with the query language's aspectual-grammaticalization distance from the dominant language (not resource level), and it is carried by a locatable, steerable representation separable from the propositional content.
Related Work: Probing work shows transformers encode telicity/duration/aspect, mostly in final layers, and are biased by tense/word order (About Time 2022; Probing Verbal Aspect in Russian 2024; Do pretrained transformers infer telicity like humans 2021), that tense/aspect are orthogonal, steerable directions (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025), that tense is easy in morphologically-marked languages but hard in Chinese (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021), and that LLMs fail cross-linguistic perfect-aspect NLI in Chinese/Japanese (LLMs Struggle with NLI for Perfect Aspect 2025). Complement-coercion work studies event recovery (Norwegian 2025). Psycholinguistics shows telicity is encoded differently across languages yet event tracking is similar (Do Cross-Linguistic Differences Influence Event Perception 2024). Crucially, ALL LLM aspect work either (i) probes/steers the surface aspect FEATURE within one language, or (ii) measures behavioral NLI failure, and treats the surface aspect as the target. NONE dissociates a shared abstract COMPLETION-STATE representation from a language-conditioned completion-INFERENCE gate, tests whether the query language causally sets whether an underspecified event is read as finished vs ongoing (biasing downstream semantic/entailment judgments), or provides a causal, steerable completion gate with an aspectual-typology-vs-resource dissociation. My prior tense proposal targeted reference-TIME (past/present/future); this targets a distinct axis: COMPLETION/boundedness. We uniquely port grammatical-aspect typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, and add a safety-critical task-completion instantiation.
Abstract: Whether an event is finished ('she was building a house' vs 'she built a house') is marked very differently across languages: Slavic and Romance grammars obligatorily encode perfective vs imperfective, English grammaticalizes the perfect, while Chinese, Indonesian and others leave completion largely to inference. A competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract completion state and, when a description is underspecified, decide whether the event counts as completed. We ask whether the language a question is asked in covertly makes that decision. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic completion-state representation but resolve underspecification through a completion-inference gate whose default is set by the query language's aspect system, so the identical event yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing readings across languages. We build ASPECT-GATE, controlled event descriptions whose completion is underspecified, paired with entailment questions that distinguish a completed from an ongoing reading (e.g., 'Is the house finished?'), rendered across 12+ languages spanning perfective/imperfective, perfect-marking, and aspect-lax typologies, with completion-forcing and completion-neutral controls. Behaviorally we measure per-language completion-inference rate on identical events. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared completion-state direction that transfers across languages including aspect-lax ones; (ii) use activation patching to show the completion state is computed similarly while a separable gate differs by language; and (iii) recover and steer a completion-inference direction to flip readings without changing the events. We include a safety-relevant subset (inferring whether an instruction/action was actually carried out) where under- or over-inference of completion causes an agent to falsely report task success. We predict the gap tracks aspectual-typology distance, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments: 1. Dataset (ASPECT-GATE): construct event descriptions whose COMPLETION is underspecified (no overt endpoint marker) paired with an entailment/yes-no question distinguishing a completed reading (endpoint reached, result state holds) from an ongoing reading (event in progress, result not yet achieved) — e.g., accomplishment verbs (build/write/cross/paint) with quantized vs bare objects, plus resultative and durative variants. Include a difficulty gradient and clearly-completed / clearly-ongoing controls. Render each in 12+ languages spanning three aspectual types: PERFECTIVE/IMPERFECTIVE-grammaticalized (Russian, Polish, Spanish, French, Greek), PERFECT-marking (English, German), and ASPECT-LAX / inference-based (Chinese, Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese). Native-speaker-validate translations and the intended reading; build a per-language aspectual-grammaticalization index (obligatory perfective/imperfective > perfect auxiliary > lexical/pragmatic only) and a resource-level proxy. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 2. Behavioral gate test: elicit completed-vs-ongoing judgments per item/language; metric = per-language COMPLETION-INFERENCE RATE on identical underspecified events, plus cross-language disagreement. Controls should agree across languages. Baselines: query in the dominant language, translate-to-English-first. 3. Aspectual-typology dose-response (dissociation): correlate per-language completion-inference rate (and its deviation from the English baseline) with the aspectual-grammaticalization index vs a resource proxy (Spearman with CIs); key contrast: a lower-resource strongly-aspectual language (Polish) vs a higher-resource aspect-lax one (Chinese). 4. Shared completion-state probe: train linear probes / logit-lens at each layer to decode the abstract completion state (completed vs ongoing) from mid-layer hidden states on held-out items; test cross-lingual probe transfer (train one language, test others) to establish a shared representation decodable even in aspect-lax languages, and contrast with a surface-aspect-morphology probe to establish the abstract-vs-surface dissociation. 5. Causal localization via patching (core test): for an item read completed in language A but ongoing in language B on the SAME event, (a) patch the mid-layer completion-state representation across runs and confirm it is present in both (patching changes little); (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the completion decision and test whether the interpretation flips, localizing the effect to a language-set gate rather than a different completion computation. 6. Completion-gate steering (causal fix/manipulation): recover a completion-inference direction (mean activation difference between completed-reading and ongoing-reading runs, pooled across languages); steer to (a) INDUCE a completed reading in an aspect-lax/imperfective-defaulting language and (b) SUPPRESS it (force ongoing) in a perfective-defaulting language, with dose-response. Metrics: induced/suppressed inference rate, propositional-content preservation (specificity: the event/entities unchanged), fluency (perplexity), output-language fidelity. Compare against explicit prompting ('assume the action is finished/still ongoing') and translate-first baselines. 7. Safety-critical subset: agentic/instruction settings where a description underspecifies whether an action was actually carried out ('The system was applying the patch' vs 'applied the patch'); measure per-language whether the model reports the task as DONE vs IN-PROGRESS, quantify the cross-lingual false-completion (falsely reporting success) and false-incompletion gap, and test whether steering the gate repairs mis-inferences. Report as a reliability finding for multilingual agents. 8. Ablations: layer sweep for where the gate is malleable; probe transfer across models; category breakdown (accomplishment vs activity vs achievement verbs); whether the default is anchored to English or the nearest high-resource language; model scale; tokenization statistics. Metrics throughout: completion-inference rate, cross-language disagreement, completion-state probe accuracy and transfer, surface-aspect probe accuracy, causal patch/steer flip rates, content-preservation specificity, safety false-completion gap and repair, Spearman with aspectual typology vs resource, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'completion state' or 'completion gate' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/suppress (Exp. 6) tests with content-preservation specificity are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 2. Whether an underspecified event is 'completed' can be genuinely ambiguous and gradient; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and include clear completed/ongoing controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might reflect genuine aspectual-norm variation rather than a gate artifact; the shared-completion-state probe transfer and the state-same/gate-differs patching test are designed to separate a different completion computation from a pure interpretation-strength shift, and translations are validated to avoid inadvertently inserting completion cues. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (Polish vs Chinese); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the grammaticalization-index operationalization. 5. Strong models may infer completion faithfully per language, shrinking the default cross-language effect; even documenting faithful language-specific aspect handling (a clean shared-state + language-set-gate architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/suppression steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. The surface-aspect feature and abstract completion state nearly coincide in strongly-aspectual languages; the aspect-lax languages and the underspecified/neutral conditions are the crucial dissociating cases. 7. Tokenization of aspect morphology varies across scripts; we use verb-final/clause-final or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics; perfective/imperfective vs perfect vs lexical cases analyzed separately. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency or content preservation; we report both. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.
